President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he met Kongsberg CEO Eirik Lie and Norwegian Defense Minister Tore Sandvik in Oslo on 21 October to discuss more NASAMS air defenses, a day after meeting US presidential envoy Steve Witkoff in the same city.
Washington has spent the past two weeks easing pressure on Russia and leaning on Kyiv, with a diesel deal, throttled Starlink, and talk of cutting intelligence, while Ukraine’s European partners move in the other direction. Russia pounds Ukrainian cities almost nightly, and the Norwegian-made NASAMS is one of the systems holding that barrage off critical infrastructure.
Kongsberg opened an office in Ukraine in 2025. Its NASAMS uses the AIM-120 AMRAAM missile built by the US defense giant RTX, the same firm behind the Patriot launchers that are Ukraine’s only means of downing Russian ballistic and hypersonic missiles. The same missile is also used in F-16s.
“They effectively protect our people and critical infrastructure from Russian missile and drone attacks virtually every day,” Zelenskyy said.
He added that Ukraine is counting on additional defense support packages next month.
A European shield Ukraine wants tested this year
The visit also advanced a joint missile-defense project. Norway is actively involved in FREYJA, a European anti-ballistic missile program that Ukraine is helping to build.
“There are already first results in creating individual elements of the system. Today we determined where we can and must speed up to reach testing by the end of this year,” Zelenskyy said.
FREYJA now draws in 10 countries and is built around an interceptor missile designed to stop ballistic threats, a capability Europe largely lacks against Russia’s fastest weapons.
A push for satellites as Starlink falters
Zelenskyy also raised satellite communications amid the scandal over speed limitations on Elon Musk’s military Starlink service that disrupted a series of front-line missions.
“We discussed in detail the start of work on new satellite-communication capabilities for our soldiers,” the president said, adding that Kyiv would bring in partners able to support them.
The push comes after SpaceX throttled the StarShield military package Ukrainian drones use. Ukraine’s 7th Air Assault Corps said the connection began dropping as drones moved at speed, negatively affecting their missions.
Read also
- Russian strikes close plant of Ukraine’s biggest aid backer. Its 3,600 workers and millions in taxes now hang in balance
- Her own city is under Russian fire, yet Kyiv woman urges killing Ukrainians among nearly 100,000 pro-Kremlin posts in two years. She faces up to 12 years
- Some of Ukraine’s artillery soldiers were TikTokers yesterday, ComBat Vision says. Their new plugin teaches them to aim

articles.title: Ukraine wants F-16 repairs at more sites, tells Lockheed
articles.body:
- Ukraine’s defense minister and army chief met Lockheed Martin Aeronautics President Orlando Sanchez Jr. to discuss F-16 support and PAC-3 interceptor supplies.
- Kyiv wants to expand F-16 maintenance to more sites in Ukraine, including through localization, to keep as many jets flying as possible.
Ukraine’s Defense Minister Evgeniy Khmara and Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapatyi met a Lockheed Martin delegation led by Orlando Sanchez Jr., president of Lockheed Martin Aeronautics, to press for steady weapons deliveries, more PAC-3 interceptors for Patriot and wider F-16 maintenance across Ukraine, the Ukrainian Defense Ministry said.
The talks centered on the F-16, which the ministry described as one of the Ukrainian Air Force’s key tools against Russia’s new jet-powered attack drones, and on Kyiv’s push to service the jets at more locations inside the country, including through local production.
“The F-16 is part of Ukrainian aviation. Ukraine is committed to a long-term partnership with Lockheed Martin. It is important to increase weapons deliveries and do everything we can to ensure that as many F-16s as possible remain in service and operate in Ukrainian skies,” said Ukrainian Defense Minister Evgeniy Khmara.
The meeting followed President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s own talks with a Lockheed Martin team in Kyiv on Oct. 19, when he praised the F-16’s record against Shahed drones and said Ukraine is counting on the program continuing. Sources at Lockheed Martin have told The Defence Blog that the company is promoting the idea of a special F-16 version tailored to Ukraine, with longer range, a new AESA radar to spot low-flying drones and cruise missiles faster, and deeper integration of European weapons, although no formal talks on such a variant are underway.
Lockheed Martin systems already make up a large share of Ukraine’s long-range firepower and air defense, from the HIMARS rocket launchers that have struck Russian logistics hubs since 2022 to the F-16 fighters and the PAC-3 interceptors that Patriot batteries fire against Russian ballistic missiles. The F-16 has become the backbone of the Ukrainian Air Force since the first jets arrived in 2024, and the type now flies roughly 80 percent of all Ukrainian Air Force sorties, with one wing alone credited with downing more than 1,000 Russian drones and cruise missiles.
Keeping those aircraft flying is a growing challenge, since Ukraine’s F-16s are older airframes donated by European NATO members and fly near-daily combat missions, which wears down engines and structures far faster than peacetime training. Expanding maintenance to more sites inside Ukraine would cut the time jets spend out of action and reduce the risk of concentrating them at a few bases that Russian missiles and drones could target, while localization would give Ukrainian industry a direct role in sustaining the fleet.
The PAC-3 request reflects Ukraine’s most urgent air defense need, since Patriot is the main system in its inventory able to intercept Russian ballistic missiles such as the Iskander-M and the Kinzhal. Lockheed Martin is ramping up production of PAC-3 MSE interceptors, and Zelenskyy said after his own meeting that Kyiv hopes to buy part of the increased output to protect more cities from ballistic attacks.
The ministry said Ukraine is ready to share its combat experience with Lockheed Martin to make the company’s weapons more effective in modern warfare, and the talks come as Lockheed Martin offers Ukraine its own version of the F-16, a variant that sources at the company told The Defence Blog would bring longer range, a new AESA radar to detect low-flying drones and cruise missiles faster, and deeper integration of European guided bombs and cruise missiles.

articles.title: Russia ready to resume talks with Ukraine and US to end war
articles.body:
Russia says it is ready to resume talks with Ukraine and US to end war
- Published
Russia is "ready in principle" to resume talks with the US and Ukraine on ending the conflict, Vladimir Putin's top aide has said.
Yuri Ushakov was speaking after Putin met US President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff in the Russian city of St Petersburg.
Ushakov said a new round could be held next month, and Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky later said he wanted this to happen as soon as possible. Kyiv and its European allies have long been pressing Moscow for resumption of the talks halted in February.
Russia has for months refused as it believes it is winning on the battlefield with Ukraine facing an acute shortage of interceptors against deadly Russian missile attacks.
Witkoff went to St Petersburg after meeting Zelensky as well as the leaders of Norway and Finland in the Norwegian capital, Oslo, on Monday.
It is not clear what specific proposals Witkoff brought to Putin, but Zelensky said after talks in Oslo that "strong" security guarantees for Ukraine and energy ceasefire proposals had been discussed.
Ushakov said their ideas were not very "useful".
Top officials from Russia, Ukraine and the US have held several rounds of talks aimed at ending the war that began in February 2022 when Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Russia blamed last month's "massive" Ukrainian strikes during its general elections for their disruption.
Speaking to reporters after Wednesday's talks in St Petersburg, Ushakov suggested that a new round could be held around 10 November in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates.
He stressed that the talks must focus on "building a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the end of the conflict."
A US official later told the BBC that Witkoff and Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, another key negotiator, had proposed at Tuesday's talks in the Norwegian capital "a trilateral meeting at the technical level between the US, Russia, and Ukraine".
"This was accepted by the Ukrainians in Oslo yesterday and by the Russians in St Petersburg today," said the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
Late on Wednesday, Zelensky told reporters: "We received feedback that Russia... supports a trilateral meeting between our teams. The American side is proposing to do this as soon as possible. We are in favour of it."
Ushakov also told reporters that President Putin reiterated to Witkoff that Russian troops were advancing everywhere across the vast front line and had a "strategic initiative".
Ukraine and its European allies are disputing Putin's claim, pointing to a virtual stalemate on the front.
On Wednesday, Zelensky said he would accept a deal that would freeze the war along the current front line.
"We call it 'ceasefire' or 'stop killings' like President Trump called it. Freeze and stop. And of course this is minimum what we need from Russia today," he told Fox News, adding that security guarantees for Ukraine could be discussed after this.
Witkoff described the latest talks as "constructive", while Kushner, who was participating via a video link, said: "There is still hard work ahead, but we have a real opportunity to move beyond this war and build a framework for lasting peace, security, and prosperity for generations to come."
The talks were held amid a growing row between Ukraine and the US.
Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to get a new president, and most recently "for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine".
Trump has blamed Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries for fuel prices which have been rising since the start of the US-led war on Iran.
He was heavily criticised by Democratic and some Republican lawmakers after lifting sanctions on Russia - allowing it to release tonnes of diesel "to the American and global marketplace".
That was despite signing legislation to authorise fresh US sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas just weeks earlier.
Zelensky - and Ukraine's European allies - criticised Trump's move.
Last week, Kyiv accused Washington of withholding critical intelligence to warn Ukrainians about incoming Russian ballistic missile launches, resulting in many civilian deaths. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday rejected such accusations as "scandalous", and Zelensky said after the Oslo talks that intelligence sharing "works now".
Ukraine's military has also complained of speed restrictions by the US satellite internet network Starlink which is owned by Elon Musk which constricted its ability to use drones to conduct strikes against Russia.
US officials have denied having requested such a slowdown and a bipartisan group of US senators has called for an urgent investigation.
Before the Putin-Witkoff talks started, Russia released Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old American citizen who had been given a jail sentence of nearly seven years for allegedly fighting on behalf of Ukraine.
Trump said the former teacher was "on his way back home" and "there was no 'swap' necessary", while Witkoff called Putin a "humanitarian" for agreeing the release.
When asked by a BBC reporter whether he agreed with such description of the Kremlin leader, US Vice-President JD Vance said: "I agree with Steve Witkoff saying something nice to a person who just released an American hostage.
"Whether you agree with the underlying sentiment or not, Steve Witkoff is a diplomat. His job is to go over there and get a job done. I care much less about what Steve said and about the fact that he is bringing an American hostage home to his family."
  - Published23 hours ago
  - Published1 hour ago

articles.title: Hegseth Highlights Defense Manufacturing Push with Visit to Future ‘Doomsday’ Planes
articles.body:
DAYTON, Ohio, and EAU CLAIRE, Wis.—Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth took his Arsenal of Freedom tour to the swing states of Ohio and Wisconsin on Oct. 20, highlighting efforts to boost defense manufacturing before the midterm elections next month, including by visiting future E-4C “Doomsday” planes.
“We plan to spend even more in the future,” Hegseth said during a visit to the Sierra Nevada Corporation in Dayton, Ohio, where he praised President Donald Trump and Sen. Bernie Moreno, an Ohio Republican.
“We are providing larger and longer and more predictable contracts to companies so that they can deliver at scale and at pace,” he added. “That means more jobs, more reliable jobs, high-paying jobs as companies invest in their people. We’re going to reward leaders who invest in their workers, who expand their capacity, and who share our utter sense of urgency.”
Sierra Nevada purchased five Korean Air 747-8i jetliners and plans to convert at least four into the new E-4C Survivable Airborne Operations Center, or SAOC. Hegseth championed the company, which won a $13 billion contract to build America’s next-generation nuclear command-and-control aircraft over Boeing. Scale AI was recently awarded a contract to integrate artificial intelligence into aircraft. And there are signs the Air Force may choose to grow the fleet.
Speaking to reporters, Hegseth discussed his recent trop to the Middle East, where he visited U.S. fighter units and Airmen, among other service members, and told Air & Space Forces Magazine he met with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. He declined to say what he had discussed with the Israeli leader, including the possibility of renewing attacks on Iran, but added that the Israeli military “has great capabilities.”
“We’ve worked with the Israeli military quite a bit,” Hegseth said. “They’ve been good partners.”
Hegseth also told Air & Space Magazine the Pentagon had not ordered a slowdown of SpaceX’s Starlink or its military version, Starshield, for Ukraine—Ukrainian officials say their access to the space internet service has been throttled, hampering their drones and air defenses.
“We haven’t changed our posture in any way to the Ukrainians,” Hegseth said. “We haven’t pulled anything back. There are terms of service that ultimately need to be complied to, and that’s where Starlink has the option to make those decisions. But nothing’s changed from our view. We haven’t made any directives or anything like that. And we wish the Ukrainians, obviously, success.”
The Wall Street Journal reported later on Oct. 20 that the move to slow Starlink was decided by Elon Musk, the chief executive of SpaceX.
But Hegseth’s trip was mainly intended as an opportunity for him to make his case for more defense spending and the Pentagon’s push to help the defense industry.
“We’re asking for a $1.5 trillion investment to make a generational investment to ensure that we remain the strongest and most powerful military in the world,” Hegseth said after touring SNC’s facilities with Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink. “And those types of investments translate directly into high-paying jobs for American manufacturers.”
The aircraft being overhauled by Sierra Nevada Corporation are due to replace the four aging E-4B National Airborne Operations Center aircraft, which are on average over 50 years old.
Boeing was eliminated from the competition to modernize the E-4 nuclear command and control fleet in 2023, leaving SNC as the sole competitor; the E-4C airframe itself is still based on Boeing’s 747-800i.
That gave SNC its largest contract in six-decade history, which is also one of the largest aircraft modernization deals given to a company that isn’t the plane’s original manufacturer. The E-4C flew its first test flight last year.
”In a doomsday scenario, SAOC provides the president with unbreakable command and control. No other nation on planet earth has these types of capabilities, serving as our nation’s ultimate insurance policy in a no fail mission,” Hegseth said.
Hegseth also touted his future of war initiative, Project Meridian, and his plans for a new four-star Autonomous Warfare Command—and the effort called the Aresnal of Freedom he has embarked on over the last year to champion American manufacturing.
Hegseth then jetted to Wisconsin to visit the rural congressional district of Rep. Derrick Van Orden, a close administration ally, who is currently locked in a tight reelection battle predicted to be a toss-up. Hegseth’s visit to the small business Riverside Machine and Engineering, alongside Small Business Administrator Kelly Loeffler, highlighted an effort to invest in small defense companies. The company is a small subcontractor that builds parts that go in radars and other equipment for BAE Systems and Lockheed Martin, including the F-35.
“Tens of thousands of small businesses are the core of our defense industrial base,” Hegseth said. “Any supply chain is only as weak as its weakest link, and if you can’t make a critical subcomponent, then ultimately that F-35 doesn’t fly or ultimately that radar isn’t working.”

articles.title: Britain sends Typhoons to guard Saudi cities from Houthis
articles.body:
- Britain will deploy Royal Air Force Typhoon jets to Saudi Arabia to intercept Houthi missiles and drones, without striking targets inside Yemen.
- The UK already supports Saudi Arabia with a Voyager refueling tanker, air defense equipment and personnel, and is extending the tanker mission by 90 days.
Britain will send Royal Air Force Typhoon fighter jets to Saudi Arabia to shoot down Houthi missiles and drones aimed at Saudi cities and critical infrastructure, the UK Defense Ministry said on Oct. 20.
CNN reported that the jets will fly defensive counter-air missions over the kingdom, and a spokesperson for the prime minister’s office said they will intercept incoming threats and will not carry out strikes inside Yemen.
The government has not said how many Typhoons are going, where they will be based or when patrols will begin. The jets join UK support already in place in the kingdom, including air defense equipment, British personnel helping counter missile and drone attacks, and a Royal Air Force Voyager tanker that has been refueling Saudi fighters since September.
“The continuing attacks from the Houthis on our ally Saudi Arabia are absolutely despicable. The targeting of the airport in Riyadh in particular shows the lengths the Houthis are going to escalate the situation in the region,” said UK Defense Secretary Wes Streeting.
Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport has been hit repeatedly this month. The deadliest strike, on Oct. 10, wounded more than 300 people, and while Saudi civil aviation authorities put the death toll at 12, CNN has since reported 13 killed, making it the deadliest attack on Saudi Arabia in more than a decade. The Houthis have also fired ballistic missiles and drones at oil facilities, and on Sept. 16 the group claimed to have shot down a Saudi F-15 over Marib, a claim Saudi authorities have not confirmed.
The fighting escalated after the Houthis announced in July that they would target Saudi shipping in the Red Sea and infrastructure inside the kingdom, following a Saudi strike on the Houthi-held airport in Sanaa. Last month the group pushed down Yemen’s western coast and took the port of Mocha and Mayyun Island in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, the narrow southern entrance to the Red Sea.
Saudi Arabia has asked regional and Western partners for air defense help. France has agreed to send military personnel and equipment, and more than 100 U.S. military advisers are providing intelligence and targeting support under a newly formed joint forces command. Pakistan already has troops in the kingdom, and Egypt’s parliament is debating a deployment after President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi called an emergency session.
The Typhoon is a familiar aircraft in the region, since the Royal Saudi Air Force has flown it since buying 72 jets in a deal agreed in 2006. Britain previously sent its Sky Sabre ground-based air defense system to Saudi Arabia earlier this year during the war with Iran.
The Associated Press reported that Britain is also extending its Voyager refueling mission by 90 days. Downing Street has described the support as defensive and limited in scope, while Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces press a counteroffensive that has so far failed to dislodge the Houthis from key positions.

articles.title: Israel's occupation, Hezbollah's arms: A looming war in Lebanon?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Israel's occupation, Hezbollah's arms: The road to a new war in Lebanon?
On 5 October, Lebanon’s Internal Security Forces stopped a van with two people on board at the Dahr al-Baydar checkpoint.
When searched, authorities discovered and then seized about 780 kg of explosives, including TNT and Composition C-4 plastic.
The two people arrested were reportedly linked to Hezbollah. They were tasked with transporting the cargo from the Bekaa region to Beirut.
The reported involvement of Hezbollah members in the explosives seizure prompted a wave of accusations from the group’s political rivals, with some suggesting they could be used for internal political assassinations.
Lebanese Forces leader Samir Geagea called the seizure “the most dangerous incident in years”, saying the weapons were probably meant for use inside Lebanon.
Kataeb leader Samy Gemayel wrote they were probably intended for a new wave of assassinations like those between 2004 and 2008, including that of former prime minister Rafic Hariri in 2005.
Lebanon’s prime minister, Nawaf Salam, also noted that C-4 had been used in previous assassinations and promised a full investigation.
However, on 15 October, Hezbollah MP Hassan Fadlallah acknowledged that the vehicle and its cargo belonged to the group. He denied allegations of an assassination plot and stated that the explosives are part of the capabilities Hezbollah uses against Israel, demanding the return of the shipment.
On the same day, US Secretary of State Marc Rubio reportedly called Lebanon’s President Joseph Aoun, urging him not to return confiscated explosives to Hezbollah.
Hezbollah’s demand for the return of the explosives has further strained its relationship with a government that has banned the group’s military activity and is pushing to disarm it.
Israel's occupation creates openings for Hezbollah to rebuild
The discovery of explosive materials comes as Israel continues to occupy swathes of southern Lebanon and launch near-daily strikes despite a US-brokered ceasefire agreed in June.
Hezbollah has halted its attacks since then, but the seizure of explosives points to efforts to rebuild its military capabilities as the risk of renewed US-Iran conflict threatens to reignite the Lebanese front.
It is not uncommon for Hezbollah to use ceasefire windows to rebuild its capabilities following a conflict with Israel.
Between the November 2024 ceasefire that ended the Israel-Hezbollah war linked to Gaza and March 2026, reports indicate that the group has rebuilt its command structure and rearmed with assistance from Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
David Wood, senior Lebanon analyst at the International Crisis Group (ICG), said that Israel’s continued occupation and attacks in Lebanon also contribute to the conditions that enable the group’s rebuilding.
“While it might be true that Hezbollah continues to operate militarily, despite the Lebanese government wanting to have a state monopoly over arms, it would be much harder for Hezbollah to do that if Israel were more willing to grant actual concessions as part of its negotiations with Lebanon and to create a viable and fair security arrangement between the two countries,” he told The New Arab.
The US-brokered framework signed in June between Lebanon and Israel has yielded limited results. Lebanon demands an end to Israeli attacks and occupation, the release of detainees, and the return of the displaced. Israel ties these conditions to Hezbollah’s disarmament, which the group rejects.
Israel has continued its military operations in southern Lebanon, occupying more than 600 square kilometres of Lebanese territory while conducting near-daily airstrikes, artillery fire, and home demolitions.
It has mostly levelled 48 of about 60 occupied southern Lebanese towns and villages. In September, Israeli forces took control of the strategic Ali al-Taher ridge near Nabatieh. They previously captured Beaufort Castle and crossed the Litani River.
Lebanon’s Health Ministry says more than 4,300 people have been killed since 2 March, following Hezbollah’s entry into the wider US-Iran war. Nearly 9,000 have been killed since 2023. Almost 330,000 people remain internally displaced.
Nicholas Blandford, a non-resident senior fellow with the Atlantic Council’s Middle East Programmes, told The New Arab that daily shelling and drone surveillance are ongoing, along with efforts to prevent reconstruction south of the Litani River, even outside the occupied zone.
“So in effect, the Israeli occupation extends far beyond where they are physically deployed. It's been quite intense over the last month,” he said.
Israel is also escalating threats to expand its southern Lebanon occupation. Last week, Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz warned that Lebanon would lose Nabatieh and the Litani area to permanent Israeli control if Hezbollah joins Iran in attacking Israel.
A renewed Iran war could draw Lebanon back into conflict
In fact, US President Donald Trump is weighing fresh strikes against Iran, with Israel reportedly pushing for renewed hostilities. Iran is likewise preparing for war, and the conflict in Yemen further fuels regional escalation.
RANE’s lead MENA and defence analyst Freddy Khoueiry explained that repeated interceptions of weapons transfers in Syria and recent seizures of Hezbollah-linked material inside Lebanon show that the group is "clearly attempting to reconstitute parts of its military capability" to rebuild supply lines and replenish stock.
“Hezbollah is likely attempting to restore enough capability to at some point defend against a potential Israeli preemptive campaign and at the same time preserve the option to participate in another regional conflict involving Iran,” he told The New Arab.
For example, Khoueiry explained that seized TNT and C-4 could be used in explosive-drone payloads, rocket and missile warheads, and roadside bombs, mines and demolition charges against Israeli forces in southern Lebanon if conflict resumes.
Dual-use items like fibre-optic cables for drones could enter Lebanon through standard commercial channels, providing Hezbollah with an alternative route to Syria.
Hezbollah may be prioritising experimenting with and expanding the use of low-cost, fibre-optic-guided FPV drones, heavily deployed against Israeli troops in southern Lebanon before the June ceasefire, as they offer a cheap, effective, and hard-to-intercept option.
On the ground, the presence of Israeli troops in southern Lebanon may give Hezbollah an opening to use guerrilla tactics, such as small units staging hit-and-run attacks from familiar terrain. Its drone operations there could also expand the pool of trained drone operators.
Wood said that while Israel has vast military superiority, Hezbollah, this year, “has still managed to make a nuisance of itself”, demonstrating that “while it can't win a military victory over Israel, it can still inflict casualties”. Hezbollah drone attacks have reportedly killed at least 12 Israeli soldiers.
However, what Hezbollah’s role would be if the US and Israel resume strikes on Iran remains to be seen.
Blandford said that Hezbollah’s involvement would depend on Iran’s ability to absorb renewed US and Israeli attacks.
“The Iranians may conclude that if they can absorb fresh Israeli and US strikes, they don’t need to involve Hezbollah,” he said. However, if Iran deems additional pressure necessary, it may activate Hezbollah to engage Israel along the border, stretching and diverting Israel's resources.
Khoueiry further explained that Hezbollah’s weakened capabilities and fragile domestic position may limit its initial involvement, though opening a Lebanese front could pressure Israel and strengthen Hezbollah’s and Iran’s negotiating leverage.
“Hezbollah could specifically seek to link pressure on Israeli military presence inside of Lebanon and potentially northern Israel again to demand an Israeli withdrawal from Lebanon, while Tehran could again attempt to incorporate the Lebanese front into a broader regional ceasefire or negotiating framework,” he said.
However, other kinds of pressures are also likely to shape Hezbollah’s calculations. The Shia community, estimated at 32% of Lebanon’s population, has borne much of the war’s human cost during the war. Last week, Hezbollah announced plans to financially help families in Lebanon whose homes were destroyed or rendered uninhabitable.
Polls diverge on Shia support for Hezbollah’s weapons, with a May poll finding that most respondents opposed disarmament and a September survey finding that most favoured placing their weapons under state control, reflecting the complexity of the group’s relationship with its constituency.
Wood said that Hezbollah weighs the suffering of its constituency but, at the same time, also weighs its deep alliance with Iran.
The group also argues that disarmament would leave the Shia community and Lebanon “wide open to Israeli abuses,” and at times, it “has used those factors to justify its decision to enter conflict in Lebanon, in the knowledge that the Shia will first and foremost pay the price”.
Blandford also argued that if Hezbollah loses Shia support, “then the game is over.”
“It doesn't matter how many weapons or how much money the Iranians give Hezbollah; if they haven't got the support of the Shia community, it's finished.”
Dario Sabaghi is a freelance journalist interested in human rights
Follow him on X: @DarioSabaghi
Edited by Charlie Hoyle

articles.title: Ukraine’s best answer to Russia’s jet Shaheds is its own jet Shahed, turned around to hunt them
articles.body:
- One of Ukraine's best and fastest interceptor drones is an air-to-air version of the Bars one-way attack drone
- Bars are some of the best defenses against Russia's fastest Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones
- But there may be too few small jet engines to rapidly scale up Bars production
Russia's latest jet-propelled Geran-4 and Geran-5 one-way attack drones fly at 500 km/h or more, nearly three times as fast as an older, propeller-driven Geran-2.
That's too fast for many of Ukraine's air defenses. In particular, the inexpensive interceptor drones that Ukrainian forces deploy by the thousand.
Russia launched more than 2,700 jet Gerans at Ukraine in September, and Ukraine is shooting down only about 55% of them, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. The speed disparity is a big part of the problem.
Ukrainian forces are scrambling for new defenses against the speedy Gerans. Among the best is actually a Ukrainian take on the Geran-4 and Geran-5: a fast, jet-propelled one-way attack drone that the Ukrainians have modified for air-to-air use.
Against jet drones, the air-to-air Bars have a hit rate of around 30%, Zelensky said during a joint press conference with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Kyiv on 4 October. "The Bars have shown positive results," Zelensky said. "They currently have the highest percentage. Others are also catching up."
Did Ukraine just unleash its first Bars cruise missiles? A 500 km strike deep inside Russia suggests it
In July, Ukraine and Germany agreed to jointly produce Bars, with Germany financing the first phase. Ukraine has reportedly been launching Bars at targets on the ground since at least the summer of 2025. But it was only recently that clear photos and videos of the drones have circulated.
Over the weekend, Ukraine’s 1021st Anti-Aircraft Missile and Artillery Brigade released footage of one jet drone hunting another. Observers identified the interceptor as a Bars and its target as a Geran-5. After launching from an elevated ramp with help from a rocket booster, the drone's operator—seeing what the drone saw through a front-facing infrared camera—steered the drone toward the Russian drone, possibly destroying it.
Exactly how the operator controlled the Bars—whether by satellite or mesh radio or some other command and control system—is unclear. Equally unclear: what kind of warhead a Bars would employ in the air-to-air role. Many smaller interceptor drones lack warheads. Instead, they simply slam directly into their targets, wrecking them in the collision.
Mystery drone
Trending Now
Bars isn't small. It likely packs an explosive warhead. Potentially one that the operator can remotely trigger when the interceptor passes near its target.
Bars is adaptable. Its maker has reworked it from a 22-kg warhead and a 700-km range to a 60-kg warhead and a stated range of more than 1,000 km, and a heavier variant can carry a 105-kg warhead.
In the air-to-air interceptor role, long range is terribly important but speed is everything. There's an obvious way for the Ukrainians to boost the Bars' speed from its reported 700 km/h top speed to potentially even faster. They could shrink the drone's warhead and its fuel load, making it lighter in order to make it faster.
That may explain how a Bars can chase down a Geran-5 even as the Russians, by one Ukrainian analyst's estimate, try to push the Geran-5 toward 700 km/h or more.
Turkey’s Korkut guns now shoot down Russian drones over Ukraine. Almost half of the jet-powered Shaheds still get through
Cost is important, too. Russia churns out Gerans for an estimated $100,000 or so per drone. The cheaper the drone, the more copies the Russians can fling at Ukrainian cities. If it takes three or more interceptor drones to take down each of those 2,700 jet Gerans, Ukraine may need to deploy 8,000 to 10,000 interceptors a month.
Ukraine already builds more than 2,000 Bars a month, its maker says, but mostly in strike versions. How many go to air defense, and how much each costs, isn't public.
The supply of small jet engines could be a constraint. “Engines are a key element; we really import them in large quantities,” Zelensky said in an interview with Financial Times. "There are also domestically produced engines, but there are not enough of them.” A Ukrainian-made engine for Bars passed final tests in September.
Read Also
- Belgium’s 10 F-16s bring Ukraine’s promised fleet to about 100 jets. Fewer than 40 are flying, as Russia’s jet drones run them ragged
- Turkey’s Korkut guns now shoot down Russian drones over Ukraine. Almost half of the jet-powered Shaheds still get through
- Russia just accidentally crashed its first Tu-95 bomber in 11 years. Its missiles will keep striking Ukraine anyway

articles.title: Ukraine’s top war charity names only way to save $25,000 to $4 million each time cheap Russian jet-powered drone is shot down
articles.body:
Intercepting a jet-powered Geran can cost anywhere from $2,000 to $4 million depending on the weapon used. Cheap interceptor drones are the only option that keeps air defense affordable, the foundation of Ukrainian top war volunteer Serhii Sternenko said on Telegram.
Russia’s jet Gerans now carry every characteristic of a small cruise missile, and Russians keep raising their speed in answer to each Ukrainian countermeasure. Former commander-in-chief Valerii Zaluzhnyi has framed the shift bluntly: an expensive Cold War missile has become a cheap weapon fired in bulk, and the drone is now “a missile in all but name,” affordable to any side, not only wealthy countries.
Sternenko heads a charitable foundation that has purchased 291,502 FPV drones, which have helped Ukraine’s military down more than 12,954 aerial targets. Also, has advised the team of former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov.
Three ways to kill a jet Geran, and what each costs
The foundation laid out the price of each method:
- Aircraft (F-16, MiG-29, Su-27, Mirage 2000): $25,000 to $1.2 million per kill. Effective, but the stock of missiles is critically low, and some air-to-air types are no longer being replenished.
- Surface-to-air and shoulder-fired systems (IRIS-T, NASAMS, Vampire, Avenger): about $30,000 to $4 million. Good for shielding key sites, but a missile capable of reaching a jet Geran at 6 to 7 kilometers costs $0.5 million to $4 million.
- Interceptor drones (makers undisclosed): from $2,000. Cheap, with trained operators ready, but not yet scalable.
Why the cheapest option is the one that matters
No single tool is enough, the foundation stresses. Downing jet Gerans still needs aircraft, small aviation and missile systems together, but it is the interceptors that make the defense affordable, taking out the cheaper Shaheds and saving costly missiles for targets nothing else can reach.
The foundation says it has found a way to counter drones that already match small cruise missiles, working with Ukrainian manufacturers, without disclosing details. The method is far cheaper than other ways of downing jet Gerans and significantly strengthens air defense, it says, as part of a wider Ukrainian push to field interceptor drones fast enough to catch Russia’s fastest weapons.
Read also
- In Oslo, US envoy pushes Zelenskyy toward deal with Russia again. Day later, in same city, Norway moves to arm Ukraine with more NASAMS missiles
- Norway bars deals with 33 more Russian financial institutions—and 22 more from India to Nigeria
- Ukraine’s interceptor crews destroyed thousands of Russian aerial targets during Vivaldi. Jet-powered Shaheds remain a challenge

articles.title: Covert CIA and Mossad operations inside Iran ahead of a possible new war - opinion
articles.body:
Middle Eastern wars do not always begin with the first missile. Their outcomes are often shaped weeks or months earlier, inside intelligence headquarters, through clandestine networks, and across the unseen battlefield of covert operations.
As the prospect of renewed conflict between the Islamic Republic of the criminal Shi’ite ayatollahs and the United States and Israel grows, the critical question is not who will strike first, but how much of the intelligence war is already unfolding inside Iran.
After eight months of war and severe military and economic losses, the Islamic Republic continues to pursue its survival through nuclear blackmail, threats to global energy security, and protracted negotiations.
President Donald Trump faces a strategic choice: accept a deal that allows Tehran to rebuild or sustain pressure until its security threats are verifiably constrained. In this confrontation, the CIA and Mossad’s intelligence capabilities, particularly their ability to identify and assess vulnerabilities within Tehran’s security establishment, may prove decisive.
Tehran has abandoned none of its tactics of intimidation, deception, and extortion. While speaking of peace, its officials impose unrealistic conditions on Washington. Mohsen Rezaei, a former IRGC commander associated with the Islamic terrorist cult of Mansouroun, insists that not a single gram of enriched uranium will leave Iran.
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has likewise conditioned reopening the Strait of Hormuz on acceptance of Tehran’s proposal. These demands reveal not a willingness to compromise, but a calculated effort to preserve leverage, prolong the confrontation, and buy time.
In intelligence warfare, time does not necessarily favor the side prolonging futile negotiations. Tehran may calculate that rising oil prices, American voter anxiety, and the November 3 midterm elections will pressure Trump into concessions.
Yet a prolonged crisis may also give Washington and Israel valuable opportunities to collect intelligence, assess military capabilities, and expose vulnerabilities within the Islamic Republic’s security apparatus. This remains a strategic assessment, not confirmation of ongoing covert operations.
Israel’s intelligence campaign against Iran’s nuclear program has already demonstrated the depth of Tehran’s counterintelligence vulnerabilities. Mossad’s 2018 seizure of Iran’s nuclear archive, sabotage attributed to Israel at nuclear facilities, and the 2020 assassination of Mohsen Fakhrizadeh exposed serious weaknesses in the regime’s security defenses.
Although the CIA’s direct involvement in these operations remains publicly unverified, US-Israeli intelligence cooperation is well established. Their shared strategic interests, however, should not be confused with evidence of joint participation in every operation attributed to Mossad.
Iran’s greatest vulnerability
For Tehran’s Shi’ite caliphate, the greatest danger extends beyond American air superiority or Israeli missile capabilities.
It is the prospect of intelligence penetration into the institutions sustaining the regime: the IRGC, counterintelligence agencies, national security decision-making centers, nuclear networks, and the increasingly compromised Intelligence Ministry.
A regime unable to protect its secrets, personnel, and command structure remains strategically vulnerable regardless of its military arsenal. Ideological loyalty and internal repression cannot compensate for counterintelligence failures.
The Strait of Hormuz represents another dimension of this asymmetric confrontation. The IRGC claims Iranian naval mines blocked three oil tankers, although independent verification remains lacking. Tehran’s broader objective is to weaponize maritime insecurity and energy-market uncertainty.
It need not win a naval battle to impose economic costs on Washington; threats to shipping can raise insurance premiums, transportation costs, and oil prices. Accurate intelligence on Iran’s actual maritime capabilities is therefore essential to distinguishing credible threats from coercive bluffing and preventing strategic miscalculation.
The Islamic Republic’s asymmetric warfare extends far beyond the Persian Gulf. For decades, Tehran’s outlaw regime has relied on terrorist militias, intelligence networks, cyberoperations, and terrorist proxies to project power and threaten adversaries.
The Iranian and Russian efforts to fuel unrest in France, alongside British counterterrorism investigations into suspected Iranian intelligence connections, underscore Europe’s growing security concerns. While allegations must be distinguished from verified intelligence, Washington cannot afford to view Tehran’s transnational threat solely through the nuclear lens.
Tehran’s refusal to relinquish its enriched uranium raises a critical question: If the regime genuinely seeks to resolve international concerns, why preserve one of its most dangerous strategic bargaining chips?
Enrichment alone does not establish an intention to build nuclear weapons. Yet uranium stockpiles, centrifuge capacity, and independent verification remain central to assessing nuclear breakout risks. Any agreement that leaves these vulnerabilities unresolved risks granting Tehran the time and strategic breathing space to rebuild.
For the CIA and Mossad, the strategic imperative is to deliver precise, independent intelligence that exposes Tehran’s capabilities, vulnerabilities, and intentions. Covert operations, however successful, cannot replace a coherent national strategy or independently guarantee regime collapse.
Intelligence achievements can degrade an adversary’s capabilities, but lasting strategic change requires political, economic, social, and security pressure working together.
Trump must distinguish between ending military operations and neutralizing the Islamic Republic’s criminal ruling apparatus. Destroying weapons, damaging facilities, and degrading IRGC capabilities does not necessarily dismantle the regime’s command structure, political will, or capacity to regenerate.
Tehran has repeatedly exploited periods of reduced pressure to rebuild its military, intelligence services, and proxy networks. American success must therefore be measured not merely by silenced missiles or a temporarily reopened Strait of Hormuz, but by the enduring degradation of the regime’s capacity to threaten regional and international security.
One strategic distinction must remain clear: Iran is not the Islamic Republic. Iranians have endured decades of repression, systemic corruption, isolation, and the regime’s regional adventurism.
Washington must not mistake the regime’s survival for Iran’s stability or sacrifice the Iranian people’s right to determine their political future in a closed-door security bargain. The demand for regime change among significant elements of the Iranian opposition deserves consideration in any serious diplomatic assessment.
This does not justify an unlimited war. Washington must weigh the human, economic, and military costs of another prolonged conflict. But avoiding war must not mean accepting a weak agreement.
Any settlement requires verifiable nuclear restrictions, independent monitoring, maritime security guarantees, and enforceable consequences for violations. Diplomacy must reduce threats, not reward their continuation.
Tehran is betting that rising oil prices, public exhaustion, and approaching US elections will force Trump to concede. Yet its leadership cannot know the full extent of American and Israeli intelligence assessments or the options under consideration. That uncertainty is a strategic factor in itself.
Covert operations may already be underway, but their existence and scope cannot be established from publicly available evidence, nor is another war inevitable.
History will judge this confrontation not by bombs dropped or facilities destroyed, but by whether a persistent security threat was durably contained. Tehran must not regain through diplomacy what it lost militarily without meaningful security concessions.
Trump must ensure that ending the war does not allow the Islamic Republic to rebuild its capacity for aggression. The intelligence battle may precede the first missile, but strategic victory requires lasting results.
The CIA and Mossad’s intelligence capabilities remain central to understanding and confronting Tehran’s intelligence apparatus. Whether their operations contribute to regime change remains uncertain, but their documented achievements deserve serious recognition.
For those seeking an end to the Islamic Republic, dismantling its machinery of repression and external aggression remains a fundamental objective. The regime’s continued existence offers no inherent guarantee of regional peace, stability, or international security.
The writer is a Middle East political analyst. His latest book, Tehran’s Dictator, examines the theocratic era of Ali Khamenei (1989-2026). @EQFard

articles.title: DIU: Russia has accumulated up to 700 ballistic missiles and more than 6,000 drones
Putin welcomes Witkoff with fresh Ukraine peace talks in offing
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin hosted U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff Wednesday to discuss new proposals for ending the war in Ukraine, amid Washington's latest push to stop Europe's bloodiest conflict since World War II.
The talks in St. Petersburg, Witkoff's ninth meeting with Putin, included a goodwill gesture from Russia: the release of a retired U.S. schoolteacher held in Russia.
The encounter prompted concerns in Kyiv and among its allies that the United States is backing away from Ukraine, at times holding back real-time intelligence on Russian attacks and hobbling Ukraine's military communications.
The latest talks came more than two years after President Donald Trump promised in his election campaign to end the Ukraine war within 24 hours.
Witkoff flew into St. Petersburg Wednesday morning, a day after conducting what a U.S. official called "constructive" talks in Oslo with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the leaders of Finland and Norway, and European and NATO representatives. President Donald Trump said it was time for Ukraine to end the war or face "a very bad thing."
U.S.-Ukraine ties have deteriorated sharply since Trump announced a diesel export deal with Russia earlier this month, which he said would help lower prices in the United States.
Since the diesel deal, Ukraine has complained of disruption to some intelligence sharing and to its use of the Starlink military satellite system, though Zelenskyy said Tuesday's Oslo meeting had reached an agreement to resolve those issues.
Citing U.S. officials and people familiar with the matter, The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday that billionaire Elon Musk ordered last week the slowdown of a military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite service that Ukraine relies on to track Russian ballistic missile strikes.
Reuters could not immediately verify the report.
Musk has said any such decision is made by the U.S. military or the president. Trump has said he was not responsible. U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth signaled Tuesday that the problem lay in the terms of service Kyiv needed to comply with.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Wednesday that Witkoff's meeting with Zelenskyy was positive and that Witkoff would share the results with Russia. He also reiterated that Washington had not pulled back Kyiv's ability to access Starlink.
"He will now, armed with those ideas, be able to go to St. Petersburg and share them with the Russian side, and let's see if we can make some progress," he said.
Despite the apparently cordial nature of Tuesday's meeting in Oslo, Trump, in comments Tuesday at the White House, remained frustrated with Zelenskyy, whom he has repeatedly rebuked and suggested should be replaced.
"He's going to have to want to make a deal, because I don't think his people are going to stand for it any longer," Trump told reporters on the eve of the talks in Russia.
Putin, who has shown few signs of compromising on his central war aims – which include full Russian control of the Donetsk region in eastern Ukraine and no NATO membership for Kyiv – received Witkoff in the Constantine Palace, an imperial edifice in his home city.
Kirill Dmitriev, Putin's special investment envoy and his key liaison for potential economic and financial deals with the U.S., also attended the meeting with Witkoff, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said.
A U.S. official said Ukraine brought new ideas and proposals to the Oslo talks, which made "meaningful progress" toward a coordinated approach to engaging with Russia.
The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said the talks covered "key elements of a comprehensive peace framework," including security guarantees for Ukraine, a postwar economic plan and a broader European security architecture.
Witkoff aimed to "create a pathway toward direct trilateral and broader multilateral negotiations," the official said. Zelenskyy said he hoped to discuss key issues on how to end the war during a trilateral meeting with Putin and Trump.
The Kremlin has repeatedly said that any Putin-Zelenskyy meeting would need to be painstakingly prepared by aides to make it worthwhile and that much legwork would be required for an overall agreement.
Trump said Tuesday he raised the idea with Putin of freeing Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old retired U.S. schoolteacher being held in Russia on mercenary charges he denies.
Putin told Witkoff that Hubbard was at the airport waiting to fly back to the U.S. with him. Witkoff thanked Putin for the goodwill gesture.
Hubbard was first detained in April 2022 and later sentenced to six years and 10 months on charges whose veracity his family and U.S.-based lawyer question.

articles.title: Israeli plans to strike Iran before election raise fears of wider regional war
articles.body:
A report that Israel planned to strike Iranian civilian infrastructure earlier this month, only to be stopped by U.S. President Donald Trump, has renewed questions about the strategic justification for another war with Tehran, particularly with Israeli elections less than a week away.
The Financial Times reported Wednesday that Israel had planned to attack Iranian infrastructure on Oct. 10, including power plants, nuclear facilities and other targets associated with the Iranian government, before Trump intervened to prevent the operation.
The report has raised concerns about why Israel would consider launching another major military campaign against Iran when previous rounds of fighting have failed to topple the Iranian government or permanently eliminate its military capabilities.
Israel has spent much of the past three years engaged in intensive fighting on multiple fronts, while damage from previous confrontations with Iran and fighting along its northern and southern borders has yet to be fully repaired.
Iran, meanwhile, continues to demonstrate its ability to disrupt shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, attacking vessels and affecting the global economy. Gulf states have largely absorbed the consequences without launching direct military responses.
Against that backdrop, questions remain over whether Israel has a clear strategic plan for another confrontation and what objectives a renewed campaign could realistically achieve.
Danny Citrinowicz, a former head of the Iran branch in the Israeli Military Intelligence Directorate's Research Division and now a senior researcher specializing in Iran and the Shiite axis at the Institute for National Security Studies (INSS), told ynet that there was no immediate military justification for launching another war.
"There's absolutely nothing that justifies a war now, either before the elections or afterward," Citrinowicz said.
"Iran is rebuilding its strength and restoring its missile capabilities. On the nuclear front, there are no indications whatsoever that they have resumed enrichment. There are the same indications that they moved certain materials to Pickaxe Mountain, but nothing beyond that."
Pickaxe Mountain, also known as Kuh-e Kolang Gaz La, is a mountainous site near Iran's Natanz nuclear complex that has attracted international scrutiny over suspected underground nuclear-related construction.
Citrinowicz questioned why Iran remained capable of launching substantial missile attacks after two previous wars that Israeli officials had described as major military successes.
"We also need to understand why, after two wars against Iran, we're still seeing them launch dozens of missiles," he said. "Apparently, they're not afraid for their arsenal."
'No justification for another campaign'
Citrinowicz said the reported Israeli interest in attacking Iran's energy infrastructure appeared to rest on two possible strategic assumptions, neither of which he considered convincing.
"What is the strategic objective of another war?" he asked. "According to various reports, Israel wants to attack Iran's energy facilities for one of two reasons: Either they think that will bring down the regime, which it won't, or they want to turn Iran into a failed state. And it's clear that would lead to a very broad Iranian campaign against Israel."
He said Iran's continued military buildup did not, by itself, justify an immediate attack.
Iran has continued replacing senior officials killed in previous confrontations, including some whose successors have adopted even more hard-line positions.
Earlier this week, Mehrdad Akhlaghi was appointed Iran's new defense minister. Like his predecessors, he warned that Iranian forces remained ready to respond to threats.
But despite the rhetoric and continued rearmament, Citrinowicz said there had been no dramatic change in Iranian behavior in recent months.
He argued that Iran's efforts to rebuild its capabilities were comparable to those of other Israeli adversaries, including the Houthis in Yemen, Hezbollah in Lebanon and pro-Iranian militias in Iraq.
Another war against Iran, he warned, could reignite fighting across all those fronts.
"The point is that there is no justification requiring a military campaign at this time," Citrinowicz said. "We need to monitor the situation and see what develops. If Iran makes a breakout toward a nuclear weapon tomorrow, then we need to attack. But right now, nothing is happening."
He described the possibility of an Israeli strike just two weeks before the election as deeply troubling.
"What's happening now is sheer madness — attacking two weeks before elections. For what?" he said.
"Iran is not on the verge of developing a nuclear weapon, and with all due respect to its missile arsenal, it still hasn't returned to where it was before Operation Rising Lion and Operation Roaring Lion," he added, using the Israeli names for the previous bouts of direct fighting against the Islamic Republic.
"There is no operational or strategic need to attack now," Citrinowicz said. "There is an attempt to incorporate political considerations, and that is serious."
The former intelligence official also questioned the lasting achievements of the previous military campaigns, noting that Iran's leadership remained in power and its military continued rebuilding.
"Yes, another strike would cause damage, but the consequences for the international system would be insane," he said. "They would set the entire Gulf ablaze."
He criticized what he described as an apparent willingness to launch another campaign without first examining why earlier operations had failed to achieve their declared objectives.
"It's as if we don't care. Just attack again. But for what?" he said.
"And this is after we were promised tremendous, unprecedented achievements in two wars, that we had 'pushed the threat back for generations.' How did we push the threat back for generations if they can attack again?"
He added that Israeli officials had previously emphasized achievements against Iran's missile capabilities, yet Iranian missiles continued to pose a threat.
"The most serious thing is the mixing of political considerations," he said. "Ultimately, there is no justification for launching a campaign two weeks before elections."
US midterm elections complicate diplomatic efforts
The prospect of another confrontation also comes as Washington approaches its midterm elections in early November, a political milestone that Citrinowicz said could influence both Iranian calculations and Trump's willingness to pursue military action.
"The elections in the United States are extremely significant because the Iranians want Trump to lose," he said. "They want to demonstrate the price of confronting them to any American president: Mess with us and you'll lose the elections."
Citrinowicz said Tehran remained open to a negotiated agreement but continued to insist on conditions unacceptable to the Trump administration.
"The Iranians are prepared to return to an agreement, but the conditions they're presenting are conditions Trump will not accept," he said.
He dismissed recent reports in the Qatari newspaper Al-Araby Al-Jadeed suggesting a diplomatic breakthrough was imminent.
"With all due respect to the reports in Al-Araby Al-Jadeed, there is no diplomatic breakthrough whatsoever," he said.
He pointed to remarks made Tuesday by Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, during a meeting with Pakistan's army chief, Asim Munir.
According to the account, Rezaei insisted that all enriched nuclear material would remain in Iran.
"All enriched nuclear materials will remain in Iran," Rezaei said, describing them as "a central asset and national wealth of the Iranian people, intended for use within the country."
Rezaei also said Iranian officials and the public agreed that negotiations should not resume until Washington took steps to rebuild trust.
"The Iranian people and officials agree that there will be no negotiations as long as the United States does not take confidence-building measures," he said, adding that the prerequisite for restoring trust was meeting Iran's stated conditions.
Citrinowicz said the statements underscored the distance between Washington and Tehran despite those reports of diplomatic progress.
He also warned that the period between November's U.S. elections and the seating of the new Congress in January could prove especially volatile.
"I think the period between November and January is very dangerous because it's the transition between Congresses," he said. "During those two months, Trump will want to do something."
However, he suggested Trump's preferred course of action might differ substantially from Israel's reported objectives.
"Perhaps he wants to deliver a single blow, then end the whole affair and declare victory," Citrinowicz said. "I'm not sure he wants to return to the idea of toppling the regime."
He described the possibility of Israel initiating another military campaign under the current circumstances as highly irresponsible.
Israeli fighter jet activity raises escalation fears
Citrinowicz also expressed concern over a Fox News report that Israeli fighter jets had flown over Syria and Iraq toward Iran as part of a military exercise.
He warned that such activity, if accurately reported, could be interpreted by Tehran as preparation for an imminent attack, potentially provoking an Iranian response.
"If that's true, it's an extremely dangerous development," he said. "We're on the brink of war, and we're conducting a simulated strike in Iraq?"
Citrinowicz questioned the logic of staging an exercise resembling an attack on Iran during a period of heightened tensions.
"Do we want to force the Iranians to fire missiles at us?" he asked.
"There's no logic in simulating an attack on Iran at the height of tensions, other than a desire to push the Iranians into attacking us, to have them fire the first shot so we'll have an excuse to respond."
He warned that another Israeli-Iranian confrontation would almost certainly spread beyond the two countries.
"Any war with Iran will once again be a regional war," he said. "Certainly involving the Houthis, certainly the militias in Iraq, and I believe ultimately Hezbollah as well."
Citrinowicz said the regional security environment had changed in ways that could make another confrontation particularly dangerous.
He pointed to the absence of a U.S. military presence in Iraq, which he said would make it easier for pro-Iranian militias to operate, as well as the presence of Houthi elements in the country.
"We'll once again find ourselves stuck in a regional war," he said.
He also highlighted concerns about Israel's and the United States' supplies of missile interceptors, which would be essential to defending against sustained Iranian attacks.
"We know we have a problem with interceptors. That's no secret. And the Americans have a problem with interceptors as well," he said.
Those shortages, he suggested, could become particularly consequential in a prolonged conflict involving multiple fronts and repeated missile barrages.
'We cannot separate Netanyahu's political considerations from Israel's strategic interests'
Citrinowicz said his central concern was the possibility that domestic political calculations were influencing decisions with potentially far-reaching consequences for Israeli national security.
"The most serious aspect of this entire situation is that it's impossible to separate Netanyahu's political considerations from the strategic considerations of the State of Israel," he said.
"That's extremely dangerous. This would be another war with Iran."
He warned that previous confrontations had demonstrated the economic and social costs of fighting Iran, with military operations disrupting daily life and economic activity across Israel.
"We know that every war with Iran paralyzes the Israeli economy and brings activity here to a standstill," he said. "And for what? What strategic objective would this war serve?"
He argued that another campaign would be especially difficult to justify given the limited prospects of removing Iran's leadership through airstrikes alone.
"We understand very clearly that we are not going to topple this regime from the air," he said.
Rather than rushing toward another confrontation, Citrinowicz called for a thorough examination of Israel's previous campaigns, including the objectives they failed to achieve and whether additional military action would serve the country's long-term interests.
"Launching a campaign two weeks before elections is madness," he said.
"Before Israel launches a campaign for which there is currently no immediate need, we must ultimately analyze what we failed to achieve in the previous campaign and why."
He said policymakers should also consider whether military force was the only available option and whether another confrontation would advance Israel's strategic interests.
"Is the kinetic solution the only one, and will it serve the interests of the State of Israel?" he asked.
Citrinowicz emphasized that Israel should preserve close strategic coordination with Washington, describing it as the foundation of Israeli policy toward Iran.
"We certainly need to maintain strategic coordination with the United States," he said. "That's a significant issue because it's the basis of all Israeli policy toward Iran."
But he stressed that coordination with Washington should not replace an independent Israeli assessment of the risks and benefits of military action.
"With all due respect to the Americans, the State of Israel needs to examine what's right for it," he said.
He concluded that Israel should not embark on another potentially more dangerous war without first understanding why previous operations had failed to achieve their stated objectives.
"Right now, it's clear that the war's objectives were not achieved," Citrinowicz said.
"Before we analyze why they weren't achieved, we shouldn't jump into another campaign, one that could potentially be even more dangerous than the previous one, because it would be extremely violent and the Iranians are learning from every confrontation."

articles.title: ‘No Kings’ protests reflect a crisis of imperial plutocracy in the US
articles.body:
‘No Kings’ protests reflect a crisis of imperial plutocracy in the US
ARIZONA- The most obvious focus of the current “No Kings” protests lies in US citizens’ immediate “bread and butter issues”: brutal cuts to education, social security, and health care ($1 trillion in cuts to Medicaid and Childre’s Health Insurance); massive inflation that makes it hard to feed families, pay outrageous costs for health insurance, and endure the exorbitant price of fuel precipitated by the perfidious war on Iran, launched for a second time since June, 2025, in the midst of negotiations.
Beyond that initial layer is the severe reduction and even obliteration of programs that help the poor, and the savage attacks against immigrants, many of whom are either legal or already citizens; yet all of them—whether Latin American or Middle Eastern—cast as either “criminals, thugs, rapists” or “threats to national security”, and subjected to imprisonment and deportation.
A distinct goal of the current protests, however, as noted by Tehran Times , is the urgent emphasis on voting in the upcoming midterm elections, since the average voter turnout in midterm elections is only 48%, despite a rise to 52% in 2022. Midterm elections occur halfway through a presidential term, and determine the composition of both chambers of Congress, Representatives and Senators. This November’s election is particularly crucial, for if Trump loses his Republican majority in Congress, Democrats plan to launch investigations into his blatantly corrupt family businesses, the Epstein files, immigration enforcement, and corporate profiteering. And if Trump also loses control of the Senate, Democrats can block Trump’s nominees for Cabinet positions, paralyze his appointment of federal judges and nominees to the Supreme Court, give Democrats subpoena power that would enhance their power to investigate the administration, and might possibly lead to impeachment proceedings.
While Trump and his base—both the “uneducated” he claims to love and the oligarchs he pampers—fear such an outcome, the rest of the country dreads that the administration may steal the election, as he attempted to do in 2020, and which Trump continues to hallucinate having won.
For more astute protesters, deeper dimensions lie beyond their immediate private afflictions and political tactics: the current regime is the malignant harvest of a systemic sociopolitical disease, an incremental process that has achieved only its most virulent embodiment in Trump. Decades of lavish tax breaks for the ultra-rich have impoverished and depleted life for the ordinary citizen, accomplished by the long assault on Labor Unions and the obscene rise in Corporate Profits. The struggle is against a system devoted to perpetual war and militarism, the rise of a surveillance state behind a shabby façade of “democracy” whose flimsy mask conceals the true face of a merciless plutocracy.
The entire society has been commodified: humanity, personhood, culture, art, law, and indeed the Earth itself are subordinated to the calculation of profit for the oligarchs. As one corporate executive affirmed, “We have to save capitalism from democracy.” [Quoted in Nancy MacLean’s masterful Democracy in Chains (2017)]. But this catastrophe did not begin with Trump, whose flagrant vulgarity, malice, ignorance and blatant corruption have reduced every ideal to a “deal”, every principle to “profit”, every fact to “fake news.” Nonetheless, Trump has crossed a threshold, representing an apotheosis of the Neoliberal ideology that has reigned since Reagan and Thatcher. Not to be confused with “Liberal” social values, Neoliberalism is not merely an economic theory but a Worldview that envisions the absolute supremacy of the spurious “Free Market”: privatization of all public space, the erasure of any regulations and responsibilities that protect workers, the public and the environment. The social fabric is devastated: citizens are reduced to mere consumers; elections succumb to legal bribery; the indivual will is divinized, while community and compassion are mocked as “Communist.”
At its root, Neoliberalism is an assault on all transcendent values, which are reduced to mere transactions: the evisceration of the Goodness, Truth and Beauty that form the very basis and deep fraternity of authentic principles that might unite the threefold Abrahamic Traditions and bridge the distance between East and West. But for the plutocracy, nothing is sacred: all life is merely “collateral damage” in the cult of money and power. Meanwhile, a perverse, heretical “Christian fascism” mirrors the Zionist desecration of Judaism and mutilates our shared dialectical heritage into a weapon of conquest.
On leaving office in January, 1961 President Eisenhower warned against the Military Industrial Complex (MIC), which over the last six decades has metastasized into the Military-Industrial-Media-Academic Complex (MIMAC), whereby Corporate Media serves as flagrant propaganda, and corporatized University Administrations silence and expel voices dedicated to the practice of critical thinking, professors who bravely stand for global justice, peace and accountability, while war crimes and genocide are upheld with lies, prevarication and impunity.
Trump has waged an assault on the very foundations of American society: the Constitution, a crucial element of which is the “separation of powers” between the Executive, Legislative and Judiciary branches, designed to avert the rise of tyranny. While Trump has attacked judges appointed by former presidents of both parties, he has fantasized that Article II of the Constitution gives him the right to do “whatever I want.”
The Will to Power and Addiction to Avarice reign supreme. In 2018, Trump unilaterally abrogated Obama’s JCPOA—the accord (in conjunction with China, France, Germany, Russia, and the United Kingdom) limiting Iran’s nuclear development in exchange for sanctions relief—despite Iran’s compliance, as verified by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA). That fateful decision resulted from pressure exerted by his billionaire donors, amid the long-established aims of the CIA in conjunction with Mossad.
What many Iranians as well as Americans grasp is that we are facing an administration of the most deeply cynical character, whose abysmal inhumanity was crystallized in the heartless retort of Matt Schlapp (chairman of the American Conservative Union), on a Piers Morgan broadcast in March: dismissing Peter Beinart’s compassionate lament that if the U.S. and Israel had not attacked Iran on February 28, the schoolgirls killed at the Shajareh Tayyibeh elementary school in Minab “would be alive”, Schlapp quipped: “They’d be alive in a burqa… in a barbaric, unequal society… with no ability to make career choices.” By Schlapp’s cavalier reckoning, the illegal, unprovoked war of aggression launched against Iran was blameless, the humanity of both the dead and living girls, their teachers and parents obliterated, along with the lives of the 73 boys whose massacre was omitted in nearly all US media reports.
Be it noted that Schlapp has faced multiple sexual harassment charges involving other men.
The bombing of Minab was no mere “accident”, given that Pete Hegseth, Trump’s Secretary of War (formerly “Defense”) openly implemented a doctrine of “More lethality and less accountability”, publicly spurning what he called “stupid rules of engagement.” Not mere bravado: he dissolved the policy to limit civilian casualties established by the Department of Defense, known as the Civilian Harm Mitigation and Response (CHMR, pronounced “Chimmer”), and fired the senior advisor at the Pentagon’s Civilian Protection Center of Excellence, Air Force combat veteran Wes J. Bryant. “We’re departing from the rules and norms that we’ve tried to establish as a global community since at least World War II,” Bryant said. “There’s zero accountability.”
As the eminent former Ambassador Chas Freeman has declared, “diplomacy… begins with empathy.” The tragic reality of US foreign policy, he laments, is quite the opposite: “We don’t do diplomacy anymore. [In] the ‘rules-based order,’ … we make the rules and decide who they apply to and who is exempt from them.”
Freeman’s grim insights are amply confirmed by Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s shameless scorn of “so-called International Law”, as the administration engages in attacking and dismantling every mechanism designed to promote and ensure human rights and global accountability, from the UN to the ICC, which Trump himself has called “an evil group of people”. For the US soars above the law, which it makes and breaks, supports or sabotages at will, in accordance with its capricious, often incoherent and myopic “interests” bereft of values, blind to principles, contemptuous of truth.
Like a lobotomized version of Netanyahu, Trump exemplifies what Marc Owen Jones has called alethocide: the killing of truth, in brash defiance of Hannah Arendt’s warning: “The ideal subject of totalitarian rule is not the convinced Nazi or the convinced Communist, but people for whom the distinction between fact and fiction (i.e., the reality of experience) and the distinction between the true and the false (i.e., the standards of thought) no longer exist.” [The Origins of Totalitarianism. Part 3, Ch. 13, §3., p. 474. (1979 ed.)].
Yet lest we be comforted by the hope that a Democratic majority would make the needful turn to empathy and diplomacy, we have only to regard the dismal Biden policy toward Palestine to sober such wishes, from its refusal to condemn the brutal evictions of Palestinian families in East Jerusalem (2021), to its audacious denials of Israeli apartheid—documented and declared from 2020-2022 not only by the UN, Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International, but by Israeli human rights organizations B’Tselem and Yesh Din—to its brazen lies and duplicity in the face of war crimes and genocide, as Biden’s minions violated US domestic law by providing Israel a flood of weapons, and “willfully enabled atrocities” in Gaza, as meticulously detailed in the recent book Crossing the Red Line by Akbar Shahid Ahmed.
As demonstrated since the Clinton presidency, the key difference between the two US parties rests in rhetoric and comportment, not in substance: while Trump spews vulgarity, racism, misogyny, megalomania and toxic fables; threatens Iran that “a whole civilization will die tonight, never to be brought back again”; declares Climate Change a “hoax” and sneers at the global scientific consensus regarding the ecocide we continue to commit—Democrats deplore his barbarity and ignorance, while urbanely praising human rights but ignoring their implementation, raise insipid procedural objections against the war, and prudently pose and gesture toward crucial shifts to renewable energy—yet only two candidates even mention “climate” on their current campaign websites.
After Gaza, the Democrats’ notoriety as “the lesser of two evils” is more woefully suspect than ever. Both parties serve the corporate and financial elite, even as they seduce and betray their constituents, far too many of whom remain complacent in the face of the fascist tide, distracted by celebrity worship, sports events, casinos, and barbecues, while vainly imagining themselves immune to the lure of “bread and circuses” and the lust for dominion and military might that leads to the suicide of empires. Trump is merely, as Chris Hedges avows, “the naked, stripped-down expression of this suicidal pact.”
The thirst for hope must not erase our nation’s long history of depredation, too rarely taught in our schools: throughout the twentieth century US support for Latin American dictators reached its peak during the Reagan administration, but the Empire emerged long before: the Mexican-American War (1846-8) was provoked by the US in order to justify stealing the territories and riches of California and Texas; Hawaii was overthrown in 1893; and the Spanish-American War of 1898—purportedly to “liberate Cuba from the domination of Spain (the erstwhile analogue of our era’s ennemis du jour, whether “Communist” or “Islamist”), but in truth to ensure US domination of the Caribbean sugar market—extended to the Philippine War (1899-1902) to annex and subjugate the archipelago under the guise of independence, freedom, and “Christian” values.
The dynamic satirized in Mark Twain’s scathing essay of 1901, “To the Person Sitting in Darkness” exposed the seething Imperialism and avarice beneath the dazzling veil of rhetorical hypocrisy in its lethal quest to “enlighten” the “savage”, “heathen”, “uncivilized” peoples and lands whose sovereignty and dignity were despoiled in our grotesque triumph.
A modicum of change will doubtless come with time, but the imperative transformation of consciousness may well arrive only with the bitter gift of regret: the inevitable collapse of our hegemonic Heart of Darkness.

articles.title: Kremlin warns of ‘extremely dangerous’ nuclear arms control vacuum
articles.body:
Kremlin warns of extreme nuclear danger
