Russia and the US urgently need to resume dialogue on strategic stability and arms control, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said. The absence of a treaty-based framework in this areas is creating a very dangerous situation, he added.
The New START treaty, the last remaining bilateral agreement limiting US and Russian strategic nuclear arsenals, expired in February without an extension or replacement.
Signed in 2010 and extended in 2021, the treaty capped each side at 1,550 deployed strategic nuclear warheads and 700 deployed delivery systems, while providing for transparency and on-site verification measures.
Following the treaty’s expiration, Russia suggested maintaining caps on warheads for another year if Washington reciprocated, but the initiative went unanswered, according to Moscow.
Russia is convinced that talks must resume soon, Peskov told reporters on Tuesday. “This is an extremely important issue,” he said. “For the first time in a long while, the world has been left without this treaty-based legal framework.” He described the situation as “extremely dangerous.”
Peskov urged an early start to negotiations, warning that they would inevitably be complex and lengthy.
The Trump administration has long insisted that any future nuclear arms control agreement should include China as well. In February, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington will press for trilateral talks with Beijing and Moscow.
On Monday, US President Donald Trump said he is open to discussing nuclear disarmament at a potential meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of next month’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China.
“We would have it to talk about nuclear weapons and denuclearization,” he told reporters. “If President Xi wants to have it, I’d have it. I’m sure we’d talk about other things like trade too.”
Peskov said Russia cannot disregard the nuclear arsenals of European NATO members, particularly Britain and France, in future strategic stability talks with the US.
Earlier this year, President Emmanuel Macron announced a “forward deterrence” initiative that could see French nuclear weapons deployed to other European countries. In March, he said France would no longer disclose the size of its arsenal, arguing that “to be free, we have to be feared.” He also outlined plans to increase its nuclear arsenal, which is currently just under 300 warheads, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI).
Moscow has warned that the strategy could backfire, saying it cannot “ignore an obvious buildup of the nuclear component of NATO’s joint potential.”
In August, NBC reported that the Pentagon was also working on a nuclear strategy that would give the US president a wider range of nuclear options in a potential conflict with Russia or China. The approach would reportedly pivot towards shorter-range tactical nuclear weapons instead of relying primarily on long-range strategic nuclear weapons.
Russia updated its nuclear doctrine in 2024, stating that aggression by a non-nuclear state backed by a nuclear power would be treated as a joint attack and that nuclear weapons could be used if conventional aggression posed a critical threat to the sovereignty or territorial integrity of Russia or its ally Belarus. Moscow also criticized the US nuclear weapons deployment to Europe as part of NATO’s nuclear-sharing arrangements.

articles.title: Ukraine, Lockheed Martin discuss F-16 upkeep, PAC-3 supply
articles.body:
Defense Minister Yevheniy Khmara and Armed Forces Commander in Chief Mykhailo Drapaty met a delegation of the American defense company Lockheed Martin, led by Lockheed Martin Aeronautics President Orlando Sanchez Jr., and discussed the importance of stable arms supplies and further cooperation, the Defense Ministry said.
"We count on mutually beneficial cooperation with Lockheed Martin for years ahead. Ukraine is ready to share unique combat experience so that together we can make defense solutions more effective in modern war," the ministry said on Telegram on Wednesday after the meeting.
The sides separately discussed the value of F-16 aircraft for the Air Force, and the ministry said it is now important for Ukraine to widen the geography of their maintenance, including through localization.
"The F-16 is part of Ukrainian aviation. Ukraine is committed to a long-term partnership with Lockheed Martin. It is important to increase arms supplies and do everything to keep as many F-16s as possible in service and working in Ukrainian skies," Khmara said.
The sides also discussed scaling up supplies of PAC-3 interceptor missiles to counter Russian ballistic missile strikes.
The ministry said Lockheed Martin products are already working to defend Ukraine, not only the F-16 and PAC-3 missiles for Patriot air defense systems, but also HIMARS rocket systems.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met the company's team in Kyiv earlier this week.
"The company is now increasing production of ballistic interceptors. We expect to be able to buy some of them to protect more lives. We are also trying to do everything so that F-16 maintenance and repair take place in Ukraine," he said after the meeting on Monday.
Zelenskyy said Patriot systems and F-16 aircraft from this company play an important role in defending against Russian ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones, and that the sides discussed ways to widen and increase supplies.
"It is important that Lockheed Martin is present in Ukraine. We are doing everything on our side to expand our partnership," he said.

articles.title: Zelensky says intelligence sharing 'works now' as US envoy to meet Putin in Russia
articles.body:
Zelensky says intelligence sharing 'works now' as US envoy to meet Putin in Russia
- Published
US special envoy Steve Witkoff has arrived in Russia to meet President Vladimir Putin after Ukraine's leader said American intelligence sharing about deadly Russian strikes "works now".
Kyiv had accused the US of recently withholding such intelligence, causing Ukrainians to lose their lives - a claim rejected as "scandalous" by Washington.
Volodymyr Zelensky was speaking after meeting Witkoff in Oslo on Tuesday for talks later described as "constructive" by a US official.
The Ukrainian president and his European allies said it was now up to Russia to respond to the proposals agreed in Oslo when Witkoff meets Putin in St Petersburg on Wednesday to discuss measures to end the war.
Putin is yet to publicly comment on the latest developments, but Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov has said the Kremlin will listen to what Witkoff offers while ruling out "any political concessions".
Finnish President Alexander Stubb, who also took part in the talks in Oslo alongside the Norwegian prime minister, said "genuine progress" had been made on proposals to achieve peace but gave no details, and warned that patience would be needed.
Witkoff was not present at their joint press conference with Zelensky after the talks, nor was President Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner who had attended via video link.
A US official later said the meeting had been "very productive and constructive" and that there was a "strong alignment at the working level" between the US, Ukraine and Europe on "next steps".
Relations between Ukraine and the US have soured in recent weeks to the extent that President Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to get a new president, and most recently "for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine".
Ahead of next month's US midterm elections, Trump has also sought to blame Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries for fuel prices which have been rising since the start of the US-led war on Iran.
Speaking after the news conference in Oslo, Trump again told reporters at the White House he wanted Kyiv to "make a deal".
He said Russia would like to "get it done" and it was "time for Ukraine to end this war".
Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.
Russian drone attacks have continued this week. Ukrainian officials said at least 10 people were killed on Tuesday - four in Kyiv and the capital region, another four in the eastern Donetsk region, and two in the central city of Dnipro.
Another attack overnight on Wednesday killed two more people near Kharkiv, the country's second-largest city.
- Trump and Zelensky appear at loggerheads despite Oslo optimism 
  - Published23 hours ago
Addressing the issue of US intelligence sharing after Tuesday's talks, Zelensky said he was "thankful that intelligence works now".
"Speaking about early warning, which is very important for our people, our children, adults, civilians because we can hear when ballistic[s] is coming - so we are thankful to American side, now it works, it's great," he said.
Zelensky also said he hoped for a good result on Starlink, after Ukraine's military had reported speed restrictions on drones using its internet network to conduct strikes against Russia.
A bipartisan group of US senators called for an urgent investigation into the restrictions last week.
The Ukrainian leader added that "strong" security guarantees for Ukraine had also been discussed, as well as energy ceasefire proposals, and restated that Kyiv was "ready for negotiations" to end the conflict.
"Of course, we are not losing this war, but we are losing people because Russia attacks," he said.
Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre meanwhile stressed that Europe needed "to be at the table" during any discussions about how to bring the fighting to an end.
Unconfirmed reports earlier on Tuesday said the transfer of more US-made Patriot interceptor missiles - the only effective weapon in shooting down Russian ballistic missiles - had not yet been approved.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters it may be true that Patriot interceptors had not yet arrived in Ukraine, but stressed that nothing had been denied to Kyiv intentionally.
European leaders have meanwhile expressed concern about recent US statements towards Russia.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz spoke of "mixed pictures and messages" on the war on Monday, and said that he was trying to convince the American government "in total that this is something we have to resolve jointly".
"It's really a big effort for our budgets, it's really a big thing for the European Union, but we are doing that and we are trying to keep on doing that until this terrible war ends," the German leader told Bloomberg TV.
Asked during an interview on Monday whether or not he saw Ukraine as a US ally, US Vice-President JD Vance said Kyiv was "certainly a partner in some ways, but we have some divergent interests from time to time, like for example... I think they should stop bombing Russian energy".
"We don't have a formal alliance as far as I know with Ukraine. They're not in Nato, I don't think they should be in Nato... we're gonna work together on some things, but also we're going to be opposite on some things too," he said.
  - Published2 days ago

articles.title: Russia Releases Imprisoned American Man as Trump Envoy Meets With Putin
articles.body:
Russia has released a retired American teacher who had been imprisoned for more than four years on charges of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine. Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff confirmed the release Wednesday, during a meeting in St. Petersburg.
Witkoff referred to Putin as a "humanitarian" and thanked him on behalf of U.S. President Donald Trump. "You talk so much about my President, President Trump, being a humanitarian—you are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that," he said.
Stephen Hubbard, 74, was sentenced to nearly seven years in a penal colony in 2024, after being detained in April 2022. Russian authorities accused the Michigan man of signing a contract with Ukraine’s military in the eastern Ukrainian city of Izyum after Russia’s full-scale invasion of the country in February 2022. The U.S. State Department under the Biden Administration declared that Hubbard, who was sentenced in a closed trial, had been wrongfully detained.
Trump said the release was secured at his request, "made directly" to Putin in a telephone conversation last week and was not part of a swap.
"Stephen is on his way back home and will soon be with his family," Trump said, noting that the U.S. "was not required to give anything in return."
Trump had hinted to reporters in the Oval Office on Tuesday that Hubbard’s release was pending. "Just stick with me," he replied, when asked about the American man’s case. "I don't want to talk about it, but everybody has been after Hubbard for a long time, long before I got here. And just remember that question for a couple of days from now, okay? Because I do things that nobody else can do."
Hubbard is the second American to be freed by Russia within the past three months. Marine veteran Robert Gilman was released on Aug. 11, having spent more than four years imprisoned on disputed charges of assaulting a police officer. Referencing Gilman's reported poor health, Trump at the time said Russia had agreed to release him "on a humanitarian basis."
Hubbard was the last American on the State Department’s list of “wrongfully detained” U.S. citizens in Russia. His release comes in the wake of Trump waiving sanctions on Russia in a bid to progress the controversial diesel deal he made with Putin as he attempts to lower fuel prices, which have soared in the wake of his war with Iran.
The deal has earned bipartisan condemnation, with several Republican lawmakers joining calls for Trump to reverse course, insisting the action will only serve to bolster Putin’s war efforts as Ukraine braces for a fifth winter under attack.
Read More: Lawmakers Argue Trump's Russia Diesel Deal 'Violates' the Law. Here's What Legal Experts Say
Meanwhile, relations between Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky have deteriorated, with the latter voicing grave concern over the U.S.-Russia diesel deal. Trump announced an “energy cease-fire” between Russia and Ukraine on Oct. 11, calling on the two countries to stop targeting each other’s assets. Zelensky accused Moscow of breaking the apparent agreement and, in turn, resumed strikes against Russian oil facilities, defying pressure from Washington. Trump called Ukraine's fresh wave of strikes a "disgrace" and said Zelensky is more difficult to deal with than Putin."
Russia agrees to resume U.S.-mediated peace talks with Ukraine, Kremlin says
During their meeting at the grand imperial palace, Witkoff asked Putin to reconsider participating in peace talks with Ukraine, with the U.S. serving as an intermediary.
"Even if we don't have a resolution today, if we just talk about and sort of consider what that next step might be, I think that would be important and the world is waiting to hear that," Witkoff said as he pitched the idea.
The Kremlin later announced that Putin had agreed "in principle" to resume trilateral talks as soon as next month, anytime after Nov. 10. Putin’s foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov told reporters the technical talks would likely focus on security guarantees for Ukraine and Russia once the war comes to an end. Ushakov suggested the sit-down could take place in Abu Dhabi.
Senior Ukrainian and Russian officials last convened in Switzerland in February for U.S.-brokered peace talks, just ahead of the fourth anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The discussions, which Zelensky suggested had been "difficult," ended without a breakthrough.
Witkoff met with Zelensky in Oslo on Tuesday ahead of his trip to Russia. Zelensky said the meeting was productive and expressed his openness to a "potential trilateral meeting of the leaders to address the issues that only the leaders can do." However, he emphasized that any meetings to negotiate an end to the war must include Ukrainian officials, insisting there should be “nothing about Ukraine without Ukraine."
Zelensky's remarks came after the Wall Street Journal reported that Putin had floated the idea of a summit with Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping to discuss a potential Ukraine deal. Trump on Monday said he was open to a trilateral summit with those attendees to discuss matters related to “denuclearization.”
U.S.-Ukraine tensions escalate
Ukraine and U.S. officials remain at odds as to why Kyiv has experienced limited access to Starshield, the military-grade counterpart of SpaceX’s Starlink commercial service. The program, which offers remote Internet connectivity from satellites in low-Earth orbit, has become a lifeline for Ukraine on the battlefield, allowing it to execute long-reach drone strike missions and counter attacks.
On Oct. 14, Ukraine said its access to Starshield was abruptly limited. Serhiy Beskrestnov, an adviser to Zelensky, said speed restrictions had been imposed, leading to the “failure” of several military missions. Beskrestnov claimed the restrictions, which he said applied to devices traveling over 100 miles per hour and using Starshield, were “related to the current political situation.” During an Oct. 18 appearance on NBC’s Meet the Press, Zelensky said he believed the limited Starshield speed was a “message” from the U.S. government. He also said that Washington had briefly stopped sharing intelligence with Kyiv, drawing a denial from U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
Zelensky’s remarks came after Reuters reported, citing two U.S. officials, that an order to limit Starshield services in Ukraine had come from inside the White House. When approached for comment, a senior U.S. official told TIME: “No such request was ever made by the President.” Some Republican lawmakers, including Representative Mike Turner of Ohio and Senator Kevin Cramer of North Dakota, have joined bipartisan calls for an investigation to determine the cause.
Addressing the matter, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately POTUS.”

articles.title: ​Europe stands by Ukraine – but how long can that last?
articles.body:
Europe woke up last Friday to another belligerent outburst from Donald Trump – this time berating Ukraine’s wartime leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy again. Just a few days after his diesel deal with the Kremlin, the US president said Zelenskyy was more difficult to deal with than Vladimir Putin and blamed Ukraine’s leader for rocketing oil prices – without any reference to the impact of his own war on Iran.
The contrast in Europe was obvious. When Zelenskyy walked into the multi-coloured summit room of the European Council headquarters in Brussels that Friday morning, the EU’s 27 leaders burst into applause, getting to their feet to offer big hugs and brisk handshakes. European Council president António Costa told Zelenskyy and the media: “This is no time to withdraw the support to Ukraine,” calling instead for increased pressure on Russia. Zelenskyy was thankful, pointedly saying he was happy to have “huge support” from “real leaders”.
The symbolism was powerful. As US support crumbles, Europe seems to be stepping up. According to the Kiel Institut’s Ukraine Support Tracker, Europe – including non-EU countries such as the UK and Norway – has spent €236bn supporting Ukraine from 2022 to April 2026, compared with a US outlay of €115bn.
While Trump is weakening sanctions, Europe is promising more. The EU has passed 21 rounds of sanctions against Russia and last year agreed to raise a €90bn loan for Ukraine – an unprecedented sum for a non-member state. Meanwhile the EU has opened accession negotiations with Kyiv and given shelter to 4.4million Ukrainian refugees.
Behind the declarations of Europe’s enduring support, the outlook is more complex and less encouraging for Ukraine, as it approaches its fifth winter since the launch of Russia’s all-out invasion.
First, Europe is not able to replace US military dominance in areas such as intelligence. This was brutally exposed by the disruption to the US SpaceX technologies that Ukraine uses in frontline drone operations and air-defences protecting civilians from Russian air attacks. Zelenskyy said the US had intentionally throttled its Starlink satellite internet access, a charge that senior figures in the Trump administration have denied.
Ukraine also depends on US-made Patriot interceptors capable of shooting down Russian ballistic missiles. Deepening the spat, Zelenskyy this week accused the Trump administration of preventing European countries from passing on their Patriot stocks to Ukraine.
Secondly, Europe’s monetary support for Ukraine is not evenly spread. Germany is the second-largest donor, having spent €54bn since the start of the war, a particularly crucial contribution since Trump ceased virtually all new US funding. But a report from the Kiel Institut describes this funding as “sizeable but not exceptional” given the scale of the German economy. Four Nordic countries together have given more than Germany, even though they total only a third of Germany’s population, the researchers note. The EU’s other big economies, France and Italy, give less than Germany.
The Nordic, Baltic and other north European states are Ukraine’s most generous donors when contributions are measured against national income, according to the Kiel Institut. Denmark, for instance, spends an equivalent to 4.17% of its gross domestic product supporting Ukraine, and Estonia 3.77%, compared with 1.49% spent by Germany, 1.1% by France, 1% by Italy and 0.86% by the UK. With Ukraine’s huge bill to defend itself growing, and Russia’s relentless attacks continuing to wreak a heavy toll, these more generous donors might arguably feel Europe’s biggest economies – and other western allies – could do more to shoulder these ever-rising costs.
Top donors to Ukraine by percentage of GDP
Thirdly, and most critically, Europe’s support for Ukraine could be reaching its limits, as Europe enters a supercycle of elections in which the far-right are expected to make gains. National votes are due in Spain, France, Poland and Italy, four of the five biggest EU member states by population. Mujtaba Rahman, managing director for Europe at the Eurasia Group, argued that the biggest risk for Ukraine is not Trump’s opinions, but the potential for European support to fragment. There is a risk 2027 will be the year “when political reality, electoral reality, policy reality, economic reality catches up with Europe and prevents it being able to go further in its support for Ukraine”, he said.
France’s elections could be the most consequential. The far-right leader and frontrunner Marine Le Pen is seeking to present herself as the candidate to restore order and security, after days of rioting and looting across French cities. She has also vowed to cease aid to Ukraine within six months of taking office “because we simply cannot do it any more”. Speaking to the Financial Times (£), Le Pen vowed to slash France’s contributions to the EU budget, which raises questions about a proposed €100bn fund for Ukraine in the upcoming 2028-34 budget cycle. Beyond Ukraine, her election could plunge the EU into a deep internal crisis that will consume political energies and attention.
Putin’s ‘strategic patience’ rewarded?
“European support for Ukraine is already fragmenting,” argued Rahman, who points out the €90bn loan for Ukraine was agreed by only 24 EU countries (Hungary, Czechia and Slovakia opted out). But a Le Pen victory could tilt the balance, especially if anti-Ukraine parties make gains in Spain, Poland and Italy. “Le Pen is the biggest gamechanger because she will provide cover for many other countries to say: ‘enough is enough, we can’t keep funding,’” Rahman said.
That scenario paints “a really dark picture for Ukraine, a really sad picture for Ukraine” he said. “Because it’s not about Ukraine’s performance on the battlefield – Ukraine has done a remarkable job of holding the line. This is the risk Europe has been talking about for a very long time, and has promised Ukraine many times it would not allow to happen: that through strategic patience, Russia gains in the negotiating room what it has not been able to gain on the battlefield. And that is precisely the risk Ukraine is now confronting.”
 
To head off this risk, EU leaders will seek to shore up support for Ukraine by agreeing another funding plan. The head of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, confirmed that Kyiv has a €70bn funding gap in 2027, although she expects Ukraine’s other international partners to help raise the sum.
Jana Kobzová, co-director of the European Security Programme at the European Council on Foreign Relations, said an EU leaders summit in December will be the moment when “we should have a clear idea and mechanism” on providing the €70bn for Ukraine ahead of key elections. “I think the urgency and the consciousness on the side of the European leaders is already there.”
To some extent, EU Russia policy is protected, after a recent decision to keep sanctions in place for three years, avoiding the need for divisive rollover decisions every six months.
But a Le Pen victory in six months’ time could lead to a bigger problem than financing Ukraine, suggests Kobzová. “If there is a huge shift in Europe as a result of these elections that are going to affect the way the EU itself works, then Ukraine might become collateral damage.”
Guardian live Q&A
At 3pm BST/4pm CEST on Friday 23 October, Guardian Europe columnists Rokhaya Diallo and Alexander Hurst will be live taking questions from our readers about the riots and protests in France. Click here to submit yours now, or join the discussion on Friday.

articles.title: The Kremlin wants Russian media to call attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure ‘Putin strikes.’ The inspiration? Stalin.
articles.body:
The Kremlin wants Russian media to call attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure ‘Putin strikes.’ The inspiration? Stalin.
Russia’s Presidential Administration has ordered state and Kremlin-aligned media outlets to begin writing about “Putin strikes” on Ukraine, two employees at such outlets told Meduza.
The Presidential Administration’s political bloc sent loyalist media recommendations advising them to report that “the effectiveness and efficiency of Russia’s strikes far exceed what the Ukrainian military has achieved.”
“Our ballistic weapons have performed flawlessly. The Ukrainian regime has lost its most important production and storage sites, where cruise missiles and drones, along with their components, were assembled and stored. ‘Putin strikes’ are far larger in scale and more effective than enemy attacks. We are shutting down the militants’ missile programs, which helps keep Russia’s regions secure,” the guidance document says.
Headlines, comments from servicemen, and articles using the phrase “Putin strikes” indeed appeared this week in major Russian media outlets.
For example, the Russian news website Gazeta.ru published an article with the following subheadline:
“SVO” veteran Konovalov: “Putin strikes” deprive the Ukrainian military of the ability to fight.
The outlet cites Vitaly Konovalov, head of the Association of Veterans of the Russia-Ukraine War in Stavropol Krai, who says the strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure are allegedly aimed at undermining supplies to the Ukrainian military. Notably, Konovalov himself never uses the phrase “Putin strikes.” It appears in the connecting phrases and generalizations added by propagandists.
Novye Izvestia published an article titled “Putin Strikes on Ukraine: Ukrainian Military Left Without Electricity and Weapons.” Rosbalt used the phrase in the headline of a news item titled “Putin Strikes on Ukraine: Ukrainian Military Losing Logistics Hubs, Substations, and Vessels.” It also appears in headlines and articles from Fedpress. Segodnia.ru writes about a “series of “Putin strikes.”” The phrase has even appeared in pro-government Instagram accounts.
A political consultant who works with the Presidential Administration’s political bloc said directly linking Putin to the strikes on Ukraine is meant to try to boost the president’s approval ratings.
According to polls by the Public Opinion Foundation (FOM), Putin’s approval rating fell from 75% in July to 71% in early October, while trust in him fell from 74% to 70% over the same period.
“In this case, [the idea is to raise the ratings] among the pro-war, ultra-patriotic segment of society, who need to be shown some successes from the war. To the question “What has been accomplished?” [at the front], the suggested answer is “Putin strikes,” by analogy with the “Stalinist strikes,”” the consultant said.
During Joseph Stalin’s rule, the term “Ten Stalinist Strikes” referred to 10 major Soviet army operations during World War II.
The source told Meduza that it is hard to assess how effective the appearance of “Putin strikes” in the press has been: “Maybe it will have some effect on the older segment [of society].”
Speaking at a press conference in Bishkek on September 1, following the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit, Vladimir Putin said he had ordered the Russian military to prepare and carry out massive strikes on Ukraine’s energy facilities. “They’re striking our people, so they’ll get a response,” he added.
In mid-October, discussing the Russian army’s strikes on Ukraine, Putin said:
They took the first step. We started responding. Now they’re whining about energy facilities too, and about other targets, including data centers and so on. They started it. They shouldn’t have started it.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].

articles.title: Lockheed Martin offers Ukraine its own version of the F-16
articles.body:
- Lockheed Martin is promoting a Ukraine-specific F-16 version with longer range and a new AESA radar, sources at the company told The Defence Blog.
- Zelenskyy met a Lockheed Martin team in Kyiv on Oct. 19, praising the F-16’s role against Shahed drones and calling for the program to continue.
Lockheed Martin is promoting the idea of a special version of the F-16 fighter built around Ukraine’s needs, with longer range, a new AESA radar and stronger air defense capabilities, sources at the company told The Defence Blog.
The idea is being floated as the U.S. defense giant expands its work with Kyiv, and it surfaced days after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met a Lockheed Martin team in Kyiv on Oct. 19 to discuss F-16 support and pilot training, the President’s Office said.
According to the sources, one option under consideration is a new F-16 variant with extended range and an AESA radar that would let pilots detect low-flying drones and cruise missiles earlier and faster than the radars on Ukraine’s current jets allow. The company is also looking at deeper integration of European weapons on the aircraft, including guided bombs and cruise missiles, which would give Ukraine more options than the mix of Western munitions its F-16s carry today.
No concrete negotiations on a new version are underway, the sources said, but the Ukrainian side has shown interest in an affordable, versatile fighter that its pilots have already mastered in combat. Lockheed Martin is counting on numerous joint projects with Ukraine, the sources added, and Zelenskyy said after the meeting that Kyiv wants the F-16 program to continue.
“It has been working from the first day the F-16 was used and still is today. Especially ahead of a difficult winter, during massive attacks with Shaheds, the F-16s destroy them. And we have a very good rate of destroying Shaheds. That is why we are very proud that we have this capability. Thank you very much. We are counting on the program continuing,” said Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
The F-16 has become the backbone of Ukraine’s air force since the first jets arrived in 2024, and the type now flies roughly 80 percent of all Ukrainian Air Force sorties, as we reported last year. One Ukrainian F-16 wing alone has been credited with downing more than 1,000 Russian Shahed-type drones and cruise missiles, and its vice commander told a U.S. audience that what Ukraine needed most was newer Block 70 jets and more missiles.
That request goes to the heart of the radar issue, since the F-16s that Ukraine received from European NATO members are older airframes upgraded under the Mid-Life Update program, which still rely on a mechanically scanned radar. Newer Block 70 aircraft use an AESA radar that can track more targets at longer range and is better at picking out small, low-flying objects such as drones and cruise missiles against the ground, which is the main threat Ukrainian pilots face during Russia’s mass overnight attacks.
At the Oct. 19 meeting, Zelenskyy also discussed work to let Ukraine service and repair its F-16s on its own territory, as well as larger deliveries of the anti-ballistic interceptors that Lockheed Martin builds for the Patriot air defense system, which the company is ramping up and part of which Kyiv hopes to buy. A Ukraine-specific F-16 would sit alongside the country’s other fighter plans, which include 16 Gripen E jets ordered from Sweden in June with deliveries from 2029 and a separate donation of Gripen C/D fighters, we reported at the time.
The sources did not say how much a dedicated Ukrainian variant would cost, how many aircraft could be involved, or which European weapons Lockheed Martin would prioritize for integration, and any such program would need approval from Washington before talks could move beyond the idea stage.

articles.title: Slovakia resumes talks with russia on energy supplies, moving away from the position of its EU allies - media
articles.body:
Slovakia resumes talks with russia on energy supplies, moving away from the position of its EU allies - media
Kyiv • UNN
For the first time since 2022, a meeting of the Russian-Slovak commission will take place in Moscow. They will discuss gas, oil, nuclear energy and cooperation.
Next week in Moscow, Slovakia will discuss the supply of Russian energy resources, resuming cooperation that was suspended after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. This step is another indication of the country’s departure from the position of its allies in the European Union and NATO, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Details
As Slovakia’s Ministry of Foreign and European Affairs reported late on Tuesday, a meeting of the Russian-Slovak intergovernmental commission on economic, scientific and technical cooperation will be held in Moscow on October 26. It will be the first such meeting since Russia’s attack on Ukraine in 2022.
According to ministry representatives, the meeting will focus on energy issues (including nuclear energy), as well as agriculture, environmental protection, sports and culture.
The publication notes that the resumption of consultations comes after several visits by Prime Minister Robert Fico to Moscow, including in May this year. Fico’s position stands out against the backdrop of the other 27 EU member states—especially after Hungary’s pro-Russian leader Viktor Orbán suffered defeat in the elections in April.
"Energy and opportunities for cooperation in ensuring the supply of strategic resources will be the key topic," the ministry said. "The Slovak side is also interested in discussing gas supplies and continuing oil supplies."
Slovakia, which purchases Russian oil and gas, is required under the EU plan to stop purchasing gas by the end of 2027. The plan is aimed at depriving Russia of the financial resources it uses to finance the war in Ukraine.
The ministry said that, while developing relations with Russia, Slovakia "continues to build its approach based on its membership in the European Union and the North Atlantic Alliance, as well as on fulfilling the obligations arising from that membership," but seeks to create space for dialogue.
In addition
Robert Fico—a populist and nationalist politician who is serving as prime minister of this Central European country for the fourth time—has repeatedly criticized EU sanctions against Russia. He also blamed Ukraine for disruptions in oil supplies to Slovakia that occurred earlier this year (while Kyiv said they were caused by Russian attacks).
Fico halted Slovakia’s provision of military aid to Ukraine, but the export of ammunition and military equipment continues on a commercial basis—including through state-owned companies. Fico said he would prefer Slovakia to be a neutral state rather than a member of NATO; he also said he does not want Slovak troops to take part in a war with Russia that could begin through the invocation of NATO’s collective defense provision.
In addition, he expressed the view that the West could provoke a confrontation with Russia, while Western intelligence services assert that the West’s actions are exclusively defensive in nature and warn of possible escalation by Russia.

articles.title: Poland has no Patriot missiles to spare for Ukraine
articles.body:
Poland has no Patriot missiles to spare for Ukraine
Poland does not have enough Patriot air defense missiles to hand over to Ukraine, Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski has said, urging other NATO members to supply Kiev with the scarce interceptors.
In an interview with the Polish Press Agency published on Monday, Sikorski warned of growing pressure on Western air defenses, citing the US-Israeli bombing campaign against Iran.
“Following the attacks on Iran, the shortage of interceptor missiles has indeed increased, and Russia is producing more missiles than we have interceptors to neutralize them. This is a real problem,” he said.
“There are NATO countries that still have such resources to contribute, but Poland is not one of them,” Sikorski said, adding that Warsaw “can only join the calls for countries possessing Patriot missiles to share them with Ukraine.”
The issue sparked a political scandal in Poland in July, when the government came under fire over the transfer of Patriot interceptors to Ukraine as part of a wider NATO-backed aid package. Opposition politicians accused Warsaw of sacrificing its own security to arm Kiev, while Prime Minister Donald Tusk insisted the deliveries would not compromise the country’s defenses.
Poland has emerged as one of the EU’s most rapidly militarizing nations, with defense spending reaching 4.7% of GDP. Warsaw has also been one of Kiev’s staunchest backers, pouring billions into military and other aid while serving as a crucial hub for Western arms shipments.
Yet Poland now faces delays in replenishing its own arsenal, with deliveries of US-made PAC-3 MSE Patriot interceptors pushed back as the war with Iran drains American weapons stocks, Polish General Ireneusz Nowak warned earlier this month.
Relations with Kiev have also soured over Ukraine’s honoring of Nazi collaborators linked to the World War II-era Volhynia massacres, in which Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) militants associated with the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN) killed an estimated 100,000 ethnic Poles. Warsaw recognizes the killings as genocide, while Kiev continues to honor figures including OUN leader Stepan Bandera.
Tensions flared again this year after Zelensky awarded a Ukrainian military unit the honorary title “Heroes of the UPA.” Polish President Karol Nawrocki subsequently stripped him of the country’s highest honor, politicians on both sides renounced state decorations, and Warsaw threatened to obstruct Ukraine’s EU accession.
The ammunition crunch is spreading across NATO. In July, the Netherlands said it had exhausted its capacity to supply Ukraine with Patriot missiles from its own stocks, having already provided interceptors and helped assemble a complete Patriot system for Kiev.
Meanwhile, Kiev is facing a critical shortage of air defense ammunition as Russia intensifies strikes on Ukrainian military and energy infrastructure. Moscow has said the attacks are in retaliation for Kiev’s continued strikes on Russian territory, including civilian targets and energy facilities.
Vladimir Zelensky has requested 300 Patriot interceptors from European backers and complained that Washington has approved only some of the missiles purchased through a NATO-backed initiative. The White House has also delayed approving additional transfers as US President Donald Trump presses Ukraine to reach a negotiated settlement with Russia.
Moscow has repeatedly maintained that Western weapons deliveries prolong the conflict, obstruct peace efforts, and risk drawing NATO countries into a direct confrontation with Russia.

articles.title: A ‘pipe dream of EU hawks’: What’s in Brussels’ new Arctic Strategy?
articles.body:
A ‘pipe dream of EU hawks’: What’s in Brussels’ new Arctic Strategy?
The EU has updated its Arctic strategy, and militarism has replaced climate activism as Brussels’ new preoccupation in the frozen north. Despite what the new strategy claims, however, the Arctic is not “the EU’s Northern Neighborhood.”
Unveiled on Tuesday by the European Commission, the ‘Strategy for the Arctic’ describes the region as a “critical” zone for trade, investment, and conservation, and a flashpoint for military confrontation with Russia.
Today, we adopt our new 🇪🇺 Arctic Strategy. The Arctic is where the tectonic plates of geopolitics collide head-on. It requires us to change our strategic posture. And work with like-minded partners that share our values ↓ https://t.co/B6GvgUOCQk
— Ursula von der Leyen (@vonderleyen) October 20, 2026
“With Russia and China increasing their footprint and ambition, the Arctic has become a front line of global power competition,” top EU diplomat Kaja Kallas said in a statement. “Our revamped Strategy reflects this new reality and puts security firmly at its core.”
To understand just how dramatic this new focus on security is, it’s necessary to turn back the clock to 2021, when the commission released its previous Arctic strategy.
The EU’s green past
Published on October 13, 2021, the strategy opened by describing climate change as “the most comprehensive threat the Arctic is facing.” Russia’s refurbishment of Soviet-era military bases along its Arctic coastline was presented primarily as something that could “further aggravate the consequences of climate change,” and the EU pledged to work with Moscow “to improve environmental and health security,” and to leave military relations with Russia up to NATO and individual member states.
Four months later, Brussels severed relations with Moscow and entered the Russia-Ukraine conflict on Kiev’s side. The title of the 2021 strategy – ‘A stronger EU engagement for a peaceful, sustainable and prosperous Arctic’ – needed an update that reflected the EU’s new militarism.
Brussels claims the Arctic
“Russia’s unprovoked and unjustified war of aggression against Ukraine has reshaped the security of the Arctic and the EU as a whole,” the new document opens, going on to assert that “the Arctic is not someone else’s frontier. It is Europe’s Northern Neighbourhood and the European Union is part of the Arctic.”
Geography is not exactly on Brussels’ side here. The 27-member union has no coastline on the Arctic Ocean, and only two of its members – Finland and Sweden – have territory inside the Arctic Circle (although a Danish dependency, Greenland left the EU in 1985). Russia accounts for 53% of the Arctic Ocean’s coastline, and 45% of all land inside the Arctic Circle.
To compensate for this, the new strategy proposes that all waters north of 60 degrees latitude be considered ‘Arctic’. The commission argues that this would allow its environmental regulations to “cover the actual footprint of Arctic shipping.” It would also dramatically expand the EU’s ‘Arctic’ territory and population by bringing almost all of Finland and Sweden into the new region, including Finland’s entire 1,340 kilometer border with Russia. It is on this frontier that the EU is preparing for conflict.
War preparations
The strategy sets out a lengthy list of military objectives, with the commission promising to:
- “Deepen engagement with NATO” and hold military exercises focused on moving troops and equipment into the Arctic
- Develop military logistics corridors from central Europe to the Arctic
- Upgrade ports and airports for military use
- Expand icebreaker capacity
- Expand satellite surveillance of the region and tracking of Russian oil tankers
- Develop polar-capable undersea drones
- Establish a “Maritime Security Hub” and increase data-sharing with NATO
- Deepen military ties with Canada, Iceland, Norway, the UK, and US
The strategy is short on some specifics, and almost all of these goals are presented without an accompanying price tag. The only actual figures listed are €260 million for ten existing European Defence Fund projects, €107 million toward the construction of an undersea internet cable to Greenland, and the €200 million Greenland ‘Partnership Package’, which was announced last month. Although the commission says that this investment package will “support resilience, security and peace in the Arctic,” none of the €200 million in funding is earmarked for explicitly military projects.
Even though these objectives make up more of a wishlist than a set of concrete commitments, one in particular has the potential to push tensions with Russia to the breaking point. The strategy states that the EU will use its ‘Copernicus’ satellite network to track Russian “shadow fleet vessels,” thus making it easier for EU states to interdict and seize them. Belgium, Estonia, Finland, France, and Sweden have detained 12 of these vessels since December 2024, a number that would likely increase with the aid of satellite surveillance.
‘Shadow fleet’ is an EU euphemism for tankers carrying Russian oil in international waters. Russian oil exporters do not abide by EU sanctions, nor do importers outside the EU. Nevertheless, EU member states have abrogated the authority to seize them, in what the Kremlin considers “flagrant violation of international law” and “outright piracy and robbery.”
Should the seizures continue, Russian President Vladimir Putin has threatened to respond in kind.
The ‘hybrid war’ deception
The EU’s militarization of the Arctic is justified, the document states, as Russia is “pursuing hybrid strategies against its neighbours… from drone incursions and Global Navigation Satellite System jamming to the sabotage of undersea cables.” In the absence of real, verifiable military action by Russia against Europe, EU and NATO leaders have taken to accusing Moscow of waging “hybrid war,” describing drone sightings, fires, and accidents at weapons factories, protests, and even natural disasters as Kremlin-orchestrated plots to destabilize the West.
A wave of “drone incursions” across northern Europe and Scandinavia last year turned out to be a hoax, with Belgium’s defense minister attempting to pass off a photograph of a police helicopter as a ‘Russian drone’. Around the same time, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s PR team lied about Russia “interfering” with her jet’s navigation systems over Bulgaria. Western spy chiefs have since admitted there is no evidence that Russia has sabotaged undersea power and internet cables.
Nevertheless, claims of ‘hybrid war’ have persisted in European politics and media, to the point where some analysts view the claims themselves as a form of “hybrid warfare” against the European public, used to justify military spending hikes and welfare cutbacks.
“When you are sure it is the Russians, or almost sure it is the Russians, attribute it to the Russians,” NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte advised the bloc’s political leaders and intelligence chiefs earlier this month.
Russia has been holding military exercises in the Arctic for decades, and the refurbishment of its Soviet-era bases in the region has been underway since before the EU published its 2021 Arctic strategy. However, the newly militarized EU is no longer content to handle this matter through old mechanisms – namely the Arctic Council – and insists that countering Russia in the north is its responsibility as well as NATO’s.
The Europeans dictate their terms
The EU’s new strategy calls on Russia to “ensure that freedom of navigation is preserved” along the Northern Sea Route (NSR), a formerly impassable navigation corridor that can now be traversed year-round, thanks to receding polar ice caps and the assistance of Russia’s vast icebreaker fleet. The NSR cuts transit time from China to northern Europe in half, and in August, the first Chinese container ship arrived at the port of Murmansk via this route.
The NSR skims along more than 24,000 km of Russian coastline, and through internationally recognized Russian territorial waters. Russia is the only state capable of rendering assistance to any ships passing through the route, and vessels wishing to pass in winter must pay to be escorted by Russian icebreakers. Moscow retains the right to deny any ships access to the NSR.
Nevertheless, the EU insists that it has a say over Russian maritime policy, even as it vows to “continue to sanction the shadow fleet entering from the Northern Sea Route” and place Russian shipping under satellite surveillance. The latest Arctic strategy states that the EU will “actively engage” with other nations to ensure freedom of navigation in the Arctic, but omits any possibility of engagement with Russia. Only “like-minded partners,” a term mentioned nearly two dozen times in the document, will be consulted.
Diplomatic and economic disputes in the Arctic were previously handled at the Arctic Council. However, seven of the council’s eight members – every one except Russia – stopped participating in high-level Council meetings in March 2022. That same month, the EU joined Finland, Denmark, Iceland, Norway, and Sweden in suspending any activities involving Russia within the separate Barents Euro-Arctic Council.
The EU’s Arctic delusion
The central fallacy of the EU’s Arctic strategy is that it presumes Brussels can regulate, with laws or with arms, what Russia does in its own back yard. It presumes that the bloc, which has no Arctic coastline, can ignore long-established forums for cooperation and directly dictate terms to a superpower that controls half of the Arctic’s land and sea area; and that by repeating the mantra “the Arctic is the EU’s northern neighborhood,” it can overcome geographic reality and the massive power differential between Russia and everyone else in the region.
In a message released by its embassy in the Netherlands on Tuesday, the Russian Foreign Ministry described the document as “another pipe dream of EU hawks.”
“A quick reality check: Russia operates a fleet of 40+ icebreakers. How many does the EU have in total?” the ministry asked. “The Arctic should be a place of cooperation, not confrontation. Maybe it’s time to stop the provocations?”

articles.title: 29 Russian Troops Captured, 108 Eliminated, 1,100+ Targets Hit: Ukraine’s HUR Summarizes Sumy Operation
articles.body:
Ukraine’s military intelligence special forces cleared more than 600 hectares (1,480 acres) of forest of Russian troops during a seven-week operation in the Sumy region, thwarting Russian offensive plans.
The Main Directorate of Intelligence (HUR) announced the operation on Telegram on Oct. 20, saying fighters from the “GROUP 10” unit of its Department of Active Operations captured 29 Russian soldiers, neutralized 108 others and struck more than 1,100 targets.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The primary objective has been achieved!” HUR said, adding that the operation prevented Russian forces from cutting off logistical routes.
The operation lasted approximately seven weeks and consisted of two phases, according to the report. Forty special forces personnel took part in active combat operations.
During the operation, HUR operatives also destroyed Russian drone command posts, artillery systems, vehicles and fortifications. After clearing the forest, the special forces handed the positions over to Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
A video released alongside the report shows footage from the operation, including Ukrainian troops taking Russian soldiers prisoner. Kyiv Post has been unable to independently verify when or where the footage was filmed.
Russian activity increases along Sumy border
The operation comes amid reports of increased Russian activity along Ukraine’s northern border.
On Oct. 21, Andrii Demchenko, spokesperson for Ukraine’s State Border Guard Service, said Russian sabotage and reconnaissance groups (DRG) had become more active over the previous several weeks, primarily in the Sumy region and also along the border in Chernihiv region.
Russia Has Up to 700 Ballistic Missiles, 6,200 Attack Drones Ready to Strike Ukraine, Intelligence Says
Ukrainian forces are deploying anti-sabotage reserves and technical equipment to detect the groups and prevent them from carrying out their plans, Demchenko said.
He also reported a slight increase in attacks by Russian infantry groups in Sumy, particularly in the Shostka and Konotop districts. However, the intensity of Russian troop deployments in the region remains below that in the Kharkiv region, he added.
“If Russia manages to secure additional resources – primarily in terms of manpower – we should expect that attacks within the Sumy region could also intensify,” Demchenko said.
In late September, Demchenko had also warned that Russian forces were repeatedly attempting to expand their zone of control near Ukrainian defensive positions in the Shostka and Konotop districts and the Yunakivka community.

articles.title: Maybe it’s personal: Europeans worry Trump just likes Putin more than Zelenskyy
articles.body:
Maybe it’s personal: Europeans worry Trump just likes Putin more than Zelenskyy
After 20 months of upheaval in transatlantic relations, EU officials fear the U.S. president dislikes Ukraine’s leader too much to push for a fair peace.
U.S. President Donald Trump and Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy are pictured on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Sept. 22, 2026. | Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images
In a throwaway comment this week, Donald Trump made clear that he does not regard the war in Ukraine as a conflict with fault on both sides. “Russia frankly has been fine on Ukraine,” the U.S. president said. “They have not been doing that much.”
To residents of Kyiv — who have endured weeks of intensifying bombardment — and Ukraine’s allies across Europe, the remark confirmed a growing impression that the U.S. is taking Russia leader Vladimir Putin’s side in the war.
“American negotiators have been trying to push Ukraine into surrender for already almost two years,” the EU’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas told the European Parliament on Tuesday. The reason Ukraine hasn’t “surrendered on Putin’s terms” so far is because Europe has been providing so much support, she added.
Advertisement
As they scratch their heads for explanations for Trump’s latest turn against Ukraine, some European officials and diplomats think it comes down to the president’s personal preferences, as much as his country’s political aims.
“I do think it’s a personal thing,” said former British Cabinet minister David Lidington, now distinguished fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, a leading security think tank in London. “Trump is self-centered — his personal predilections for dictators and autocrats, his desire to give opportunities to U.S. businesses … are very important parts of his motivation.”
In private, EU officials agree. “Trump doesn’t like [Ukrainian President Volodymyr] Zelenskyy. He just doesn’t like him,” said one government official who has observed both men closely. “That makes it harder to get the U.S. to help on peace. Everything is a rational business deal with Trump, until it’s not.”
A diplomat from an EU country — granted anonymity, like others in this report, to discuss sensitive matters — said the inconsistent Trump could change his mind again and reverse recent moves against Ukraine. The U.S. president has chopped and changed on many issues, “except one thing,” the diplomat said. “He seems to be supportive of the Russians.”
“He’s been critical of Ukraine, the EU, NATO, but hardly ever said anything critical about Putin. It is striking. We have to deal with an administration that seems to be more pro-Russian than anything else,” the diplomat said.
The White House didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
Advertisement
Mounting losses
For Ukraine and its European allies, the idea that nothing can or will change Trump’s feelings about Zelenskyy is a bleak one. After four-and-a-half years of war, Kyiv is running low on funding, air defenses and — amid swelling support for Europe’s populist right — facing a potential loss of political support in the months ahead.
Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff met the Ukrainian president and the leaders of Norway and Finland for talks in Oslo on Tuesday, and will head to St. Petersburg to discuss peace proposals with the Russian leadership on Wednesday as the White House pushes hard for a ceasefire. One option Putin will be offered is a three-way leaders’ summit with Trump and Zelenskyy.
Previous efforts to get the Russian president to attend such a meeting have failed, however, and EU diplomats do not believe Putin is showing any genuine desire for a ceasefire. That is partly what makes Trump’s hostility toward Zelenskyy so problematic.
“There is a clear consensus across Europe that Putin does not want peace,” a second EU diplomat said. “He will need to be forced into peace.”
Trump greets Russian President Vladimir Putin as he arrives for talks in Anchorage, Alaska, on Aug. 15, 2025. | Andrew Harnik/Getty Images
But instead of making demands of Putin, Trump has ratcheted up his pressure on Zelenskyy, even amid escalating Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities this month. Ukraine’s leader is feeling the strain, as he told his EU counterparts in private meetings in Brussels last week, according to the first diplomat.
In a succession of highly critical comments in recent days, Trump has said Zelenskyy “doesn’t care” and “doesn’t want to end this war;” and should be replaced as leader or as Ukraine’s negotiator. “President Putin would like to see a settlement,” Trump said. “President Zelenskyy could have solved this war, or he could have made a deal, many times.”
Advertisement
The Oval Office beating
Trump’s animosity may date back to an incident during his first term in 2019, when he urged the Ukrainian leader to help with an investigation into Joe Biden, who eventually defeated Trump in the following presidential election, Lidington said. A succession of hostile encounters in the years since — including in the Oval Office in February 2025 — have reinforced the impression, he said.
“It was clear that in the infamous meeting in the White House that Trump and [Vice President JD] Vance had planned that public beating-up of Zelenskyy and it struck me then that there was a strong personal element to this,” said Lidington.
“I think there’s another element, which is that if you look at the people Trump tries to court, it tends to be autocratic strongman — and it is ‘man’ — leaders,” Lidington said.
He recalled attending a dinner with world leaders in 2018 to mark the centenary of the end of World War I in Paris. French President Emmanuel Macron and the German chancellor at the time, Angela Merkel, were playing joint hosts “at the top table,” but Trump was not interested in making small talk with either of them, Lidington said.
“It was pretty obvious from the body language that Trump was impatient with them and one of the people he really wanted to talk to was [Turkish leader Recep Tayyip] Erdoğan and other people who were a bit more in that strongman image that he likes to portray himself,” he observed.
‘Strange stories’
A senior official from a European country familiar with the Ukraine talks said Trump’s motives were partly political, partly about calculating what would be profitable and partly about personalities.
Advertisement
“They are currently in an election cycle and need someone to blame for rising prices,” the official said. “In general, Trump tends to like various types of people and leaders. He actually has a fondness for successful and cheerful people.”
In recent days, Zelenskyy has warned his country is suffering more civilian casualties because the U.S. has cut back on support, including Starlink and Starshield services that help Ukraine defend itself against Russian attacks and plan operations. “We still have no explanation for this, just different strange stories,” Zelenskyy told U.S. congressmen on Monday.
This month, the advanced warnings of incoming Russian missile attacks from U.S. partners have failed to come through as normal. Ukraine is also running low on Patriot missile interceptors, he said.
The Pentagon has not issued an official comment on the Ukrainian complaints. The U.N. Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine said 328 civilians were killed and more than 2,000 wounded across Ukraine last month, an 85% increase compared to September 2025. The U.N. said that the first two weeks of October were among the deadliest for civilians in Ukraine in years, driven by increased missile and drone strikes.
The first EU diplomat quoted above said many European governments were irritated that Trump had cut them out of his conversations with Putin so far. “There is probably much more dialogue between the Americans and the Russians than we might know,” the diplomat said.
Tuesday’s meeting with Witkoff in Norway raised the possibility that direct engagement with Putin might be back on the cards, for Zelenskyy at least.
“Today was a good day for peace,” Finland’s President Alexander Stubb said after attending the talks in Oslo. “On a substantive and technical level we have actually made a lot of progress under the radar in the past week or so,” Stubb said.
The process is now going in the right direction again, he added. “Hopefully, we don’t do any backtracking.”

articles.title: Lockheed Martin Wants to Build Ukraine Its Own F-16 to Hunt Russian Drones and Missiles
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Lockheed Martin Wants to Build Ukraine Its Own F-16 to Hunt Russian Drones and Missiles
US defense manufacturer Lockheed Martin is considering a specialized version of the F-16 fighter jet for Ukraine, featuring extended flight range, upgraded radar systems, and improved capabilities to intercept Russian drones and cruise missiles.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Defence Blog on October 21, citing sources within Lockheed Martin, the proposed aircraft could feature an active electronically scanned array (AESA) radar and expanded compatibility with European-made weapons.
The proposal remains at an early stage, with no formal negotiations underway. However, Ukrainian officials have reportedly expressed interest in obtaining a modern, cost-effective fighter based on an aircraft already operated by Ukrainian pilots.
One of the main improvements under consideration is an AESA radar capable of detecting and tracking multiple targets, including small drones and low-flying cruise missiles, more effectively than the mechanically scanned radars installed on Ukraine’s existing F-16s.
Ukraine currently operates older F-16 aircraft transferred by European NATO members. These fighters have undergone modernization but lack some of the advanced systems available on newer Block 70 variants.
Lockheed Martin is also exploring the integration of additional European weapons, including precision-guided bombs and cruise missiles, potentially expanding the aircraft’s operational flexibility.
The proposal follows an October 19 meeting in Kyiv between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Lockheed Martin representatives, during which the parties discussed F-16 maintenance, pilot training, and further cooperation.
During the meeting, Zelenskyy emphasized the aircraft’s role in intercepting Russian aerial attacks, particularly Shahed-type drones.
“It has been working from the first day the F-16 was used and still is today. Especially ahead of a difficult winter, during massive attacks with Shaheds, the F-16s destroy them. And we have a very good rate of destroying Shaheds. That is why we are very proud that we have this capability. Thank you very much. We are counting on the program continuing,” Zelenskyy said.
