articles.title: Trump may completely halt the supply of Patriot missiles to Ukraine – NATO warns of the risks
articles.body:
Trump may completely halt the supply of Patriot missiles to Ukraine – NATO warns of the risks
Kyiv • UNN
NATO fears a complete halt to U.S. arms deliveries to Ukraine due to tensions between Zelenskyy and Trump. Patriot deliveries are already being delayed.
NATO representatives warned Ukrainian officials about the risk of a complete halt to the supply of U.S. weapons, including missiles for Patriot systems, due to deteriorating relations between Presidents Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Donald Trump. Bloomberg reports this, citing informed sources, writes UNN.
Details
According to the publication, the Alliance's leadership fears that relations between Kyiv and Washington could deteriorate completely. NATO representatives are urging the Ukrainian side to reduce tensions in its communication with the Trump administration in order to avoid further restrictions on military aid.
The PURL program, under which European countries purchase U.S. weapons for Ukraine, is a particular concern. The United States currently supplies only about 12 Patriot interceptor missiles per month, four times fewer than during Joe Biden's presidency.
U.S. delaying deliveries of missiles already paid for by European allies
Zelenskyy previously stated that U.S. missiles were arriving irregularly, despite European partners having already paid for the corresponding deliveries. In addition, according to him, the Pentagon failed several times to warn Ukraine about Russian missile attacks.
The situation is complicated by limited stocks of U.S. interceptors. According to Mark Cancian, an expert at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, the United States has approximately 800 Patriot missiles. At the same time, the Pentagon seeks to preserve reserves for operations in the Middle East and a potential conflict with China.
As The Washington Post previously reported, Washington is also delaying approval of the transfer of Patriot missiles to Ukraine from European countries. According to the publication's sources, U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has neither approved nor rejected the relevant requests, leaving them without a final decision.

articles.title: Pentagon Starting with Resilient Energy for Sweeping ‘FORTRESS America’ Project
articles.body:
Looking to make a quick start on Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s sweeping “FORTRESS America” program to make every military base in the U.S. more self sufficient, the Pentagon is dialing up its efforts in an area the Air Force has been working for several years: energy resilience and independence.
Hegseth unveiled FORTRESS—a long-winded acronym for Federal Operations for Resilience, Troop Resources, Energy, Supply, and Survivability—during his Sept. 30 “State of the Force” speech, and in a subsequent memo outlined five “pillars” of the effort: energy independence; supply chain and defense industrial base resilience; a strategic defense reserve; installation hardening and cyber resilience; and resilience in space and spectrum.
At an Oct. 20 Defense Writers Group roundtable, a senior U.S. defense official said that first pillar is a key early priority.
“That’s absolutely what we’re moving on, is on the energy side of that, comprehensively,” he said, adding: “This is not a wait-and-see kind of a thing. We want to move out pretty quickly to get to that energy [resilience]. Those solutions can include investments in microgrids, battery backup storage.”
Other pillars may take years, the official acknowledged; another of Hegseth’s initiatives, the Next Great American Base project to build a new military base from scratch, will likely act as a “pilot” for ideas to feed into FORTRESS America, he added.
But “first and foremost, it’s doing the assessments of the installations to make sure we understand power generation and where we’re going to go with that, and then getting those deployed,” the official said.
There are already plenty of ideas and projects in the works to address energy resilience—officials have recognized that many bases are reliant on the civilian grid for electricity and water, and adversaries have figured out ways to hack or attack those grids. A ransomware attack shut down the Colonial Pipeline in 2021, causing fuel shortages and panic up and down the East Coast. In 2024, U.S. intelligence agencies warned that Chinese hackers were working to preposition themselves in the cyber networks for critical infrastructure like water and electrical grids. And both the wars in Ukraine and with Iran have featured plenty of attacks on energy infrastructure.
“The attack, as we know it, will not look like an attack,” former Air Force Assistant Secretary for Energy, Installations, and the Environment Ravi Chaudhary told Air & Space Forces Magazine. “It will look like a systematic shutdown of community capabilities. Our adversaries are going to start with making it hard to get on base, and they’ll go for the softest targets they can, which won’t be military. It will be public works.”
Back in 2021, the Department of the Air Force released an Installation Energy Strategic Plan warning of the possibility of extended power disruptions lasting 30 or more days, due to severe weather or cyberattacks. Around that same time, Congress mandated that the Pentagon work to make 99.9 percent of the energy load required for critical missions resilient, and Air Force bases started running Energy Resilience Readiness Exercises—essentially pulling the plug on bases and seeing how units, commanders, and backup systems responded.
Increasingly, officials started looking at building “microgrids”—power sources outside of the larger civilian energy grid. In 2022, the Air Force started work on a project to build a nuclear microreactor at Eielson Air Force Base, Alaska. Kadena Air Base in Japan deployed a microgrid with generators and solar power in 2023. More nuclear microreactors may be going to Buckley Space Force Base, Colo., and Malmstrom Air Force Base, Mont., under a program with the Defense Innovation Unit.
Chaudhary, who served in the Biden administration, also came aboard in 2023 and helped author the Department of the Air Force’s 2024 Installation Infrastructure Action Plan. Among its action items was a direction to install microgrids at two Space Force bases and 14 Air Force bases by fiscal 2030.
FORTRESS America is wildly more ambitious—Hegseth said in his speech that “every major military installation in America is going to generate its own power, independent of the civilian grid.”
Hegseth did not specify how long that would take or how much money would be devoted to that goal, and the senior U.S. defense official noted Oct. 20 that details are still being worked out as the officials consider the needs of around 500 bases in the continental United States.
“The assessment timeline that we’re in right now is trying to determine what is this going to cost,” the official said.
The assessment isn’t as simple as multiplying the cost of a nuclear microreactor by 500, the official said. Indeed, it could take decades to fully achieve the objective. To move as quickly as possible, the Pentagon aims to used a variety of solutions tailored the the particular needs of each base—including renewable options like geothermal and solar energy, as well as fossil fuels like natural gas, the official said.
Chaudhary agrees with that approach.
“We need to acknowledge this reality that our bases are not a monolith, and they’re vulnerable in different ways, and our adversaries have demonstrated the capability and intent to attack our installations in kinetic and nonkinetic ways,” he said.
While not every base is the same, one that might prove instructive to the entire FORTRESS America effort is Tyndall Air Force Base, Fla. After Hurricane Michael wreaked catastrophic damage on the base in 2018, the Air Force considered walking away completely before deciding to rebuild Tyndall as its “Base of the Future.” That included infrastructure hardened against the worst storms, but also a microgrid, advanced facilities, and more. Chaudhary sees it as a model for many of the elements of FORTRESS America.
“My general thought is that in some way, shape, or form, the Base of the Future of Tyndall is going to be replicated in this new strategy by the Department of War,” he said.
The senior U.S. defense official praised Tyndall’s “very, very thoughtful design work” and seemed to indicate the “Base of the Future” would indeed influence the new program.
“They are incorporating a lot of the things that we ask them: microgrids, smart systems, their ability to to do preventative maintenance by a centralized hub, so they can see across all their facilities and know when things are going to go down,” the official said. “Those are technologies and things that we want to invest into all of our installations, so that we can not only reduce costs, but more importantly, it increases the life of the facility, so that we’re making better investments in the time frame to keep those.”
All that work on Tyndall wasn’t cheap though—the Air Force has spent $5 billion or so restoring the base. And while not every base will need to be rebuilt from the wreckage of a hurricane, the cost of FORTRESS America figures to be scores of billions of dollars, if not hundreds of billions.
To bear that cost, both Chaudhary and the senior defense official cited the need for public-private partnerships.
“We’re a capital-intensive country,” Chaudhary said. “How do we leverage that capital to best serve our national security needs? And that really lends itself to public-private partnerships.”
The defense official wondered: “Are there other partnerships, other ways to make these investments that they’re valid and viable … Are there other means by which I can do private investment, other public things? … All of that is what we’re working on right now through the FORTRESS team to get that assessment.”

articles.title: Ukraine Counts on Beijing’s ‘Constructive Role’ as Sybiha Meets Chinese Ambassador
articles.body:
As the Kremlin claimed China is already preparing a trilateral summit with Russia and the US, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha met Beijing’s ambassador in Kyiv to discuss further steps Beijing could take toward a just peace.
The meeting focused largely on reviving bilateral dialogue ahead of the 35th anniversary of diplomatic relations between the two countries, Ukraine’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement on Wednesday, Oct. 21.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Political contacts and visits, as well as additional coordination in international organizations, growing trade and wider access to the Chinese market for Ukrainian goods were also on the agenda.
“The Ukrainian side is counting on Beijing to play a constructive role,” the ministry said, adding that Sybiha thanked the ambassador and his staff for continuing work in Kyiv despite daily large-scale Russian attacks.
Beijing prepares for a trilateral summit
Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov claimed that China was already preparing a meeting among the Russian, US and Chinese leaders. The idea was reportedly brought up during talks between Russian President Vladimir Putin and senior US envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg on the same day. None of the three capitals had rejected it.
“The hosts of the APEC summit will take charge – or rather, are already taking charge – of the preparations,” Ushakov said according to Interfax-Russia on Wednesday.
“And, should circumstances prove favorable, they – our Chinese friends – will certainly incorporate this meeting into the program of events in Shenzhen,” he continued.
‘We Need to Move On’: Zelensky Won’t Wait in Oslo for Witkoff After Putin Meeting
Neither Washington nor Beijing has publicly confirmed this account, and Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning previously said on Oct. 19 that China has no information on the rumored trilateral meeting.
Meanwhile, President Volodymyr Zelensky warned against excluding Ukraine on Tuesday, Oct. 20, insisting Kyiv must participate in any talks concerning its sovereignty and the war’s outcome.
According to the Wall Street Journal on Oct. 19, Putin first proposed the format during an Oct. 9 telephone call with US President Donald Trump, hoping to settle the war with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping on terms favorable to Moscow.
During that same telephone discussion, Trump struck a controversial diesel deal with Russia that led to a week of escalated tensions between Kyiv and Washington.
The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit will be held in Shenzhen on Nov. 18-19, Bloomberg reported, noting that the Russian president rarely travels abroad because of security concerns – primarily Western sanctions and a 2023 International Criminal Court (ICC) arrest warrant.
However, he plans to attend the summit in person for the first time since 2017.
Moscow open to talks with Kyiv
Ushakov also said, according to Russian state-owned media TASS, that Putin told Witkoff Russia was “in principle, ready to resume” trilateral negotiations with Ukraine and the US in November.
Moscow wants the talks to focus on postwar security arrangements for Russia and Ukraine, he said.
Witkoff had arrived with documents outlining approaches to ending the war, developed during his talks with Zelensky, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb in Oslo, Norway on Oct. 20.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Putin would review the proposals, while Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov ruled out political concessions.
Beijing – Moscow’s longstanding partner
Although China presented itself as neutral in Russia’s war, its military and economic ties with Russia have continued to deepen since the full-scale invasion was launched in 2022.
Ukraine’s Military Intelligence (HUR) told Kyiv Post in July that more than 550 Chinese service members have trained at Russian military institutions, while over 180 Russian troops completed similar internships in China in November 2025 alone.
China was also the largest buyer of Russian fossil fuels in August, at €8.4 billion ($9.7 billion), according to the Center for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA).
Cut off from Western technology by the European sanctions, Russia has increasingly turned to Chinese suppliers.
Chinese components, including turbo-jet engines, have helped Moscow build faster Shahed-type drones that are significantly harder for Ukraine to intercept due to their speed, able to reach 400-600 kilometers per hour (250-370 miles per hour).
On Oct. 16, The Insider reported that Shenzhen Xingkai Technology, a Chinese company, offered to supply nearly $2.9 million worth of communications equipment for attack drones, potentially helping Russian unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) operate deeper inside Ukraine.
The offer included 500 mesh modems to a factory in Russia’s Alabuga special economic zone.
Days prior, Zelensky warned that Beijing is assisting Russia’s efforts in building their own domestic Starlink rival, “Rassvet.” The system, still under development, could strengthen military communications, reconnaissance capabilities, and long-range drone operations.
“It is a pity that China is not on our side in this war – politically. It is not even about weapons,” Zelensky said on Sept. 17, noting that Beijing has enough influence to push Putin to the negotiating table, but chooses not to.

articles.title: Putin orders release of jailed American as he meets Trump envoy for Ukraine talks
articles.body:
Vladimir Putin ordered the release of an American man from a Russian jail as he met Donald Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg on Wednesday for fresh talks on ending the war in Ukraine, amid increasingly close relations between Moscow and Washington.
Trump had previously asked Putin to free Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old former teacher who had spent more than four years in Russian jails on charges of fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine.
His release appeared to be Moscow’s latest calculated move to bring Trump further into line with Putin’s position on Ukraine, while offering the US president a diplomatic victory before the midterm elections.
Hubbard was released unilaterally by Russia, rather than as part of a prisoner exchange as has often been the case with previous releases of Americans held in the country.
Writing on social media after the release was announced, Trump said it followed a request he had made “directly” to Putin last week.
He wrote on Truth Social: “The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return – an unprecedented situation for Russia … There was no ‘swap’ necessary for this release.”
Witkoff, meanwhile, lavished praise on Putin during their meeting at the grand Constantine Palace in St Petersburg, describing the Russian president as a humanitarian.
“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian. You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that,” Witkoff told Putin. He also conveyed Trump’s thanks for a deal to resume Russian diesel exports to the US.
The Russian president is wanted by the international criminal court (ICC) as a war criminal, in relation to the deportation of Ukrainian children to Russia during the war.
More than 17,500 civilians have been confirmed killed in Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, according to the UN, which says the true toll is likely to be significantly higher.
The warmth of Witkoff’s remarks stood in stark contrast to the increasingly hostile rhetoric directed at Volodymyr Zelenskyy by senior US officials, most notably Trump, who has called for the Ukrainian president to resign and portrayed him as the main obstacle to peace.
Witkoff travelled to Russia from Oslo, where he had met Zelenskyy and European leaders a day earlier in an attempt to inject momentum into stalled negotiations, with Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine now in its fifth year.
Witkoff told Putin during a televised portion of their meeting: “We’ve brought some papers. It’s really some ideas, some sort of peace deal between Russia and Ukraine, and you’ll read that at your leisure.”
The visit was Witkoff’s ninth to Russia since Trump tasked him with brokering an end to the war.
Witkoff described his meeting with Putin as “constructive” but said “important work” remained and trilateral talks between the US, Russia and Ukraine “at the technical level” would follow.
The Kremlin said it had agreed “in principle” to the talks, which would focus on how to guarantee the security of Ukraine and Russia once the war ended.
The latest rupture in relations between Washington and Kyiv was triggered by Trump’s surprise decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel as part of a deal with Putin, followed by his call for Zelenskyy to be replaced after Ukraine refused to halt its strikes on Russian oil refineries.
Kyiv has since complained of disruptions to US intelligence-sharing and restrictions on its access to Starshield, the military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite network.
Zelenskyy said on Tuesday that Washington had resumed providing advance warnings of Russian missile attacks after his meeting with Witkoff in Oslo.
But Ukraine continues to face restrictions on Starshield, although it remains unclear who ordered them. The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday that Musk had personally ordered the slowdown, while Reuters, citing sources, said the directive had come from inside the White House.
During Wednesday’s meeting with Witkoff, Putin thanked Trump and his wife, Melania, for “their attention to efforts to end the war”.
Yet there are few signs of an imminent breakthrough. Despite repeated Ukrainian calls for a ceasefire, including a halt to attacks on energy infrastructure, Moscow has given little indication that it intends to end its bombardment of Ukraine as winter approaches, apparently confident that continued pressure will help it extract greater concessions from Kyiv.
The Russian leader remains intent on sticking to his maximalist war aims, including his demand for full Russian control of Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region.
Putin also sought to emphasise the prospects for closer economic ties between Russia and the US once the war ends, suggesting that Moscow could significantly increase its exports of fertilisers to the American market.
Russian officials said the first tanker carrying diesel to the US would depart on Thursday as part of an initial shipment of about 300,000 tonnes.
Energy analysts and traders have questioned whether Trump’s agreement to temporarily resume Russian diesel imports will deliver meaningful relief to US consumers before the midterm elections, arguing that the volumes involved are too small to significantly ease the global supply squeeze.
The talks on Wednesday also touched on a possible meeting in China next month between Putin, Trump and the Chinese president, Xi Jinping. The Kremlin said Beijing was already making preparations for what it described as an unprecedented summit between the three leaders.

articles.title: Rubio: Musk Sets Ukraine’s Starlink Access, Not White House
articles.body:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Wednesday, Oct. 21, that decisions about Ukraine’s access to Starlink rest with SpaceX and Elon Musk rather than the White House, amid conflicting accounts of restrictions affecting Ukrainian military operations.
Speaking to reporters during a visit to India, Rubio said a private commercial contract governs the service, Reuters reported.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The agreement determines “how their stuff can be used and what speeds they’ll allow it to be used at,” he said.
Rubio said he was not aware that the administration knew about the decision beforehand. Musk and SpaceX did not respond to Reuters’ requests for comment.
WSJ says Musk ordered the restrictions
The remarks followed a Wall Street Journal report published on Tuesday, Oct. 20, which said Musk ordered restrictions on the military-grade satellite service used by Ukraine, citing US officials and people familiar with the matter.
The newspaper said the decision disrupted Ukrainian offensive and interceptor drones and caused confusion inside the Trump administration.
Accounts differed over the timing of discussions with Trump. One source said Musk, Trump, and White House officials discussed the matter before the restrictions, while two said Musk and the president discussed it afterward.
Reuters has separately cited two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter as saying the decision ultimately came from the White House. The administration has denied that account.
Kyiv Mayor Klitschko Accuses Government of Staging Anti-Mayor Protest
Conflicting accounts from Washington and Musk
Trump previously denied ordering the restrictions and said he did not think Musk was responsible either.
His comments came despite Ukrainian reports that satellite connections were failing during military operations. Kyiv has repeatedly sought an explanation and the restoration of full service.
Musk, meanwhile, said on Oct. 14 that limits on Ukraine’s military Starshield terminals were determined by the US military and ultimately the president.
The distinction between Starlink and Starshield has also become a point of contention. Rubio has said Ukraine never had access to Starshield, while President Volodymyr Zelensky has described disruptions affecting both services.
Why speed limits matter for Ukraine
The restrictions concern the speed at which a terminal can move while remaining connected, a separate issue from how quickly it transfers internet data.
Zelensky said on Oct. 17 that terminals in Ukraine disconnected above 161 kilometers per hour (100 miles per hour), causing Ukrainian forces to lose control of interceptor drones.
He said Ukrainian specialists tested terminals traveling at 180 kilometers per hour (112 miles per hour) in EU territory without experiencing the same disconnections. He argued that the comparison showed the limits were specific to Ukraine.
The effects are concentrated on faster aircraft relying on satellite links, including drones used to intercept Russian jet-powered Shaheds and conduct strikes beyond conventional radio range.
Stationary ground terminals and most short-range first-person-view drones, which normally use direct radio links, have been largely unaffected by the movement-speed restriction.
Starlink also carries military communications, targeting information, and logistics data, making the network important well beyond individual drone missions.
Kyiv seeks answers as Europe weighs alternatives
During a virtual meeting with US lawmakers on Monday, Oct. 19, Zelensky said Washington had still not explained the satellite restrictions or failures to provide advance warnings of Russian ballistic missile attacks.
He raised the issues with a bipartisan group from the Senate and House as Ukraine sought to restore communications needed for its defenses.
European governments have also been examining alternatives, but EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas warned on Oct. 16 that Europe could not replace Starlink’s capabilities in the short term.
The European Commission has been discussing Ukraine’s participation in GOVSATCOM, a program pooling satellite resources for secure government communications. Brussels has not confirmed that it could meet the same battlefield requirements as Starlink.

articles.title: Elon Musk ordered the Starlink restrictions that disabled Ukrainian drones, defenses - report
articles.body:
Elon Musk was behind the speed restrictions placed on the military-grade version of Starlink used by Ukrainian forces, the Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday night, citing US officials and people familiar with the matter.
SpaceX first placed a limit on some services in Ukraine on October 13 without warning. Ukrainian officials at the time feared the move by Musk's company may have been made at the request of US President Donald Trump.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced that Ukraine was unable to use its interceptors against Russian drone attacks as a result of the restrictions on Saturday, saying that Ukraine had been told that they had been caused by technical issues.
Musk claims POTUS behind any decisions on speed limits as Trump denies responsibility
Trump said on Friday that he did not think he or Musk was responsible for Ukraine losing Starlink access in a way that affected its military operations against Russia and told reporters on Monday that he didn't know who was responsible but "would like to find out."
Musk posted that "any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," to his X/Twitter account shortly after the slowdown was publicized.
According to the WSJ report, some US officials said that Musk acted without any order from Trump. However, a person familiar with the situation told WSJ that Musk had communicated with multiple senior administration officials, including Trump himself, before imposing the new speed cap.
This comes amidst strained US-Ukrainian ties, with Trump accusing Zelensky of sabotaging peace efforts and Zelensky accusing the Trump administration of withholding intelligence, which the White House has denied.
"There has not been some deliberate political directive to go out and harm Ukraine," US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told journalists on Tuesday.
Rubio added that he had had a 45-minute conversation with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Tuesday. Zelensky said the topics included ballistic missile interceptors, early warning of Russian attacks and the situation with Starlink and Starshield satellite services.
Trump criticizes Zelensky's attack on Russian diesel
Trump has criticized Zelensky for attacking Russian diesel refineries, saying on October 10, days before the Starlink restrictions, that he told Zelensky, "You can do whatever you want to Russia, but don’t hit the refineries because that’s a world problem.’ And what does he do? He goes and hits the diesel fuel. He better damn well stop.”
Trump reiterated his criticism in a Truth Social post on Sunday, saying that Zelensky "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did," calling on the Ukrainian leader to stop attacking Russian diesel facilities.
Musk has publicly agreed with Trump's criticism, responding to a video of Trump telling Zelensky to stop the attacks with "Zelensky has gone too far," on X, four days before drone operators reported losing unrestricted access to Starlink.
Ukraine is still “waiting for the official response from contacts with the Pentagon and SpaceX at the leaders' level to understand what has happened, but also to understand whether the connection has been restored or will be restored,” Ukraine's top diplomat in Washington, Denys Sienik, told the WSJ on Tuesday.
Amichai Stein and Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title: WSJ: Elon Musk personally ordered Starlink restrictions for Ukraine
articles.body:
WSJ: Elon Musk personally ordered Starlink restrictions for Ukraine
The Wall Street Journal has written that Elon Musk ordered the speed of the military version of Starlink to be reduced in Ukraine, leaving some Ukrainian attack and interceptor drones practically unusable.
Source: The Wall Street Journal, citing sources
Details: The WSJ noted that both Musk and US President Donald Trump have expressed dissatisfaction with Ukraine over its strikes on Russian oil refineries in recent weeks. Trump sees these attacks as a reason for high energy prices.
Sources told the WSJ that Musk was behind the restriction of the speed at which Ukrainian equipment could connect to the satellite network last week, rendering some attack and interceptor drones practically useless.
Two sources said Musk and Trump had discussed the decision on Starlink during a phone call shortly after news of the speed restrictions became public.
One source also claimed that Musk and Trump had discussed the issue even before the decision to restrict Starlink speeds was made.
Public complaints by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who said Ukrainians could die if unrestricted access to the service was not restored, led to widespread confusion over who had ordered the speed reduction and an unofficial investigation at the White House.
According to the sources, as the controversy unfolded, SpaceX representatives contacted their counterparts at the White House in an attempt to reach a common understanding and issue a joint statement saying that the company and Trump's administration had coordinated their actions before Musk issued the order.
Hours after news of the speed reduction became public, Musk wrote on X (Twitter): "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," using the acronym for president of the United States.
Trump told journalists on 19 October that he did not know who was responsible for reducing Starlink speeds, "but I would like to find out".
Some US officials claim that Musk had acted unilaterally and that Trump had not specifically ordered any retaliatory measures against Ukraine.
However, a source familiar with the situation said Musk had spoken to several administration officials, including Trump, before introducing the new speed restriction. Ukrainian officials said the restriction had allowed Russian missiles to bypass their air defence systems.
Background:
- Reuters reported earlier that the order to restrict Starshield, a satellite system Ukraine uses for battlefield communications and to control interceptor drones, came directly from the White House.
- US Republican Senator Thom Tillis is seeking an investigation into the Pentagon's actions with regard to problems with Starlink satellite communications systems encountered by the Ukrainian Armed Forces.

articles.title: US Restores Ballistic-Missile Warnings to Ukraine as Russia Hits Kyiv High-Rise, Killing 2
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
US Restores Ballistic-Missile Warnings to Ukraine as Russia Hits Kyiv High-Rise, Killing 2
Washington has restored critical early-warning intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches just as Kyiv was hit again—this time by a strike on a 24-story residential tower that killed two people.
The United States has restored early-warning intelligence sharing with Ukraine on Russian ballistic missile launches, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on October 21, as a Russian strike hit a 24-story residential building in Kyiv, killing at least two people and injuring two other persons.
Explosions were heard across the Ukrainian capital in the morning, with one strike hitting the Sviatoshynskyi district.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the projectile struck the high-rise at approximately the 20th-floor level, triggering a fire.
“In the Sviatoshynskyi district, there was a strike on a 24-story residential building at the level of the 20th floor. There is a fire. Emergency services are heading to the scene,” Klitschko said.
Kyiv City Military Administration initially reported one fatality before authorities confirmed that the death toll had risen to two. Two additional people were injured.
Against the backdrop of the latest Russian strike, Zelenskyy said Washington has resumed sharing intelligence used to provide Ukraine with warning of incoming Russian ballistic missiles—a capability he has repeatedly described as critical because such weapons leave civilians only a short window to reach shelter.
“I am talking about early warning, which is very important for our people, for children, adults, and civilians, because we can receive a warning about an approaching ballistic missile,” Zelenskyy said.
The Ukrainian President said Kyiv was grateful that intelligence cooperation with the US was functioning again. He made the remarks after a meeting with US presidential special envoy Steve Witkoff and noted that he had also discussed intelligence sharing with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
The restoration comes after Zelenskyy recently said Ukraine had stopped receiving some US warnings about Russian ballistic launches amid mounting tensions between Kyiv and Washington.
Earlier, reports emerged that Russia has carried out 2,147 attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure since July 16, with strikes recorded every day.

articles.title: Pentagon chief denies directives restricting Starshield in Ukraine, points to priority of replenishing US air defense arsenals
articles.body:
The US Department of War maintains an unchanged position on supporting Ukraine and has refrained from issuing any directives on restricting the operation of the Starshield satellite network, while on the supply of interceptor missiles Washington's priority is to provide its own armed forces with as many as possible, US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has said.
"We have not changed our position on the Ukrainians in any way, but on things like interceptor missiles, of course, we want to make sure our guys are also supplied with as many as possible. So that is the case, and President Zelenskyy knows it," Hegseth said.
According to Hegseth, press reports about a change in the Pentagon's approach to Ukraine are false. He noted the heroic efforts of Ukrainians and recalled that under the previous American administration Kyiv was given large volumes of military aid that drained American stockpiles, so the department is now replenishing these stocks on the instruction of US President Donald Trump.
Commenting on reports about reduced speeds and restricted coverage of the Starshield military satellite system in Ukraine, the Pentagon chief assured that the US defense department had left service volumes unreduced and had refrained from issuing such orders. Hegseth explained that the use of terminals is governed by the terms of service, and the authority to decide on compliance with them rests directly with the Starlink operator, and he wished the Ukrainian side success.
As reported, the administration of US President Donald Trump is holding back, without consideration, the transfer of anti-aircraft interceptor missiles for Patriot systems for Ukraine from partner countries, which coincides with a sharp deterioration in diplomatic relations between Washington and Kyiv over disagreements about strikes on Russian oil refineries.

articles.title: Britain’s cargo drone becomes a low-cost drone interceptor
articles.body:
- A BAE Systems TRV-150 drone armed with a three-pod APKWS launcher intercepted several attack drones during a Pentagon experiment at Eglin Air Force Base.
- The adapted Malloy T-150 fired laser-guided rockets at multiple targets in one flight without landing to reload.
A heavy-lift cargo drone built by BAE Systems subsidiary Malloy Aeronautics has shot down several one-way attack drones with laser-guided rockets during a Pentagon experiment in Florida, firing one rocket after another without having to land and reload.
The modified aircraft, known as the TRV-150, carried a three-pod launcher loaded with BAE Systems’ APKWS rockets during the Joint Readiness Experimentation exercise run by the Office of the Under Secretary of War for Research and Engineering at Eglin Air Force Base from Sept. 21 to 25, BAE Systems said in a statement on Oct. 21.
The TRV-150 is a version of Malloy’s T-150 quadcopter, a British-built electric drone designed to carry cargo, which Maryland-based SURVICE Engineering adapted to meet U.S. Army requirements while BAE Systems’ FalconWorks division developed the APKWS kit and integrated it on the aircraft. BAE Systems says the trials show that low-cost precision weapons can be fitted to uncrewed platforms to counter drone threats on the battlefield, and the company now wants to take the same setup to sea to protect ships from similar attacks.
“Our customers are facing drone threats right now, so we’ve worked at pace with our partners to move from concept to a proven system, which can engage multiple targets in a single mission,” said Thomas Lancashire, head of UAS business development at BAE Systems FalconWorks.
APKWS, short for Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System, turns an ordinary unguided 70 mm (2.75-inch) Hydra rocket into a precision weapon by fitting a laser-guidance section between the warhead and the motor, which makes it far cheaper than the air-to-air missiles traditionally used to shoot down drones. The rocket has become one of the U.S. military’s main low-cost answers to cheap attack drones, and in May the U.S. Navy awarded L3Harris a contract worth up to $98.4 million for proximity fuzes that make APKWS more effective against drones, while BAE Systems test-fired the rocket from a Royal Air Force Typhoon in March as it adds counter-drone rockets to the fighter.
The Eglin trials build on the first firing of a precision munition from an adapted T-150 in July 2025, when the drone launched a single APKWS rocket, and this time the team used a production-ready three-pod launcher to engage targets in the air. The ability to fire several shots in one sortie matters against attack drones, which often arrive in groups and leave little time for a launcher to land, reload and take off again.
“Supporting the warfighter has been at the core of SURVICE’s mission since its founding over 45 years ago. Bringing the TRV-150 to the US warfighter and now adding APKWS as a proven, precise, and cost-effective capability to our TRV-150 UAS platform is exactly the type of innovation SURVICE was designed to deliver,” said Gregory Thompson, president of SURVICE Engineering.
BAE Systems bought Malloy Aeronautics in 2024, and the T-150 is already in service with British forces as a logistics drone. During the Royal Navy Carrier Strike Group’s eight-month deployment to the Indo-Pacific last year, the drone carried supplies between ships throughout the voyage, and SURVICE is one of several partners BAE Systems is working with around the world to turn the aircraft into a multi-role counter-drone system.
BAE Systems has not said when an armed TRV-150 could enter service, but the company’s next step is to adapt the rocket-armed version for maritime use, where it would help defend ships against the kind of drone attacks that have hit vessels in the Red Sea and the Black Sea.

articles.title: Rostec develops attack drones with characteristics comparable to cruise missiles
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 21. /TASS/. Russia’s state corporation Rostec is developing and manufacturing strike drones with performance characteristics on par with those of cruise missiles, the corporation said.
"As technology advances, the distinction between a drone, a cruise missile, and a loitering munition is disappearing. The Dan-T is already a full-fledged cruise missile in terms of its capabilities. The Rostec State Corporation is working to advance this field, and several other comparable projects are underway. These systems are becoming increasingly intelligent – all of them feature elements of artificial intelligence to one degree or another.
The next models, which we will be able to present as early as next year, will fly farther, faster, and will be considerably more advanced in terms of intelligence," Rostec said in a video presentation of its latest Dan-T aerial strike drone.
The state corporation presented this system at the El Alamein International Airshow 2026 in Egypt.
About the munition
The Dan-T is a loitering munition with a range of up to 450 km. With a weight of up to 270 kilograms and equipped with a compact turbojet engine, it can be launched from both aircraft and helicopters. The Dan-T is designed to fly in stealth mode to evade air defense systems and operates fully autonomously after launch from its carrier. The munition can approach its target at speeds of up to 500 km/h while following the terrain, thereby reducing the likelihood of interception by enemy air defense systems.
The Dan-T can be launched from Russian-designed aircraft and helicopters, including the Yak-130, MiG-29, Mi-28N, and Mi-8. It can also be integrated with foreign combat aircraft.
As Rostec told TASS, the munition’s effectiveness has been confirmed by hundreds of successful launches against enemy targets during the special military operation in Ukraine.

articles.title: Putin and U.S. envoy Witkoff hold talks in St. Petersburg as Washington pushes a new plan to end the war in Ukraine
articles.body:
Putin and U.S. envoy Witkoff hold talks in St. Petersburg as Washington pushes a new plan to end the war in Ukraine
Steve Witkoff, the U.S. president’s special envoy, flew to St. Petersburg this morning for a meeting with Vladimir Putin, part of a renewed U.S. effort to restart talks on ending Russia’s war against Ukraine. Jared Kushner, the U.S. president’s son-in-law, who usually accompanies Witkoff on such trips, did not travel to Russia because of illness but is taking part in the meeting by video link.
Kirill Dmitriev, the Russian president’s special representative, met Witkoff at Pulkovo Airport. The meeting with Putin began around noon Moscow time at Konstantinovsky Palace, and its opening was open to the press. Witkoff thanked Putin for agreeing to the “diesel deal” and said he hoped the Russian president would consider resuming trilateral talks. He also said he had brought documents outlining approaches to a peaceful settlement.
Putin announced that Russia had released U.S. citizen Stephen Hubbard, who had fought for Ukraine’s armed forces. After he fell into Russian captivity, a court sentenced him to nearly seven years in prison on charges of mercenary activity.
Witkoff met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Oslo the day before his meeting with Putin. The talks also included Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, Finnish President Alexander Stubb, and representatives from the EU, NATO, France, the United Kingdom, Germany, and Poland. Kushner took part in the meeting online.
After the talks, Stubb said they had made “real progress on two levels”: in the short term and in a broader context. He said the discussions touched on key issues including air defense, energy facilities, and the possibility of a partial ceasefire.
Zelensky said Ukraine and the West have “clear ideas about how to achieve peace,” including organizing a trilateral meeting with Trump, Putin, and Zelensky himself “to resolve issues that only leaders can resolve.”
Moscow has repeatedly said it sees the point of that meeting only in the final stages of negotiations. After the talks in Oslo, Trump said he believes Putin and Zelensky do not “don’t have to be in the same room” at a trilateral meeting.
Sources cited by Axios said the discussions in Oslo focused on drafting a framework agreement to end the war, which would then be proposed to Russia. The outlet reported that the parties made “meaningful progress” and reached a “strong alignment at the working level” on further steps. Axios sources said Kushner again asked Ukraine at the meeting to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries.
Witkoff is expected to leave Moscow later today and return to Oslo, where he will meet again with Norwegian Prime Minister Støre to brief him on his talks with Putin.

articles.title: India, US ‘perfectly aligned’ on key issues: Marco Rubio; defends ties with Pakistan
articles.body:
Rubio is set to visit Jamnagar for talks on bilateral ties, energy cooperation and commercial investment.
US secretary of state Marco Rubio urged businesses to view the India-US relationship as a strategic partnership spanning technology, trade and security, saying the two countries were “perfectly aligned” on issues that would shape the 21st century, even as he acknowledged that disagreements between them would persist.Addressing a gathering of India Inc’s leading business figures at a Freedom 250 event at BKC, Rubio said the relationship between the two countries could help shape the future of the global economy, particularly as advances in artificial intelligence and quantum computing transform industries and societies.
“I truly believe the relationship between US and India is defining, in many ways, in a positive way, what the 21st century can look like,” he said.The gathering included Noel Tata (Tata Trusts), Anand Mahindra (Mahindra Group), Kiran MazumdarShaw (Biocon), Ashok P Hinduja (Hinduja Group), Amit Dixit (Blackstone), Hitendra Dave (HSBC India), K Balasubramanian (Citi India) and Rahul Badhwar (JPMorgan Chase).Rubio identified emerging technologies and secure trade routes as two areas in which the countries’ interests converge. “US and India are perfectly aligned,” he said, referring to the challenge of harnessing new technologies for public benefit.
“We have the same expertise. We have the same talented people working on it, from engineers to creative thinkers and innovators.”He linked economic growth to the security of international shipping routes, arguing that businesses needed the freedom to move goods across borders and reach markets.For India and US, he said, this required “a free and secure Indo-Pacific” in which “no nation can claim dominance or ownership of international shipping lanes”.“No two nations on earth will ever be perfectly aligned on every issue,” he said. “But on the core issues that matter..., alignment between our countries is extraordinary.”The speech did not signal any immediate change in tariffs or market access.
Rubio said he believed US should engage more frequently with India, and he planned to return in three months.
US secy of state defends ties with Pakistan
US is required to have relationships with countries, including with those with whom it may have some disagreements, said secretary of state Marco Rubio while defending ties with Pakistan and condemning terrorism. Rubio also confirmed the next Quad leaders’ summit would take place in Manila next month.“In the case of Pakistan, it’s a country that we have to have a relationship with, a country that possesses nuclear weapons. It’s a country that from a geographic standpoint, we need to be able to interact with them in much the same way as govt of India has to have and has a relationship and meets with leaders from Iran,” said Rubio speaking to Network 18.“... It could be a positive thing because if... we can speak to them, it perhaps puts us in a position to help discourage the kinds of things India is worried about,” he added.

articles.title: Some of Ukraine’s artillery soldiers were TikTokers yesterday, ComBat Vision says. Their new plugin teaches them to aim
articles.body:
Ukraine receives Western weapons, but the code that teaches soldiers to aim them is increasingly its own. Developers of the Ukrainian battlefield reconnaissance and coordination system ComBat Vision have released a new plugin that turns the abstract math of artillery fire into a visual tool, letting crews simulate firing and learn to adjust it, the team says.
The developers built the tool around a problem they name plainly: the quality of specialists entering the military is falling rapidly.
“Artillery soldiers are sometimes yesterday’s TikTokers or "tanks" players,” the team explain, so the plugin makes firing and aiming as visual as possible to teach indirect fire quickly.
On screen, it draws a round’s flight path from the weapon’s firing tables and the dispersion ellipse for that gun and munition, warns of obstacles on the calculated trajectory, and simulates the shell after the shot with a training error added. It then shows real or simulated bursts, averages the correction across a series of hits, and lets the user enter corrections, including by voice, and watch the result.
The plugin draws its ballistics from MyGun, an app by Yaroslav Sherstiuk that automates ballistic and fire calculations for artillery. ComBat Vision itself coordinates troops and shares object data, integrating with optical sensors such as drones, ground robots and security cameras to fix targets in space.
From a single app to a platform with a plugin store
ComBat Vision’s bigger move is becoming a platform rather than a single app. The developers say they will open a plugin store within a week, where units can download the new artillery feature and others, such as repeater-coverage calculations and remote control of minefields.
The team has announced plans to open it, not results from using it, so its payoff, letting one platform add new tools without building a separate system each time, is a claim to watch rather than a proven gain.

articles.title: Kyiv’s Donors Expected Peace in 2027, but Russian Escalations Left 2026 Funding Unfulfilled
articles.body:
Each year since Russia’s full-scale invasion, Ukraine’s donors have bet on peace the following year.
Each year, Moscow has proved them wrong.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
As of late 2026, Ukraine has been trying to work out how to counter jet-powered Russian drones, which have caused more civilian deaths and cost $1.5 billion in tax revenues by year-end, per the prime minister’s estimates. Moscow is also expanding the Alabuga-Volokno factory to raise Geran/Shahed drone production by 78%, according to Politico, even as the IMF reported that its economy grew only 1% this year.
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR) chief Oleh Ivashchenko told Ukrinform that Russia may have enough resources to continue until 2028. And the Bank of Finland Institute for Emerging Economies (BOFIT) wrote in its mid-term forecast that Russia can still sustain a full-scale war thanks to higher oil prices, despite weaker economic activity and a widening fiscal deficit.
“Even with the risks of continuing the war, there are no signs that the economy faces an immediate collapse into crisis,” it wrote in its latest Forecast for Russia for 2026-28.
Kyiv’s mission: two months to find almost $50 billion
The aid plans assume a happier ending in 2027, which isn’t the case in Ukraine.
In autumn 2026, the finance ministry received a bill from the defense ministry for an additional $27 billion to fund costlier warfare, and the treasury needed another $29 billion more for donor-backed social wages.
Ukraine May Have 300-500 Russian Spies Working for Kyiv
It had neither: In October, the government delayed $2.3 billion in development payments, and businesses went without value-added tax (VAT) refunds for a while.
Part of the problem also lies with Ukraine’s lawmakers, most of whom don’t see the worst of the war coming or the need to vote for reforms that will unlock the cash. The finance ministry has been sounding the alarm in finance for almost a year, since Ukraine signed the new $8.1 billion IMF program with benchmarks lawmakers must vote on.
The EU’s reform-tied Ukraine Facility also lists steps that parliament and the government have not adopted since 2025. The list deadlocked parliament from early 2026, as the government and lawmakers failed to agree until the treasury emptied. The EU, which had earlier accepted compromises, now refuses 2026 aid unless Ukraine implements the bills.
Now, Kyiv must find financing for 2026 and 2027 in under two months. The president and defense ministry team is negotiating weapons funding – one half of the financing – while the prime minister, finance ministry and central bank work on social spending, pensions and wounded businesses.
                                                                                                                                                                         (Chart by Olena Hrazhdan / Kyiv Post)                             
If lawmakers fail to vote for reforms, Ukraine may have nothing to pay for its survival and could resort to printing money and face protests.
“We will lose communications with international donors. The IMF program will be impossible to maintain with quantitative easing,” Finance Minister Serhiy Marchenko said at the tax committee meeting in September.
Ukraine printed money in 2022 and landed softly, but doing so again risks Argentinian or Venezuelan-style inflation.
If the IMF blocks a tranche over poor performance, Ukraine automatically loses the ability to attract aid from others, as the IMF’s green light signals that the country can be trusted. Defense needs make this funding a lifeline as Russia shows no desire to end the invasion.
But Ukraine’s delegation has options: reassure donors that the reforms have been voted on, and again negotiate the use of Russian assets.
To complete the mission, Kyiv must clear three quests: convince the IMF in Thailand, agree on funding with the EU, and push the Ukrainian parliament to do its one job.
Ukraine’s parliament and 2026 IMF Annual Meetings funding quests
For 2026, the EU told Ukraine it will receive the committed cash for its budget needs as parliament votes on the bills, a person familiar with the matter told Kyiv Post.
“In recent weeks, the IMF team has been in talks with various partners – primarily from the European Union – regarding the mobilization of additional funds to Ukraine. But Europeans gave a clear signal we need to fulfill the conditions necessary,” the person said.
Almost immediately after taking office, the new prime minister, Serhii Koretskiy, rushed to push through the reform decisions his predecessor, Yulia Svyrydenko, left undone.
Under Koretskiy, the government adopted six decisions that missed deadlines in 2025 and the first half of 2026. Eight Ukraine Facility steps and six of 12 Ukraine Support Loan conditions remain unmet, per the RRR4U monitoring, and President Volodymyr Zelensky still has not signed the digital-platform income tax bill, another IMF benchmark.
Finance Minister Marchenko did not attend the IMF’s Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Thailand; instead, he kept a close eye on the lawmakers. When the state treasury became nearly empty, it partly worked: On the third attempt, they voted for an IMF benchmark scrapping the VAT exemption for parcels worth up to €150 ($174), and parliament began filling six of 11 Accounting Chamber seats.
                                                                                                                                                                         From left: IMF Alternate Executive Director Vladyslav Rashkovan, Deputy Minister of Finance Olha Zykova, IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva, National Bank of Ukraine Governor Andriy Pyshnyi and IMF European Department Director Mateusz Szczurek during a meeting on the sidelines of the IMF and World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok. (Photo courtesy of Ukraine’s Ministry of Finance press service)                             
The mood was somber as delegations headed to Bangkok for the IMF Annual Meetings, but the last-minute vote reassured them.
“We came to Bangkok on a low, and we leave on a high. The Rada vote changed the mood. It showed once again that, against all odds, Ukraine continues to deliver on its reform agenda,” a well-informed source told Kyiv Post.
Before the meetings, the source was skeptical that the parties would arrive with any “significant headline announcements.”
Ukraine’s finance ministry is also happy.
“For our key partners, Ukraine’s performance is no longer in question. The discussion has now shifted to determining how to ensure and structure the necessary financing for 2027 in a sustainable and predictable manner,” Deputy Minister of Finance Olha Zykova told Kyiv Post.
                                                                                                                                                                         Ukraine’s finance ministry delegation at the IMF and World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok. From left: Deputy Ministers of Finance Yuriy Drahanchuk, Olha Zykova, Government Commissioner for Public Debt Management Yuriy Butsa and Finance Ministry press service staff. (Photo courtesy of the Ministry of Finance)                             
Kyiv Post still does not know whether Ukraine’s defense ministry shares that optimism. It did not answer Kyiv Post’s request on its $27 billion gap, but wrote that it freed up $354.5 million, 1.3% of the gap, by revising arms purchases.
Quest 2: Cash for 2027 and European partners
Immobilized Russian sovereign assets in the EU, amounting to €210 billion ($243.6 billion), remain key to Ukraine’s 2027 plan, despite earlier objections from Belgium.
Signed programs cover $20 billion for 2027, leaving $32.6 billion unfulfilled. Kyiv Post found that the EU has agreed to cover part of this, and Kyiv should find the rest outside the union.
“Depending on the final size of the EU contribution to cover the budgetary needs in 2027, we calculate the residual amount to be covered by other donors in the range of $10-15 billion,” the second source participating in the discussions told Kyiv Post.
“It’s important to obtain those financing assurances, including from the EU, by the next IMF review scheduled by the end of the year,” the person added.
                                                                                                                                                                         (Chart by Olena Hrazhdan / Kyiv Post)                             
Kyiv Post was told that Kyiv’s allies are doing “a lot of work on [a] technical level” to secure Ukraine’s 2027 funding needs, with further details remaining undisclosed.
One potential option is a second Extraordinary Revenue Acceleration (ERA) loan backed by Russia’s frozen sovereign assets.
“The European Commission is working on developing various options,” a person familiar with the matter told Kyiv Post.
Partners seem less willing to confiscate the principal of the frozen assets, according to the source. And with the US, which took part in the earlier ERA Loan, also showing less enthusiasm, another option could be a new EU-backed Ukraine Support Loan, the person added.
“They can find the resource if they have the political will and simultaneously Ukrainian authorities deliver their promises,” the person said.
Negotiations should turn to specific financing assurances by early December, Zykova told Kyiv Post.
“The focus is on finding the right combination of support from the EU and our non-EU G7+ partners, while safeguarding Ukraine’s debt sustainability,” she said.
The second IMF review is planned for November, when Ukraine will again report on whether Kyiv did its homework, and partners will face another checkpoint on whether they did theirs amid a looming increase in Russian escalations across Ukraine in the months to come.

articles.title: MSM ‘sources’ contradict Musk on Starlink for Ukraine
articles.body:
MSM ‘sources’ contradict Musk on Starlink for Ukraine
The Wall Street Journal has challenged Elon Musk’s denials over alleged restrictions on satellite services used for Ukrainian drone strikes deep inside Russia. The outlet has cited anonymous White House sources who have claimed that the SpaceX founder and Starlink owner had personally ordered restricting the service.
Ukrainian officials last week claimed that SpaceX’s Starlink satellite communications service and its military-grade version, Starshield, which Kiev uses for frontline drone operations, stopped working on drones traveling faster than 160 kph (100 mph). Neither Starlink nor SpaceX has publicly acknowledged a technical “signal or service failure,” leaving the questions of whether an actual service restriction took place, and if so what could have caused it, unconfirmed.
What has Ukraine claimed about Starshield?
Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky initially claimed, without evidence, that Kiev had been told “technical malfunctions” had caused a service slowdown. He later shifted the blame to Washington. On NBC’s ‘Meet the Press’ on Sunday Zelensky claimed, again without citing evidence nor being asked to provide it, that an order had come from the US government. According to Zelensky, Kiev had even secretly despatched cars to the EU, where they could drive "legally" at 180kph (110mph) where tests allegedly surfaced discrepancies in Starlink performance between the EU and Ukraine.
What has Musk said about Starshield?
Musk has categorically denied that he instructed SpaceX to restrict either service, nor has he confirmed that any restriction or slowdown took place.
The WSJ cited anonymous sources who contradicted him, alleging on Tuesday that he personally ordered speed limits on Ukrainian hardware connected to the satellite network.
Even the WSJ's sources accounts differed. Some claimed that Musk acted unilaterally; others said he consulted senior administration officials, including President Donald Trump, before making the decision. The outlet also claimed that SpaceX representatives contacted the White House to coordinate their accounts of whether the restrictions had been agreed on with the administration.
What has the US government said about Starshield?
Musk earlier insisted that Starshield is owned and controlled by the US government, meaning any speed or usage restrictions are determined by the US military and ultimately Trump – who denied that he ordered the restrictions, though he said on Monday he “would like to find out” who did. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent both said the administration was not behind the restrictions, with Bessent rebuking Zelensky for making “reckless” allegations.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio also rejected the claims. Questioned about the allegation during a visit to India on Wednesday, he warned Kiev against escalating the dispute, saying Ukraine “would not exist” as a sovereign state without US support.
Relations between Zelensky and Washington have effectively collapsed in recent weeks over sanctions on Russia and Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure. Both Musk and Trump have sharply criticized Ukraine’s attacks on Russian diesel refineries, blaming them for global fuel shortages and soaring prices at the pump.
Speaking at the Oval Office on Tuesday, Trump warned Zelensky that he is “going to have to want to make a deal.” He also criticized the cost of supporting Kiev, saying the US has received “absolutely nothing back” except “grief, death and tremendous monetary loss.”
What did Kiev say about Starshield?
Despite Zelensky’s evidence-free assertions and there being no record in the public sphere to support it, the Western press and Ukrainian diplomats are echoing the claims regardless. Ukraine’s ambassador in Washington, Denis Senik, said on Tuesday that Kiev is still “waiting for the official response from contacts with the Pentagon and SpaceX” to understand what happened.
What did the Kremlin say about Starshield?
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said last week that Moscow is unaware of the reported Starlink restrictions, but stressed that “overall, of course, it would be better if such amazing technology… was not used for military purposes at all.” Moscow has condemned Western military assistance for Kiev, arguing that it only prolongs the conflict and obstructs peace efforts.
Is there any proof Starshield was slowed down?
There is no proof on the public record or in the public domain that the Starshield was affected. The only suggestions supporting the idea such an incident took place are Vladimir Zelensky's uncontested claim that Ukrainians sent cars to the EU with Starlink terminals to compare data and the claims of an anonymous Ukrainian officer who told German media giant Axel Springer's Global Reporter's Network, seemingly during the alleged service restriction, that all operations were on hold.

articles.title: Witkoff could meet with Putin soon – Kremlin
articles.body:
Witkoff could meet with Putin soon – Kremlin
Moscow expects US President Donald Trump’s special envoy, Steve Witkoff, to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin in the near future, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said. US mediators held talks with Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky in the Norwegian capital, Oslo on Tuesday.
Russia highly appreciates US mediation efforts, Peskov said at a news briefing on Tuesday, adding that Moscow sees every meeting between Putin and Trump’s envoys as “very important and well-timed.” He did not provide any details about the date or place of a potential meeting, but said the Kremlin expects Witkoff to inform Moscow about the results of Tuesday’s talks with Zelensky and his European backers.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said on Tuesday that Russia is willing to discuss any economic and financial initiatives Washington puts forward, provided they are “advantageous to us.”
He stressed that Russia will not make one-sided political concessions, warning that any deals with the US might not last beyond Trump’s term in office.
“The history of the American presidency is notable for a well-established political tradition… whereby a new president is not bound by any decisions made by their predecessor,” Lavrov said, adding that this gives the US leverage in talks and that Moscow is well aware that Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, could try to “arrange something” with this in mind.
Russia should not expect “some political favor to carry us through all global affairs,” Lavrov said. “We must rely solely on ourselves.”
Earlier on Tuesday, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, who hosted the meeting between Zelensky and the US negotiators, said Witkoff will travel to St. Petersburg on Wednesday for a meeting with the Russian leadership.
According to Store, the list of proposals Trump’s special envoy could put forward might include a three-way summit between Trump, Putin, and Zelensky. Ukrainian media also reported that other potential proposals included an energy ceasefire.
Last week, the Financial Times reported that Washington proposed unfreezing billions of euros in Russian assets held in the EU to give impetus to Ukraine peace talks during negotiations in Miami with officials from Ukraine, France, Germany, Britain, the EU, and NATO. The idea was vehemently opposed by Kiev’s European backers, including German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
Russia has said the stance of Kiev’s European backers is one of the main obstacles to settling the conflict. The EU is still clinging to the idea of “strategically defeating Russia,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov reiterated last month.
Moscow has also rejected the idea of a temporary truce, insisting on a long-term peace deal that addresses the root causes of the conflict. With negotiations stalling and no breakthrough in sight, Ukraine has maintained its megaphone diplomacy, publicly calling for new negotiations and demanding an unconditional ceasefire.
The renewed diplomatic push follows a spat between Trump and Zelensky over Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil facilities. The US president has demanded that Kiev stop the attacks, blaming them for surging fuel prices globally and in the US. The dispute has since widened, with Zelensky accusing Washington of withholding intelligence on Russian missile attacks and restricting Ukraine’s access to the Starlink satellite network.

articles.title: Netanyahu ‘completely lacks legitimacy’ to launch new war ahead of elections: Opposition leader Golan
articles.body:
Yair Golan, leader of Israel’s opposition Democrats party, said Wednesday that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu “completely lacks the legitimacy” to launch a war ahead of Oct. 27 legislative elections, Anadolu reports.
His remarks came after The Financial Times reported that US President Donald Trump had rejected Netanyahu’s plan to strike infrastructure and nuclear facilities in Iran, a military campaign that was reportedly set to begin on Oct. 10.
Trump opposes any military escalation ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm congressional elections in the US, fearing negative repercussions for the Republican Party’s electoral prospects, according to the report.
Golan, also a former deputy chief of staff of the Israeli army, said in a post on US social media platform X: “Netanyahu is a sick and weak leader clinging to power by force, willing to put Israel’s security at risk to save himself.”
The upcoming general election is seen as crucial to Netanyahu’s political future.
He is standing trial on corruption charges, including bribery, fraud, and breach of trust, which could result in imprisonment if he is convicted.
Golan further criticized Netanyahu, saying he “completely lacks the legitimacy to drag Israel into another military campaign, driven by personal and political calculations, on the eve of the election.”
Netanyahu, who is wanted by the International Criminal Court over war crimes in the Gaza Strip since 2023, has headed the current government since late 2022.
READ: Netanyahu, opposition blocs tied as 55% back unity government if election inconclusive: Poll
Since October 2023, Israel has launched a genocidal war in Gaza.
It has also waged wars against Lebanon and Iran, carried out airstrikes on Yemen and Qatar, and conducted near-daily ground incursions into Syria.
Golan called on Israeli army’s Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir and security establishment leaders to “oppose any military action intended to serve personal interests under the pretext of security needs,” while also urging voters to go to the polls to “save Israel from this dangerous government.”
Separately, Gadi Eisenkot, head of the opposition Yashar party, said Netanyahu’s claim of destroying Iranian nuclear bombs was “an outright lie.”
“Iran has never possessed nuclear bombs,” Eisenkot said in remarks carried by Israel’s public broadcaster KAN, arguing that he sees “no direct and immediate threat that requires action.”
Eisenkot is widely viewed as the opposition figure with the strongest potential to challenge Netanyahu in the upcoming elections.
A Channel 12 poll released Monday found that 45% of respondents considered Eisenkot better suited to serve as prime minister, compared with 33% for Netanyahu, widening Eisenkot’s lead to 12 percentage points from 10 in the previous survey.
However, polls generally suggest that neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor the opposition is likely to secure a parliamentary majority, raising the prospect of another election unless one side agrees to form a coalition with Palestinian parties in Israel.
In a separate statement on X, the Israeli military said Wednesday that its personnel had begun early voting, including troops stationed in occupied territories in Gaza, Lebanon, and Syria.
