articles.title: German sniper detained after deserting Ukrainian Army – FSB
articles.body:
German sniper detained after deserting Ukrainian Army – FSB
A German sniper who deserted the Ukrainian military after failing to receive a promised payment has been detained by Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB), the agency announced on Wednesday.
In footage released by the agency, the man said he had served with German forces in Afghanistan between 2004 and 2010, took part in fighting in Somalia from 2006 to 2008, and later fought as a mercenary in Syria between 2008 and 2010.
The former Bundeswehr soldier said he then served as a sniper with Ukraine’s 25th Territorial Defense Battalion near Donetsk between 2016 and 2018, alongside fighters mainly from Britain and Georgia.
He later moved to Switzerland before returning to Ukraine in November 2025 to sign another three-year military contract the following month. The man said he held the rank of corporal and served as a sniper.
“After signing the contract, I was promised a payment of 100,000 hryvnias ($2,200). However, I did not receive this money and was forced to flee the Ukrainian armed forces,” he said in the testimony.
The FSB released copies of the German national’s military documents and contracts, with his identity concealed, as well as photographs showing him alongside other fighters. The agency said he could face criminal charges for mercenary activity under Russian law.
The detention comes a week after the FSB apprehended Swedish national Freddy Mikael Stalkrantz Lindholm in Russia’s Pskov Region. According to the agency, he crossed the border illegally to carry out sabotage and terrorist attacks on Russian military facilities, posing as a prospective recruit for the Russian Army.
Lindholm previously commanded a drone unit in Ukraine’s Aidar battalion, which Russia has designated a terrorist organization. He faces charges of illegally crossing the border, while investigators are considering additional charges related to terrorism and mercenary activity.
US investigators have also reportedly uncovered a scheme in which Mexican drug cartels sent their members to Ukraine to gain battlefield experience and paid officials close to Vladimir Zelensky for their “training,” Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service said on Tuesday.
Kiev has increasingly turned to foreign fighters as its military struggles with manpower shortages, draft evasion, and desertion. In March, then-Defense Minister Mikhail Fedorov identified the recruitment of more foreigners as one of the measures aimed at tackling Ukraine’s mobilization crisis.
At least 20,000 foreign mercenaries have fought for Kiev since 2022, Russian diplomat Yulia Zhdanova told the OSCE Forum for Security Co-operation earlier this month, saying most came from the US, UK, Canada, and Georgia.
Moscow has repeatedly pursued criminal cases against foreign fighters fighting for Kiev, including prosecutions in absentia, and has warned that mercenaries are not entitled to prisoner-of-war protections under the Geneva Conventions.

articles.title: Ukraine and Norway Race to Test FREYJA Ballistic Missile Interceptor by Year’s End
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine and Norway Race to Test FREYJA Ballistic Missile Interceptor by Year’s End
Ukraine and Norway are accelerating development of the FREYJA anti-ballistic missile defense program, with initial components already showing progress and the first tests targeted for the end of 2026.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced the development on October 21 following a meeting with Norwegian Defense Minister Tore O. Sandvik, Kongsberg CEO Eirik Lie, and representatives of the Norwegian defense company.
According to Zelenskyy, Norway is actively participating in the European FREYJA program, which aims to develop new capabilities for intercepting ballistic missile threats.
The Ukrainian president confirmed that work on individual elements of the system has already produced initial results. During the meeting, Ukrainian and Norwegian officials identified areas where development could be accelerated to begin testing before the end of the year.
Kongsberg, one of Norway’s leading defense manufacturers, produces the NASAMS air defense system, which Ukraine currently operates to protect cities and critical infrastructure against Russian missile and drone attacks.
The discussions also addressed additional military assistance from Norway. Zelenskyy said Ukraine expects new defense support packages to arrive as early as November, although he did not specify their contents.
Another priority was the development of new satellite communications capabilities for Ukraine’s Defense Forces. Zelenskyy said the initiative would involve additional international partners with the necessary technological resources.
Earlier, Ukrainian defense manufacturer Fire Point upgraded its FP-7.x Freyja interceptor missile with a dual-mode infrared and radar seeker. Developed as part of the European FREYJA program, the missile is designed to counter ballistic threats, including Russia’s Iskander-class missiles, while offering a lower-cost alternative to US-made Patriot interceptors.
Discuss this article:

articles.title: Zelenskyy Says Starshield Limits Remain as US Restores Missile Intelligence Sharing
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Zelenskyy Says Starshield Limits Remain as US Restores Missile Intelligence Sharing
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated that Starlink and Starshield services used by Ukrainian forces remain restricted, although US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has promised to work on resolving the issue, Fox News reported on October 21.
“Regarding Starlink and Starshield: they are still restricted, but the secretary of state told me that he will work with his team to unblock this issue,” Zelenskyy stated in an interview with Fox News.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Hegseth also addressed the Starshield restrictions, stating that the Pentagon had not ordered any reduction in support for Ukraine. “We haven’t pulled anything back,” he stated, adding that any restrictions were tied to Starlink’s terms of service rather than a US directive.
Zelenskyy also confirmed that the US had restored intelligence sharing with Ukraine, including information about Russian ballistic missile launches.
The restrictions on Starshield terminals emerged overnight on October 14, when SpaceX imposed new speed limits in Ukraine without advance warning.
The restrictions were reportedly imposed directly by Elon Musk. The Wall Street Journal reported that Musk personally ordered the October 14 Starshield slowdown, disrupting Ukrainian drone and interceptor operations, even though he later wrote that speed and usage limits were controlled by the US military and ultimately the president.
The terminals stopped functioning at speeds above roughly 160 kilometers per hour, disrupting systems used by Ukrainian forces to intercept Russian jet-powered Shahed-type drones.
Discuss this article:

articles.title: Air defenses intercept 150 drones used by Russia to attack Ukraine overnight
articles.body:
Air defenses intercept 150 drones used by Russia to attack Ukraine overnight
According to Ukrinform, the Ukrainian Air Force Command reported this on Facebook.
"On the night of October 21 (from 18:00 on October 20), the enemy attacked with Iskander-K cruise missiles launched from the airspace over Russia's Rostov region and 186 strike drones, including Shahed-type UAVs (88 of them jet-powered), S8000 Bandеrol/Dan-T, Gerbera, and Parodiya decoy drones, launched from Oryol, Kursk, and Primorsko-Akhtarsk in Russia, the temporarily occupied city of Donetsk, and Hvardiiske and Chauda in the temporarily occupied Autonomous Republic of Crimea," the statement said.
The air attack was repelled by aircraft, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine's Defense Forces.
"As of 08:30, preliminary data indicates that air defenses shot down or suppressed 150 enemy UAVs, including Shahed-type drones (63 of them jet-powered), S8000 Bandеrol/Dan-T, Gerbera, and drones of other types," the statement said.
Ten attack drones remain in the air, with combat operations ongoing.
Hits by enemy aerial attack weapons were recorded at 27 locations, while debris from downed targets fell at 13 locations.

articles.title: Ukraine’s interceptor crews destroyed thousands of Russian aerial targets during Vivaldi. Jet-powered Shaheds remain a challenge
articles.body:
The commander of an interceptor battalion in Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps said his unit destroyed several thousand Russian aerial targets during Operation Vivaldi, ArmyInform, the Defense Ministry’s news agency, reported on 21 October.
Operation Vivaldi is a Ukrainian counteroffensive north of Lyman in Donetsk Oblast, where the 3rd Army Corps has reported liberating settlements. In its third phase, Ukrainian forces reclaimed five settlements and expanded their gains to 176 square kilometers. Strikes on Russian logistics and electronic warfare likely neutralized Russia’s drone defenses before Ukraine sent in armor, the Institute for the Study of War assessed.
The commander, who uses the callsign “Betsyk,” leads the interceptor battalion of the 1030th Anti-Aircraft Missile-Artillery Regiment “Aquila,” part of the 3rd Army Corps. He said Russian forces deployed large numbers of reconnaissance drones to locate Ukrainian positions after the corps began advancing.
Betsyk named Zala, Orlan, Supercam, Merlin, and Knyaz Veshchiy Oleg among the reconnaissance drones used by Russian forces.
Russia also brought in reinforcements and units operating strike drones, including first-person-view (FPV) quadcopters, Molniya fixed-wing FPV drones, and Lancet crews, he said. At one stage, Russian forces deployed crews from their Rubicon drone unit to disrupt the advance, but the move did not change the situation.
Ukraine retook Kolodiazi north of Lyman as its drones hit 200-plus Russian vehicles in Operation Vivaldi’s last phase, Ukrainian drone officer says
Betsyk said his battalion’s work deprived Russian forces of the ability to strike Ukrainian troops and track their movements.
Jet-powered Shaheds: speed is the main challenge
The regiment also works against Russian strike drones heading for targets behind the front line. Betsyk said interceptor crews had destroyed some jet-powered drones, but not in significant numbers.
The main difficulty is speed, he said. Interceptor drones need to reach 500–600 km/h to intercept Russian jet-powered attack drones, according to Betsyk.
For now, the regiment mainly uses conventional air-defense systems against these targets: self-propelled anti-aircraft systems, surface-to-air missile systems, and portable surface-to-air missile systems. Betsyk said these systems were historically designed to engage jet-powered targets.
He compared the current challenge with the early use of piston-powered Shaheds. Those drones initially posed a serious threat but later became easier for Ukrainian air defenses to counter. Russia has largely stopped using piston-powered Shaheds on most fronts since summer, he said, but continues to use piston-powered Gerbera drones, which are relatively cheap and can partly exhaust Ukrainian air defenses. The main drones Russian forces use now are jet-powered Shaheds, he said.
Betsyk expects Russian forces to adapt if Ukraine fields effective interceptors against jet-powered drones. They will seek ways to evade the interceptors, increase speed, improve navigation, and change their tactics, he said. However, he added that the battalion had not observed a major evolution so far and did not expect the drones’ speed to double.
What the corps says Vivaldi achieved
Separately, 3rd Army Corps commander Andrii Biletskyi said Ukrainian forces retook 277 square kilometers and 16 settlements during Operation Vivaldi, Ukrainska Pravda reported. Biletskyi also said Russian losses exceeded 8,000 personnel, according to ArmyInform. These figures are Ukrainian claims and have not been independently verified.
Read also
- Russia’s Rubicon hunts Ukrainian drone pilots. In Vivaldi, it became the target, and its morale fell sharply, says the Ukrainian general
- Russia’s jet drones fly near 600 km/h now. Ukraine is building simulators for the 900 km/h ones it expects next
- Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps took the lessons of the failed 2023 counteroffensive into Operation Vivaldi. It fought small, and won.

articles.title: How Egypt's Saudi pledge aims to curb Israel's Gulf ambitions
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
How Egypt's Saudi pledge aims to curb Israel's Gulf ambitions
Egypt, a regional military power, has pledged to provide all forms of assistance to defend Saudi Arabia amid escalating Houthi attacks from Yemen, in a move aimed at maintaining its strategic position in the Gulf.
But analysts view another geopolitical objective behind the Egyptian support for Riyadh: countering Israel’s bid to play a security role in a region vital to Cairo’s political and economic interests.
On 17 October, President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said Egypt would take any necessary measures to protect Saudi Arabia if Riyadh requested assistance. He called an emergency parliamentary session to authorise possible troop deployment.
The following day, the National Defence Council, Egypt’s top security body, pledged to provide all necessary and possible support to safeguard Saudi Arabia’s security, stability, and territorial integrity.
The Egyptian pledge came after US President Donald Trump said on 16 October that Israel had been helping Saudi Arabia counter Houthi attacks from Yemen and suggested Riyadh should accept further Israeli assistance.
It followed Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s visit to Cairo last month to seek support against the Iran-backed Houthis. The visit highlighted the importance of Egyptian-Saudi coordination on issues affecting the Red Sea and wider regional stability.
For Cairo, which has longstanding strategic ties with Riyadh, the prospect of Israel becoming a more prominent security partner for the kingdom adds urgency to its efforts to reinforce its role in regional security.
“Egypt’s interest lies in doing everything possible to strengthen its ties with Saudi Arabia, or at least to ensure that its relationship with Riyadh is closer than Israel’s,” Ahmed Aboudouh, an associate fellow at Chatham House in London, told The New Arab.
Strengthening ties with Saudi Arabia offers Egypt significant economic and geopolitical benefits as Cairo seeks foreign investment, financial support, and foreign currency. The kingdom is also important for millions of Egyptians working there, whose remittances provide a vital source of foreign currency.
Closer coordination with Riyadh also helps Egypt protect its interests in the Red Sea, particularly shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key route to the Suez Canal and a major source of revenue for Cairo.
During Trump’s first term, the US brokered the Abraham Accords in 2020 to normalise relations between Israel and Arab countries, including Saudi Arabia’s neighbours, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and Bahrain, allowing Tel Aviv to expand its economic, diplomatic, and security partnerships in the Gulf.
The American president has also pushed for normalising ties between Saudi Arabia and Israel, but Riyadh insists that any normalisation depends on resolving the Palestinian issue, including the establishment of a Palestinian state.
If Riyadh accepts any Israeli assistance against Houthi attacks, cooperation in areas such as intelligence sharing and air defence could expand, potentially giving Israel a greater role in Gulf security.
For Egypt, that possibility raises concerns about a changing regional balance in which Israel could become a more influential security partner for Arab states traditionally linked to Cairo.
Cairo's bid to keep Israel at bay
“Egypt would oppose any attempt by Israel to become a player in the Arab world’s collective security, regardless of who was involved, and Saudi Arabia would certainly stand with Cairo. This means keeping Israel out of regional military and intelligence cooperation,” Egyptian military expert Samir Ragheb told The New Arab.
Egypt was the first Arab country to sign a peace treaty with Israel in 1979, following decades of conflict and several wars, but their relations have remained largely cold despite formal diplomatic ties.
The relationship has been marked by mutual distrust, periodic tensions, and regional competition, particularly over Gaza and broader Middle East security arrangements.
Egyptian political analyst Mokhtar Ghobashi said Egypt’s pledge to defend Saudi Arabia could deter Israel from seeking a security role in the Gulf.
“Relying on Israel as a security guarantor for a country in the Arab world, amid divisions and conflicts between Arab states, is an extremely dangerous proposition,” he told The New Arab.
Since the 2020 Abraham Accords, security cooperation between Israel and some Gulf states has expanded, including arms sales and coordination on air and missile defence amid shared concerns over Iran.
Egypt’s support for Saudi Arabia reflects its interest in preserving its regional influence and maintaining a central role in shaping the security arrangements in the Middle East.
Cairo could face greater competition for influence if Riyadh turns to Israel for certain defence capabilities. While this would not necessarily weaken Egyptian-Saudi relations, it could reduce Egypt’s role in shaping the kingdom’s security policy.
The implications extend beyond bilateral relations. Closer security ties between Israel and Saudi Arabia could give Tel Aviv a greater role in shaping regional responses to threats, from Yemen’s Houthis to Iran.
Protecting Egypt's strategic interests
Red Sea security is another concern for Cairo. A broader Israeli security role in the Gulf could give Tel Aviv greater influence over decisions affecting the Bab el-Mandeb, a vital maritime corridor central to Egypt’s national interests.
Aboudouh said another objective behind Egypt’s pledge to defend Saudi Arabia is to protect its strategic interests in the Red Sea and around Bab el-Mandeb.
“Egyptian officials may have concluded that expanding the country’s regional role is now crucial to protecting maritime traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait against any Houthi attempt to exploit a conflict with Saudi Arabia to disrupt shipping, as they have done in the past,” he told The New Arab.
Egypt has been hard-hit by regional instability following Israel’s war on the Gaza Strip and Houthi attacks on shipping in the Red Sea since 2023, losing an estimated around $20 billion in Suez Canal revenues.
Sisi framed Egypt’s potential role in Saudi Arabia as defensive, saying Cairo had no intention of attacking any party but was prepared to defend Saudi Arabia if requested. “We do not want to fight or attack anyone. We will only defend Saudi Arabia,” he said.
Egypt joined the Saudi-led coalition that intervened in Yemen against the Houthis in 2015, but its role remained limited. A deeper commitment now could expose Cairo to a costly conflict, particularly if operations extend beyond the defence of Saudi territory.
It could also strain Egypt’s resources and increase its exposure to instability along the Red Sea.
The extent and form of any Egyptian assistance will therefore be crucial. Intelligence-sharing, logistical support and maritime security cooperation would carry different risks from deploying troops to Yemen.
Cairo may seek to bolster Saudi Arabia’s defences while avoiding involvement in an open-ended conflict.
Mohamed Sabry is an Egyptian journalist based in Cairo with over two decades of experience covering Egypt, regional politics, foreign policy, and diplomacy. His work has appeared in Al-Monitor and InsideOver
Follow him on X: @MohamedSabry079
Edited by Charlie Hoyle

articles.title: U.S. Navy taps portable reactor to power Indiana base
articles.body:
- The U.S. Navy selected Radiant to install a 1-megawatt Kaleidos microreactor at Naval Weapons Station Crane in Indiana under the U.S. Army’s Janus Program.
- The Department of War wants the Navy’s first shore-based microreactor operating at Crane no later than September 2028.
The U.S. Navy has selected Radiant to install its Kaleidos nuclear microreactor at Naval Weapons Station Crane in Indiana, putting a commercial company in charge of the service’s first shore-based advanced reactor, which the Department of War wants running no later than September 2028.
Radiant announced the selection on Oct. 20, about six weeks after the Department of War named Crane as the site for the Navy’s first microreactor without saying which vendor would build it.
Kaleidos is a factory-built reactor that produces 1 megawatt of electricity and is designed to be moved by truck, ship or aircraft and set up at a customer’s site without cooling water, major excavation or extensive construction. Each unit runs for up to five years before it needs refueling, over a planned service life of 20 years, and at Crane it is meant to keep power flowing to the base independently of the regional grid, which matters for an installation where the Naval Surface Warfare Center, Crane Division, works on microelectronics, high-voltage systems and weapons.
The reactor will be installed under the U.S. Army’s Janus Program, the Pentagon effort to put commercially owned and operated microreactors on military bases so they can keep critical facilities running through grid outages. Before it reaches Crane, the project still has to move through design refinement, prototype testing, environmental review, site preparation and coordination with the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, with technical support from the Naval Nuclear Propulsion Program, the organization that runs the reactors on the Navy’s carriers and submarines.
“The Janus Program was built from day one to deliver real, reliable hardware and systems to solve energy resilience challenges across all of the Services,” said Dr. Jeff Waksman, Principal Deputy Assistant Secretary of the Army for Installations, Energy and Environment. “We are excited to partner with the Navy to place a Janus reactor at NWS Crane, and by doing so to deliver the state of Indiana its first advanced microreactor.”
Crane is the second military base Radiant has lined up this year under Janus. In August, the U.S. Army awarded contracts worth up to $2.2 billion to five reactor makers, with Radiant receiving the largest share, up to $750 million to deploy 15 Kaleidos units by 2030, as we reported, starting with three reactors at Fort Benning in Georgia that will back up Lawson Army Airfield and other critical facilities, we reported in September. The company also has a deal with the Defense Innovation Unit and the Department of the Air Force to deliver a Kaleidos unit by 2028, and it now says it is the only nuclear company working with the U.S. Army, U.S. Navy and U.S. Air Force at once.
“Our installations are foundational warfighting platforms and ensuring their resilience is essential to supporting the Fleet,” said Vice Adm. Brad Collins, Commander, Navy Installations Command. “By investing in advanced capabilities like this microreactor at Crane, we are providing our Shore infrastructure with the resources needed to sustain the mission and empower our warfighters.”
Radiant has not yet proven the design at full scale, and the reactor is now going through a year-long test campaign at the Idaho National Laboratory’s DOME facility, where the Department of Energy gave the company exclusive access after a competitive selection. The company says the test uses the same reactor design and the same type of fresh fuel that will go to military customers, running at full power for an extended period to show the performance and reliability needed before deployment.
The Navy brings decades of reactor experience to the project, since the Naval Nuclear Propulsion Program, founded in 1948, has logged more than 7,500 reactor-years of operation and over 171 million miles under nuclear power without a reactor accident.

articles.title: Ukraine hits Russian heavy rocket launcher near Black Sea coast
articles.body:
- Ukraine’s Prymary drone unit destroyed a Russian Tornado-S rocket launcher near Skadovsk in occupied Kherson Oblast, hitting it with several kamikaze drones.
- OSINT analyst Dominik geolocated the strike to Ulyanivka, while HUR said the unit also hit a Buk-M3, an Orion drone and four radars.
Ukrainian drones have destroyed a Russian 9K515 Tornado-S heavy multiple launch rocket system in occupied Kherson Oblast, hitting the launcher with several different kamikaze drones in succession in a strike carried out by the Prymary unit of Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR), which released the footage on Oct. 20.
OSINT analyst Dominik geolocated the strike to the village of Ulyanivka just outside Skadovsk, at coordinates 46.189524, 32.964916, which places the launcher close to the Black Sea coast and well behind the Dnipro River front line.
The video shows the Tornado-S being struck by drones of different types one after another, a method Ukrainian operators use against high-value vehicles so that a second or third drone can finish off a target that survives the first hit before the crew can drive it away. HUR did not give the exact date of the strike, saying only that it took place over the past month, and Russia has not commented on the loss.
The Tornado-S is one of the most valuable launchers in Russia’s rocket artillery, since it is a modernized version of the Soviet 9A52 Smerch that fires 300 mm (11.8-inch) rockets from a 12-tube launcher mounted on an eight-wheeled Kamaz truck. Built by NPO Splav in Tula, part of the state-owned Rostec group, the system uses digital fire control and GLONASS satellite navigation so its three-person crew can prepare and fire a full salvo without leaving the cab, and its guided rockets can reach targets up to 120 km (75 miles) away.
That range lets Russian crews fire on Ukrainian cities from deep inside occupied territory, and in the south the system has repeatedly been used against Kherson and other towns along the Dnipro from positions in the occupied part of the region. Ukrainian units put a high price on each launcher they destroy, and after a drone strike on a Tornado-S in the Huliaipole sector in July, the Pomsta Border Guard Brigade estimated the vehicle’s value at more than $15 million.
The Skadovsk strike is the latest in a series of Tornado-S losses this year as Ukrainian drones reach further behind Russian lines. In February, the Ptahi unit of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces destroyed a launcher in occupied Zaporizhzhia Oblast with FP-2 strike drones guided by reconnaissance drones, we reported at the time, and in March a long-range Fire Point drone hit three Tornado-S launchers and a transport-loader near Karakul in occupied Crimea, as we reported. Two more launchers were hit near Melitopol within a few days in late April, followed by the July strike in the Huliaipole sector.
“Big names, formidable specifications and the millions invested in military equipment do not guarantee the occupiers’ immunity,” Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence said in its statement.
The Tornado-S was the centerpiece of a wider monthly report from Prymary, which HUR said also hit a Buk-M3 air defense system, an Orion reconnaissance and strike drone, a Kasta-2E low-altitude radar, a Nebo-U long-range surveillance radar and two P-18 early warning radars. The unit also struck a drone assembly and repair site and a building housing troops of the 4th Air Assault Battalion of the 108th Air Assault Regiment, although HUR gave no dates or locations for those strikes and did not say whether every target was destroyed or only damaged.

articles.title: Putin, Witkoff meet in Russia for Ukraine war talks
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Putin, Witkoff meet in Russia for talks on Ukraine war
Russia's Vladimir Putin began talks with US envoy Steve Witkoff on ending the Ukraine war in Saint Petersburg on Wednesday, with the American official saying he had brought "ideas" for a possible peace deal.
Witkoff travelled to Russia from Norway, where he met Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky in talks Washington described as "positive."
The meeting is taking place as the United States pushes an end to Europe's worst conflict since World War II, with Russia pounding Ukrainian cities ahead of winter and amid a bitter feud between Donald Trump and Zelensky.
As Witkoff touched down in Putin's home city, Russia announced it would soon begin shipments of diesel to the United States under a deal with Trump, and that it had freed a US citizen—Stephen Hubbard—held by Moscow since the start of the war on allegations of fighting as a "mercenary" for Ukraine.
"We've brought some papers. It's really some ideas, some sort of peace deal between Russia and Ukraine, and you'll read that at your leisure," Witkoff—Trump's business partner and envoy—told Putin in Saint Petersburg's Konstantinovsky Palace.
Putin thanked Trump for his efforts to resolve the war and said he was eager to be informed about the US meeting with Zelensky.
The longtime Russian leader has repeatedly refused to hold face-to-face talks with Zelensky and said that Moscow intends to seize the rest of eastern Ukraine.
Witkoff told Putin he hoped trilateral talks can resume.
"I'm hoping that you might consider that as a next step in the peace process so we can begin to have technical teams discussing what are those next steps," he told the Russian leader.
Putin thanked Trump for his "attention" to the conflict and said the US leader had "insisted that it was necessary to end this conflict" in their last phone call.
Russia's war against Ukraine has killed hundreds of thousands of troops on both sides as well as thousands of civilians.
As Witkoff arrived in Saint Petersburg, Kyiv said Moscow's strikes killed at least four people —including two in the capital and an elderly couple in the eastern Kharkiv region.
'Momentum' in talks
Meeting Putin, Witkoff described his talks with Zelensky as "productive."
"I think there's some degree of momentum and I hope that today can be another step forward in the peace process and discussing how we resolve the Ukrainian conflict," he said.
Zelensky on Tuesday thanked Washington for the resumption of US intelligence sharing on Russian strikes.
The Witkoff-Zelensky meeting in Norway followed days of friction between Washington and Kyiv, with Zelensky urging the US not to side with Russia and Trump calling for the Ukrainian leader to be replaced.
Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner is also due to participate in Wednesday's talks with Putin remotely.
US-led talks on the conflict have so far not led to a breakthrough and Moscow insists it intends to press on with its offensive.
Witkoff also told Putin that Washington was "grateful" for a diesel deal—met with astonishment in Kyiv and across Europe—that saw US sanctions on Moscow eased to allow Russian fuel to flow to the United States.
The deal has been seen as a way to try to lower fuel prices for American consumers ahead of testing midterm elections in the US next month.
Washington was interested in further "business and economic cooperation" with Russia when the war ends, Witkoff said.
"We even talk about it now openly with the Ukrainians to give them some sort of sense about what the possibilities will be when this whole conflict is over," he said.
Kyiv has pleaded with Western countries to put more pressure on Moscow and not lift sanctions.
Ahead of the talks, Putin announced that Stephen Hubbard, an American taken captive by Russian forces in Ukraine in 2022 and later sentenced to almost seven years in prison, had been freed.
Trump had asked the Russian leader to free Hubbard, a retired English teacher in his 70s who had always denied the charges he was a "mercenary" fighting for Ukraine.
Witkoff hailed the move and called Putin a "humanitarian".
Trump later said that Hubbard was on his way to the Unites States and that the release had not been part of a swap deal.

articles.title: Kallas lashes out at US over Ukraine peace efforts
articles.body:
Kallas lashes out at US over Ukraine peace efforts
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas has accused Washington of trying to force Ukraine to surrender to Russia, attacking President Donald Trump’s diplomatic efforts to end the conflict.
Speaking to the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Tuesday, Kallas credited Europe’s military and financial backing of Kiev with prolonging the conflict and preventing Ukraine from accepting Moscow’s terms.
“American negotiators have been trying to push Ukraine into surrender for already almost two years, one and a half years now,” she said, as quoted by Euronews.
Moscow has cited Kiev’s aggressive posture and the hostile position of its European backers as major obstacles to a peace settlement. Ukraine has consistently rejected Russia’s conditions, insisting on joining NATO and restoring control over all territories it claims.
Kallas’ remarks came a day after US President Donald Trump said negotiations were making “great progress,” defending his decision to ease economic pressure on Russia to keep diplomacy moving.
Trump has stepped up his criticism of Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky, describing him as “more difficult to deal with” than Russian President Vladimir Putin. He has accused Zelensky of prolonging the conflict and taking Washington’s extensive support for granted, and has criticized Kiev’s continued attacks on Russian refineries for disrupting global diesel markets. Zelensky has said he feels betrayed by Trump.
Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports earlier this month to curb rising energy prices ahead of the US midterm elections. On Friday, he suspended tariffs targeting China, India and other major buyers of Russian oil and gas. Trump defended the measures, saying he did not want to drive Moscow away from the negotiating table. The decisions drew criticism from European officials, with Kallas describing the diesel agreement as a “gift to Putin.”
US special envoy Steve Witkoff held talks in Oslo on Tuesday with Zelensky, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, with Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner joining remotely. Witkoff is expected to travel to St. Petersburg on Wednesday for another round of discussions with Russian officials, according to Store.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Monday that Moscow “highly appreciates” Washington’s continued mediation efforts.
Russia has insisted on a long-term peace deal that addresses the root causes of the conflict, rejecting the idea of a temporary truce. Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has accused Zelensky of repeatedly undermining negotiations, suggesting that any agreement acceptable to Moscow and Washington would threaten the Ukrainian leader’s hold on power.
Further financial support for Kiev has also become a source of disagreement within the EU. At Friday’s EU summit in Brussels, Zelensky demanded another €70 billion ($78.5 billion) for next year, in addition to €90 billion already pledged by the bloc to bankroll Kiev’s war effort.

articles.title: Ukrainian Partisans Cut Moscow Military Comms to Help Drones Slip Through Russian Air Defenses
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukrainian Partisans Cut Moscow Military Comms to Help Drones Slip Through Russian Air Defenses
Agents of the ATESH partisan movement are sabotaging Russian military communications around IXcellerate, one of Moscow’s largest commercial data centers, in an effort to disrupt air-defense coordination and help Ukrainian drones reach their targets, the group said on October 21.
“We are disabling enemy channels, disrupting command and control, and helping UAVs reach their targets,” ATESH said.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
IXcellerate is a major part of Moscow’s digital infrastructure, supporting banking applications, card payments, telecommunications operators, and business services.
ATESH claims that Russia’s Defense Ministry also uses infrastructure connected to the facility for military communications and air-defense command systems, effectively embedding military traffic within civilian server networks.
According to the movement, drone strikes depend not only on the aircraft themselves but also on disrupting the communications networks that connect Russian air-defense crews and command posts.
Cutting those links on the ground, ATESH says, can delay target information and reduce coordination between air-defense units.
Without stable communications, Russian air-defense crews can lose situational awareness, receive targeting information too late, and struggle to cover the routes used by incoming drones, the group said.
ATESH claims its agents are identifying military communications infrastructure concealed within civilian facilities and disrupting those networks from inside Russia.
The group said Moscow’s attempts to hide military traffic inside civilian server infrastructure have not prevented partisan cells from locating and targeting the communications links supporting Russian military operations.
Previously, ATESH claimed responsibility for sabotaging a critical electrical substation in Azov, Russia’s Rostov region, disrupting power to a defense manufacturing facility that produces guidance systems and other components for Russian missiles.

articles.title: Report: Netanyahu planned massive Iran attack, but Trump blocked it
articles.body:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu planned to launch a major new military offensive against Iran earlier this month, but President Donald Trump blocked the operation over concerns about restarting the war ahead of the November 3 U.S. midterm elections, the Financial Times reported Wednesday, citing three people familiar with the plans.
According to the FT, Netanyahu instructed the Israeli military to prepare a multi-day bombing campaign for the weekend of October 10, targeting Iranian nuclear facilities, power plants and other civilian infrastructure, as well as sites associated with the regime. The planned offensive was intended to surpass the intensity of the joint U.S.-Israeli military campaign launched in February.
The operation was ultimately shelved because of Trump's opposition, although both leaders have continued threatening renewed military action against Tehran. One person familiar with the discussions told the FT that another round of strikes in the coming weeks remained a realistic possibility, potentially involving both Israel and the United States.
"There will either be a deal or an attack," the person said, suggesting that Washington hopes to force Iran into an agreement addressing its nuclear program and control of the Strait of Hormuz, the strategic waterway through which much of the world's oil passes.
The report said Israeli officials had presented their American counterparts with an updated list of Iranian targets based on newly collected intelligence. The list reportedly includes civilian infrastructure sites that were not attacked during the previous campaign.
U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth visited Israel on Monday for talks with Netanyahu and other senior officials, according to an Israeli official cited by the newspaper. It remains unclear whether Washington had been expected to participate directly in the operation originally planned for October 10.
Another person familiar with the matter suggested that Israel's military preparations could also have been intended to increase pressure on Tehran during negotiations, emphasizing that the ultimate decision on renewed hostilities rested with Trump.
Deputy White House spokesperson Anna Kelly told the FT that Iran was in extremely poor economic and military condition and that U.S. efforts to blockade Iranian ports while facilitating Gulf oil exports were succeeding. She explicitly ruled out American strikes before the midterm elections.
The revelations come amid heightened military readiness in Israel ahead of the October 27 parliamentary election. IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir has ordered troops to remain on their bases beginning Thursday, suspending leave through election day to ensure voting can proceed safely.
Trump has meanwhile publicly endorsed Netanyahu's re-election bid and intensified his warnings to Tehran. On Sunday, he suggested that Washington could be forced to confront Iran without Israeli support if Netanyahu lost, while threatening further military action unless Iran changed course.
In a video released Monday from an Israeli air base, Netanyahu told Trump that they had unfinished business to complete together. Trump responded by praising the Israeli prime minister and expressing confidence in their partnership.
According to the FT, current and former Israeli security officials fear that a new war launched so close to the election could undermine the democratic process. Even if Netanyahu loses, he could remain caretaker prime minister for weeks while coalition negotiations proceed, retaining the legal authority to order military action.
The prime minister's office did not respond to the FT's requests for comment, while the IDF declined to comment.

articles.title: Suspicious drones spotted flying over French military sites
articles.body:
Members of the French navy stand on the deck of the Dixmude amphibious helicopter carrier in Toulon, France on Feb. 17, 2026. | Thibaud Moritz/AFP via Getty Images
PARIS — Suspicious drones flew over military facilities in southeastern France earlier this month, the French navy said on Wednesday.
During a large-scale armed forces exercise that lasted from Oct. 5 to Oct. 16, "unauthorized drones were detected in the no-fly zone, near and above military sites," the navy said in a press statement.
"In each instance, the planned security measures were activated by the deployment of anti-drone devices, in coordination with domestic security forces," it continued, adding that a judicial investigation was opened.
Advertisement
Suspicious drones are increasingly spotted in several European countries including Denmark, Germany and France, close to military sites and defense industry facilities. In July, a Moldovan man was arrested on suspicion of espionage after flying an unmanned aerial vehicle over a KNDS factory in Munich. Some of these drone incursions are attributed to Russia, as Moscow intensifies its hybrid attacks against European countries.
The French navy's statement confirms local media reporting about drone sightings around Toulon. The southeastern town is home to one of France's largest naval bases, which hosts the country's aircraft carrier Charles de Gaulle as well as attack submarines.
According to local broadcaster Ici Provence, the drones flew at night above the naval base, the General Directorate of Armaments facility in Toulon, and the 54th Artillery Regiment in Hyères. The military exercise, dubbed Typhon, was precisely aimed at training against drone sightings.
The navy said that no sensitive infrastructure was threatened. "The Ministry of the Armed Forces and Veterans Affairs reminds the public that unauthorized drone flights near or over military facilities are strictly prohibited," the statement concluded.

articles.title: Witkoff urges Putin to restart trilateral talks on Ukraine
articles.body:
United States special envoy Steve Witkoff has proposed that Russian President Vladimir Putin consider resuming trilateral talks involving Ukraine, the United States and Russia at the level of technical groups, and has handed over documents setting out approaches to a peace settlement of Russia's war against Ukraine, Russian media reported.
"I also hope you will consider resuming trilateral talks involving Ukraine, Russia and the United States, within which we could discuss next steps toward a settlement," Witkoff said at a meeting with Putin in St. Petersburg on Wednesday.
The talks could involve representatives of technical groups and experts who would work through the relevant issues in detail, he said. Witkoff expressed hope that the sides could discuss the proposal even if they do not reach a final decision at the current meeting.
The American envoy also said he had brought documents setting out approaches to a peace settlement and asked Putin to look at them. United States special envoy Jared Kushner was to join the meeting by phone, and, according to Witkoff, also wanted to present a few ideas.
After the Oslo talks on October 20, attended by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Witkoff and European representatives, Finnish President Alexander Stubb said the sides had discussed security, the economy, air defense, energy infrastructure and a partial ceasefire, including in the context of energy and food security.
Zelenskyy said the proposals worked out by Ukraine and its European partners provide for a move to a potential trilateral meeting of leaders to resolve issues that require decisions at the highest level. He said Witkoff was to pass these proposals to the Russian side.

articles.title: Russian-born Kazakhstani billionaire Timur Turlov is the new president of world chess. His election has divided Ukrainian officials, and Russia has abruptly dropped its case against him.
articles.body:
Russian-born Kazakhstani billionaire Timur Turlov is the new president of world chess. His election has divided Ukrainian officials, and Russia has abruptly dropped its case against him.
The election of a new head of the International Chess Federation (FIDE) has sparked a political scandal in Ukraine. Ukraine’s national chess federation criticized the choice of Timur Turlov, a Kazakhstani businessman who lived and did business in Russia for many years. But Turlov received unexpected support from Mykhailo Podolyak, an adviser to the head of President Zelensky’s office. A week later, Russia’s Prosecutor General’s Office withdrew its lawsuit seeking to seize Turlov’s income for the Russian state. Writing for Meduza, Ukrainian journalist Konstantin Skorkin explains everything that is known about FIDE’s leadership changes and the events that followed.
How the FIDE presidential election unfolded
Many international sports federations readily recruit influential businesspeople and politicians to lead them, using their connections to secure support and funding for their sports. For example, Sebastian Coe, a former member of Britain’s House of Lords, heads the International Association of Athletics Federations; Swedish billionaire Johan Eliasch leads the International Ski and Snowboard Federation; and French politician David Lappartient heads the International Cycling Union.
For the past two decades, FIDE has been led by Russians. Since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russians’ presence in international sports has often been seen as legitimizing the aggressor state. Some members of Russia’s elite have left international sports federations because of sanctions. Billionaire Vladimir Lisin, for example, no longer heads the International Shooting Sport Federation.
Others have held on to their positions. Alisher Usmanov, who had headed the International Fencing Federation since 2008, temporarily stepped aside in 2022 to keep the personal sanctions imposed on him from affecting the federation’s work. Just two years later, however, Usmanov won reelection.
The chess world has been home to a particularly large number of influential Russians. From 1995 to 2018, FIDE was headed by Kirsan Ilyumzhinov, who was president of the republic of Kalmykia when he was elected. Ilyumzhinov sought to make Elista, which hosted international chess tournaments, a global center for chess. In the late 1990s, a complex called City Chess was even built near the city.
In 2018, FIDE’s leadership called on Ilyumzhinov to resign: He had been placed under U.S. sanctions, which were hurting the federation’s work. Ilyumzhinov refused to leave voluntarily, however, and FIDE’s ethics commission had to remove him.
His successor was another Russian politician, former Deputy Prime Minister Arkady Dvorkovich, who had served in the leadership of the Russian Chess Federation. By the time he was elected head of FIDE, he was already chairman of the supervisory board of the Russian Agricultural Bank.
Dvorkovich is the son of the well-known chess coach Vladimir Dvorkovich, who was part of the coaching team that trained world chess champions Anatoly Karpov and Garry Kasparov.
The younger Dvorkovich led the world chess federation until July, when, like his predecessor, he was placed on a sanctions list — in his case, the EU’s, for “publicly supporting the actions of the Russian Federation” — and was forced to step away from FIDE’s leadership.
Earlier that year, in February, Ukraine had sanctioned the former deputy prime minister for supporting “Russian aggression,” along with nine Russian athletes.
The Ukrainian president’s website says the sanctions list was drawn up in response to a petition by Ukrainian skeleton racer Vladyslav Heraskevych. During the 2026 Winter Olympics, Heraskevych was disqualified for wearing a helmet bearing portraits of Ukrainian athletes killed during the war. Dvorkovich’s name, however, did not appear in Heraskevych’s petition, which was published on the Ukrainian government’s website.
The former FIDE head currently holds no government or political posts. Since leaving the chess federation, he has been working as a professor at the New Economic School in Russia. It recently emerged that Dvorkovich plans to challenge the European sanctions in an EU court.
Russia’s FIDE membership was suspended in June because the Chess Federation of Russia had established branches in occupied Ukrainian territory: the Donbas and the annexed parts of the Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions.
The election for a new FIDE president took place in September in Samarkand. Ilyumzhinov tried to run again but did not even make the official list of candidates.
Three candidates made the list:
- Vadim Rosenstein: A German businessman and founder of the WR Chess team, born in the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic, who holds Russian and German citizenship
- Jan Henric Buettner: A German businessman who invests heavily in chess championships
- Timur Turlov: A Kazakhstani businessman of Russian origin who has headed Kazakhstan’s chess federation since 2023
Delegates from FIDE’s national member federations elect its president. Delegates from 196 of the 202 countries eligible to vote officially registered for the election in Samarkand and received ballots.
Turlov and Rosenstein received the most votes in the first round. In the second round, Turlov won 110 votes to Rosenstein’s 85, with one FIDE delegate abstaining.
Who is Timur Turlov?
After Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Timur Turlov was among the Russian businesspeople who tried to distance themselves from Russia.
Born in Moscow, he graduated from the Tsiolkovsky Russian State Technological University (MATI) and began his business career as a trader for Moscow companies operating on the U.S. stock market. In 2008, Turlov founded Freedom Finance, which gave clients access to U.S. stock market infrastructure, including initial public offerings.
In 2012, he opened a subsidiary in Kazakhstan and began doing business there. In 2015, he established Freedom Holding Corp., registered in Nevada. It brought together the Russian and Kazakhstani Freedom Finance companies, the Freedom24 app, and Freedom Finance Bank. Turlov became the main shareholder. Freedom Finance Kazakhstan Bank joined the holding company in 2020, followed in 2021 by Freedom Finance Insurance, a group of Kazakhstani insurance companies.
In October 2019, Turlov listed Freedom Holding Corp. on Nasdaq. It became the first financial institution from the Commonwealth of Independent States to be listed on the exchange.
In January 2021, Turlov’s holding company acquired Prime Executions Inc., a U.S. broker-dealer registered with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. This gave the holding company’s clients direct access to the U.S. market. That same year, Turlov entered the Forbes global billionaires list in 1,517th place, with a fortune of $2.1 billion.
In June 2022, Turlov obtained Kazakhstani citizenship. To do so, he had to give up his Russian passport and the “offshore” passport he had previously obtained from St. Kitts and Nevis. At the same time, he announced that he was ending his business ties with Russia. By October 2022, the company’s Russian operations had been transferred to co-founder and Deputy CEO Maxim Povalishin. The deal was worth $140 million; the company soon rebranded as Tsifra.
According to Forbes Kazakhstan, Turlov ranks second among the country’s richest people and sixth among its most influential. In December 2025, he expanded his influence by acquiring the Kazakhstani telecommunications operator Transtelecom. Around the same time, his holding company began publishing a local edition of the glossy magazine Tatler.
After 2022, Turlov became involved in charitable projects in Kazakhstan. In spring 2023, he founded Kazakhstan’s QJ League for youth soccer and became chairman of its board of trustees. Late that year, Turlov launched Qalam, an online publication “devoted to the history and culture of the world as seen from Kazakhstan and Central Asia.”
His company spent a total of $66 million on charity in 2023, its representatives said.
Severing his business ties with Russia, however, did not help Turlov avoid sanctions. In October 2022, Ukraine placed him and his holding company’s Ukrainian subsidiary on its sanctions list alongside other figures in Russian or Russia-linked businesses. More than 2,500 individuals and 1,300 companies were sanctioned at the time. Others listed alongside Turlov included businessmen Mikhail Fridman, Oleg Deripaska, and Alexey Mordashov; pro-Russian Ukrainian politician Viktor Medvedchuk; and members of Alexander Lukashenko’s circle.
Turlov called his inclusion on the sanctions list “a clerical error.” The company promised to challenge it, though it took no concrete steps to do so. In 2023, Hindenburg Research investigated Freedom Holding Corp. and accused it of evading sanctions. The holding company’s shares fell 8% as a result. The investigation also drew the attention of the SEC, which launched its own inquiry. In January 2024, Freedom Holding Corp. commissioned an independent review that refuted Hindenburg’s findings.
Turlov has been involved in chess since January 2023, when he became head of Kazakhstan’s federation. He told journalists that he regularly plays as an amateur on Chess.com. “I try to enjoy the game itself,” Turlov said. “I’m not out to prove anything to anyone in chess.”
Why Ukraine’s federation opposed Turlov’s election as FIDE president — and where Mykhailo Podolyak comes in
The news outlet Agentstvo, citing an acquaintance of Turlov’s, reported that he has close ties to Kazakhstani President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and “does nothing without his approval.” In July, the outlet reported, Kazakhstan’s president met with Vladimir Putin and asked him to help Turlov win the FIDE election. Another source told Agentstvo that Putin agreed. After Turlov won the FIDE presidential election, Tokayev personally congratulated him.
Turlov’s victory sparked another scandal. The Ukrainian Chess Federation issued a statement saying it did not support his candidacy. It had initially nominated its own candidate, federation head Oleksandr Kamyshin, an outside adviser to Ukraine’s president and a former minister for strategic industries. Kamyshin, however, declined to run, saying his “priority during the war is developing chess in Ukraine.”
The FIDE presidential election uses a secret ballot, and it is not known whom the Ukrainian delegate voted for. Champion, Ukrainska Pravda’s sports website, reported that Ukraine’s federation most likely supported Buettner, who failed to reach the second round, because Ukrainian media also suspected Turlov’s main rival, Rosenstein, of doing business with Russia.
According to the news outlet UNIAN, revenue at 2R Integra, a company linked to Rosenstein’s family, grew roughly 40-fold after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and its website advertised services for supplying industrial equipment and electronics to Russia in circumvention of sanctions.
After Turlov’s victory, he received unexpected support from Mykhailo Podolyak, an adviser to the head of the Ukrainian president’s office. At the new FIDE president’s invitation, Podolyak became a vice president. Indian grandmaster and former world champion Viswanathan Anand became first vice president.
The alliance between Turlov and Podolyak came as a surprise for several reasons.
First, there had been no previous public reports of contact between the Kazakhstani businessman and the Ukrainian adviser. They also had no business ties or known history of political cooperation.
Second, Podolyak had no connection to the chess world and had never expressed an interest in the game. Discussing his new post in interviews, he gave an exclusively political rationale: He wanted to use the vice presidency to reduce Russian influence in the chess world while leaving sporting matters to the Ukrainian Chess Federation.
Yet it was with the Ukrainian Chess Federation that his relationship soured. Turlov arranged the appointment without involving the national federation, which sharply condemned Podolyak’s decision. The federation said it had received no offer to nominate a Ukrainian representative to the new FIDE head’s team, and its regional organizations sent a letter of protest to President Zelensky. The letter said:
By working with sanctioned individuals [Turlov — Meduza], Mykhailo Podolyak is legitimizing Russians’ presence in FIDE’s leadership and helping Russia maintain its influence over international chess. This undoes the efforts of Ukrainian chess players who have spent years fighting that influence.
Podolyak, in turn, criticized the Ukrainian Chess Federation for its “passive stance.” In his view, its officials had not done enough to counter Russian influence within FIDE. “They weren’t involved at all in getting rid of Dvorkovich’s team. They did absolutely nothing. Not publicly, not behind the scenes,” Podolyak said.
Ukrainian Chess Federation Vice President Volodymyr Kovalchuk maintains that Turlov is part of Dvorkovich’s team and simply “swapped in” for the sanctioned Russian. In Kovalchuk’s view, Podolyak helped legitimize this “castling” maneuver. Kovalchuk believes that “nothing will change” under Turlov:
Only the name has changed — Turlov will replace Dvorkovich. But I’m sure Dvorkovich will keep handling all of FIDE’s affairs. The entire Russian team is still there, and Dvorkovich will be the one actually running things, while Turlov will keep running his business. After all, he’s a Russian oligarch who made his money in Russia and is now investing it in Kazakhstan.
One detail supporting Kovalchuk’s prediction is the appointment of former Russian Sports Minister Alexander Kolobov as second vice president.
Podolyak continued to defend Turlov, calling Ukraine’s sanctions against the businessman “strange.” “When the full-scale invasion began, he became a Kazakhstani citizen and left Russia — which, unfortunately, still exists — behind for good. He also invested in humanitarian programs in Ukraine for a long time,” Podolyak said on Instagram.
Citing sources, Kommersant reported that Russia’s Prosecutor General’s Office moved in early October to have Turlov declared an “extremist” and his Russian assets confiscated over that humanitarian support. Law enforcement officials cited Freedom Holding’s transfer of 2 million euros for humanitarian aid to Ukraine. The money was intended to buy ambulances. A representative for Turlov said the businessman no longer had any assets in Russia.
In mid-October, it emerged that the Prosecutor General’s Office had withdrawn its lawsuit and the court had dismissed the case against Turlov. A representative of the prosecutor’s office did not give a reason for the decision.
In Ukraine, sanctions against Turlov’s company have begun to ease. In January 2025, Zelensky issued a decree allowing Ukrainian clients of Turlov’s brokerage to recover their assets. Their accounts had been frozen when sanctions were imposed three years earlier on the company, through which Ukrainians invested in government bonds and other securities.
For now, however, lifting the sanctions entirely is not on the table. Although the restrictions against Turlov were imposed for five years and expire in late 2027, his holding company acknowledges in its annual report that there is no guarantee he will be removed from the sanctions list.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].
To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter.

articles.title: Her own city is under Russian fire, yet Kyiv woman urges killing Ukrainians among nearly 100,000 pro-Kremlin posts in two years. She faces up to 12 years
articles.body:
Russia bombs Kyiv almost every day. Inside the same city, a single account spent two years pumping out nearly 100,000 posts in Russia’s favor. Ukraine’s Security Service has served notices of suspicion on six more pro-Kremlin agitators across the country, among them the Kyiv woman behind those posts, which included calls to kill Ukrainians, the agency said.
Social media has become a channel for spreading hatred during the war, and the scale is striking. Except for Russian narratives, the Kyiv suspect also incited violence against a national minority and called for destroying the churches of religious communities, the agency said.
The agency framed the six as part of a wider effort to justify Russia’s aggression and inflame ethnic and religious hatred. Investigators notified them of suspicion.
Six accounts, one message from the Kremlin
The others span the country. In Mykolaiv, SBU cyber specialists detained a person they say acted on a Russian handler’s orders, administering a local Telegram channel of more than 13,000 subscribers in support of Russian forces, investigators said.
In Cherkasy Oblast, the wife of a priest of the Moscow-linked Ukrainian Orthodox Church allegedly praised Vladimir Putin and denied Russia’s aggression in Telegram chats, while a Russian citizen with permanent residence in Ukraine allegedly called the full-scale war an “internal civil conflict.” In Zakarpattia region, two women allegedly urged the region’s “separation” from Ukraine.
What the suspects face, and where this fits
The charges are grave. The suspects were notified under several articles of Ukraine’s Criminal Code, including inciting ethnic and religious hatred combined with threats and justifying Russian aggression, and face up to 12 years in prison with confiscation of property, the agency said.
The sweep continues a long campaign against homegrown pro-Russian propagandists. In February, the SBU detained three suspected agitators who used Telegram and TikTok to call for missile strikes on Kyiv and to justify Russian war crimes, part of a pattern in which Moscow recruits users online to spread its narratives.
