articles.title: De-Modification: India’s “Cockroach” party is challenging the country’s slide toward autocracy
articles.body:
Authorities in Delhi have shut down the metro, cut off mobile internet, and detained hundreds of opposition members — including the leader of an opposition youth movement called the Cockroach Janta Party. Narendra Modi’s government is cracking down on a wave of protests inspired by his decision to strike 130 million voters from the rolls. The opposition and human rights activists claim that the ruling Hindus are disenfranchising mainly Muslims, and the government has used force to break up protests whose stated goal is the resignation of the head of the national election commission. It appears that, despite the years Modi spent “conditioning” Indian society, he has so far failed to turn the world’s largest secular democracy into a truly authoritarian nationalist state.
The Indian youth protest movement Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has hit a sore spot in the cult carefully constructed around the figure of Prime Minister Narendra Modi. After pro-government media questioned the education of CJP leader Abhijeet Dipke, Dipke proposed that he and Modi release their diplomas at the same time. The hint is easy to read: the head of the government apparently has no authentic higher education documents, and such blows to Modi’s vanity obviously irritate the ruling elites.
The diploma scandal has not emerged out of nowhere: India, once “the planet’s largest democracy,” is gradually degenerating into an authoritarian regime with decorative elections. The government consistently subjugates the courts and the election commission, persecutes political opponents, and encourages a nationalist Hindu doctrine. Harassment of Muslims — in particular the demonstrative demolitions of the homes of those who stand up for the rights of religious minorities — has become the norm. The authorities follow the principle “for friends, everything; for enemies, the law,” with the regime catering to the interests of big business and politicians close to it. Meanwhile, police brutality reigns on the streets against those whom the regime has designated as its enemies.
India, once “the planet’s largest democracy,” is gradually degenerating into an authoritarian regime
For a long time, the status quo rested on two fundamental pillars: the conformism of the urban middle class and mass handouts to the poor through digital platforms. These measures helped the Modi regime mask deep social tensions.
However, there are checks and balances slowing India’s slide into a full-fledged autocracy: the ruling party’s loss of an absolute majority in the 2024 general election, the defiance of regional authorities in the Indian states, and economic problems, especially unemployment among educated youth. With social mobility jammed, the monopoly on fear has cracked — it is being displaced by caustic grassroots protest, symbolized by the Cockroach Party.
Authoritarianism with a democratic facade
Since the early 1950s, India has been considered the world’s largest democracy — hundreds of millions vote in general elections where turnout regularly exceeds 60%, election commissions reach even the most remote Himalayan villages with portable electronic voting terminals, and transfers of power historically take place without military coups. However, over the past few years, international research centers have revised their categorizations of the country’s political system.
Sweden’s Varieties of Democracy (V-Dem) Institute at the University of Gothenburg has moved India into the category of “electoral autocracy,” placing it 106th out of 179 countries. The U.S.-based NGO Freedom House has downgraded the country’s rating from “free” to “partly free,” with an overall score of 62 out of 100. The analytical unit at The Economist has shifted India down to its level of “flawed democracies.”
The country has not yet grazed the bottom of this particular ranking (“hybrid” or “authoritarian” regimes), but in 2022 India fell to last place in the global Environmental Performance Index (EPI) — a decline largely explained by the Indian government consistently dismantling independent environmental monitoring groups, persecuting environmental NGOs as “anti-national” structures, and blocking civil society’s participation in decisions on the construction of large industrial facilities.
This depreciation predictably irritated Delhi, with officials accusing Western analysts of bias and colonial thinking. Nevertheless, the researchers’ conclusions rest on a fundamental postulate of modern regime theory: competitive elections alone cannot protect a society from authoritarian degeneration.
Competitive elections alone cannot protect a society from authoritarian degeneration
The Indian model showcases an authoritarian transformation typical of the 21st century. Unlike stereotypical dictatorships of the past, India has not abolished the constitution, dissolved parliament, or declared a state of emergency. The multiparty facade remains intact, and the government relies on a real majority of votes in the legislature.
However, the electoral process unfolds simultaneously with an ongoing destruction of the system of checks and balances on executive power and the subordination of independent institutions to it, the neutralization of the courts’ independence, and the suppression of any organized resistance outside of the voting procedure.
Nationalism for the loyal, lawlessness for the rest
One of the key concepts describing the Indian political system is nationalist populism, which relies on carefully cultivated ressentiment, which the government successfully exploits to mobilize the cultural and historical grievances of the national majority. The dismantling of the institutional system of checks and balances is then presented to society not as a usurpation of powers but as a necessary defense of the people from corrupt elites and threatening minorities.
In Indian political practice, this model is implemented through the doctrine of Hindu nationalism, or Hindutva, which serves as the main tool for promoting majoritarian identity and the systemic marginalization of the Muslim minority (about 14.2% of the population). According to expert reports, the number of documented cases of incitement to hatred against religious minorities in India rose by 97% between 2023 and 2025.
Internationally, researchers find direct parallels between Indian nationalist mobilization and the building of an “illiberal democracy” in Viktor Orbán’s Hungary, where appeals to the nation’s historical traumas likewise became the main fuel for changing the constitutional order.
Indian nationalist mobilization under Modi is compared to Hungary’s exploitation of historical traumas under Orbán
Another important mechanism for retaining control is the effect of “increasing returns to scale,” characteristic of many modern electoral autocracies in Latin America and Asia. Essentially, a political force that has gained an initial electoral advantage uses the status of incumbent to radically and irreversibly change the playing field in its favor.
In today’s India, loyalist security forces work to eliminate the opposition’s sources of financing. While no one cancels regular elections on paper, rivals of the authorities have their campaign money taken away on false pretexts.
Along the way, critics are methodically squeezed out of the media, culture, and universities, leaving the state as the sole contender in the battle for minds. Regular campaigns to find and persecute so-called “anti-national elements” in Indian universities, as well as the establishment of control over the editorial policy of leading television holdings, largely repeat the typical authoritarian moves that were used to build the one-party systems of the 20th century.
India’s authoritarian transit has birthed the model of a “dual state,” one in which the legal system is split into two distinct circuits. The regulatory circuit — for big business and the loyal majority — has clear rules of the game, civil courts, and a stable investment climate. For the opposition, activists, and the independent press, however, a zone of selective arbitrary use of force is created, where the norms of law give way to political expediency under the pretext of protecting national security. This resembles the Jim Crow regime in the U.S. South, where until the 1960s court verdicts depended largely on the racial identity of victims and defendants.
Modi-fication of the state
The central figure and chief architect of this political transformation is Prime Minister Narendra Modi, whose approach to governance has changed the mechanics of Indian power. His policy is built on deeply personalized state institutions and the creation of a direct emotional bond with the electorate.
Publicly, Modi cultivates the image of a man of humble origins who started out selling tea at a railway station, devoted himself to serving the nation, and firmly opposes the out-of-touch dynastic elites of the past. This image allows him to retain voters’ trust even during economic downturns. Modi’s governing style is marked by strict centralization: key decisions are made by the prime minister’s office, while the role of the government and parliament is merely to formally approve ready-made initiatives.
Modi prefers to communicate with citizens directly, avoiding open press conferences where journalists could challenge him with uncomfortable questions. His regular radio addresses, social media presence (utilizing armies of bots), and carefully orchestrated mass rallies create the illusion of Modi’s personal presence in the country’s everyday life. Every significant achievement, be it a successful space mission, the development of a vaccine, or a social assistance program, is branded with Modi’s name and portrait. Such an approach makes the state bureaucracy part of the leader’s personal political brand, and loyalty to the state begins to be equated with loyalty to the prime minister personally.
Whereas the former Indian establishment built a secular republic based on the state’s neutrality toward religions, the fundamental task of Modi’s team is to reassemble the country as a Hindu civilizational state. In this concept, India must not merely become an economic superpower but also take the place of a universal spiritual mentor for the whole world. In school textbooks, Hindu civilization is presented not only as the most ancient in the world but also one that once possessed unique technological achievements.
Claims that in the Vedic period aviation, plastic surgery, and genetic manipulation somehow existed became the foundation for Modi supporters’ assertions of India’s civilizational superiority and a way to overcome the inferiority complex tied to the colonial past. Pro-government scholars have openly begun to claim that Isaac Newton and Albert Einstein were wrong and that gravitational waves should be renamed “Narendra Modi waves.”
The use of Sanskrit and ancient philosophy in international discourse and the promotion of yoga and Ayurveda as “India’s contribution to global development” serve as soft-power tools meant to secure for India the status of a “civilizational state.” The ultimate goal of this process is to establish Hindu nationalism as the only legitimate basis of statehood, finally pushing secular pluralism to the margins of political life.
War on the opposition, journalists, and Muslims
Political scientists describe what is happening in India as “autocratization through legality,” a process well illustrated by the familiar principle “for friends, everything; for enemies, the law.” The ruling Bharatiya Janata Party has mastered the use of the apparatus of state coercion to formally follow procedural norms while making political competition unequal from the start.
The main lever of pressure on the opposition is specialized investigative and fiscal bodies — first of all, financial crime departments. Over the past ten years, the vast majority of cases brought by these agencies against politicians have involved members of the opposition camp.
The vast majority of criminal cases against politicians under Modi are cases against the opposition
In the run-up to the recent election, even sitting leaders of opposition states ended up under arrest, and the country’s oldest political force, the Indian National Congress (INC), lost access to its bank resources, which paralyzed its election campaign. At the same time, criminal prosecutions against politicians who are willing to switch to the ruling coalition’s side are often suspended.
Anti-corruption investigations are launched against opposition leaders and prominent regional administrators, their party and personal accounts are frozen, and the leaders themselves are held in prison for months without a verdict. This is made possible by the specifics of anti-money-laundering legislation, which places the burden of proving innocence on the accused and practically rules out release on bail at the investigation stage.
Statistics on criminal cases against political opponents under Modi bear out what human rights activists say. The Enforcement Directorate (ED), India’s main financial investigation agency, has been especially active. Before Modi was elected prime minister in 2014, the ED carried out 112 politically motivated searches; under his rule, the number of raids reached 2,974, and the total number of registered cases exceeded 5,400.
The total value of assets seized from opposition members and public figures grew from 53.46 billion to 1.16 trillion rupees (roughly $14 billion). From 2004 to 2014, 14 out of 26 politicians under investigation were prominent opposition figures (54%). After Modi’s election, this figure rose to 95% — of the 121 major politicians who came under ED investigation, 115 already belonged to opposition parties.
Human rights organizations document the degradation of the country’s election oversight institution. India’s Election Commission, once an independent arbiter, has gradually lost its autonomy after the government changed the procedure for appointing its members. Now this “Putin-style” oversight body regularly shows a selective approach during campaigns, ignoring the use of hate speech and religious polarization by the ruling party but harshly cracking down on violations by the opposition.
The information space has suffered comparable erosion. The largest TV channels and newspaper holdings have come under the control of business conglomerates closely tied to the government. These media do not merely broadcast the authorities’ position but also deliberately stigmatize critics of the regime, activists, and human rights defenders, declaring them a threat to national security. The authorities use tax audits, searches, and harsh antiterrorism legislation against independent digital platforms and investigative journalists. India has also become the global leader in the number of localized internet shutdowns.
The largest Indian media holdings have come under the authorities’ control and harass critics of the regime
In parallel, Modi’s authoritarian regime has paralyzed the work of the nonprofit sector. By tightening the requirements of the foreign funding law, the authorities cut off access to grants for thousands of nongovernmental organizations. Leading think tanks, along with environmental and human rights groups, came under pressure, lost their licenses to receive foreign aid, and were forced to wind down operations or abandon a critical agenda for the sake of physical survival.
As part of this new ideological course, Indian Muslims have begun to be systemically marginalized. Amendments to the Citizenship Act have made religious affiliation an official criterion, and laws against interfaith marriages are being passed at the state level.
A commonplace practice that has become part of everyday life is so-called “bulldozer justice.” Under the pretext of fighting illegal construction, municipal authorities who enjoy police backing demolish the homes and shops of people suspected of antigovernment crimes or participation in street protests. This practice of collective punishment is applied selectively and hits mainly Muslim communities and other vulnerable groups, turning the threat of instant loss of property into an effective instrument of intimidation.
Researchers note that violence by radical groups often goes without due attention from law enforcement. Extremists carry out extrajudicial reprisals against Muslims involved in the meat trade or cattle transport, but instead of investigating attacks, police often open criminal cases against surviving victims or their relatives on charges of cow slaughter, destroying the secular foundation of the state.
The judiciary shows noticeable indecision in standing up to the executive. The Supreme Court periodically issues rulings in defense of basic rights, but on the most politically sensitive questions judges dodge adjudication, putting off consideration of key constitutional suits for years and thereby allowing the government to accustom the country to political arbitrariness.
Authoritarianism finds its limits
In the context of the global confrontation with China, most Western capitals view New Delhi as an indispensable partner in Asia — an important market and a manufacturing alternative. To preserve the strategic alliance, international diplomacy (with rare exceptions) prefers to overlook the dismantling of legal institutions in India, instead sticking with the familiar rhetoric of shared democratic values.
Nevertheless, Indian society shows the limitations of this political model. The results of the 2024 parliamentary election demonstrated that autocratization is not total: voters dissatisfied with economic inequality and unemployment deprived the ruling party of an absolute majority, proving that social problems can still counterbalance the effects of state propaganda and erode universal consolidation around Modi’s nationalist ideology.
The loss of an absolute majority turned Narendra Modi’s one-man rule into a classic coalition government, with all of the compromises that entails. Open anti-Muslim polarization has eased because of the ruling party’s dependence on moderate secular allies in the regions, whose success in local elections, in turn, depends on religious minorities.
The adoption of the most radical ideological laws — including the national Uniform Civil Code, which would restrict the religious freedoms of Muslim and Christian communities — has also been put on hold. Also postponed are controversial labor market reforms that shifted the balance of power in favor of employers by dismantling basic social guarantees for workers.
Although Modi has retained control over the security apparatus and media, the strengthened opposition is trying to revive real debate in parliament and prevent the government from pushing through laws without public consultations.
Total control in exchange for food
The presence of the state in the everyday life of ordinary Indians has expanded greatly during Narendra Modi’s twelve years in power. The most noticeable change for the average voter has been the creation of a digital distribution pipeline for social benefits.
In the past, the provision of assistance depended on convoluted local bureaucracy, influential village elders, or local self-government bodies — panchayats — which inevitably generated corruption and patronage at the local level. However, the introduction of the national biometric Aadhaar system and a direct cash transfer mechanism allowed the federal center to send subsidies directly: for buying cooking gas, laying water pipelines, and building toilets (under the Clean India program).
This technological breakthrough earned the government a colossal new base of supporters — the so-called “labharthis,” or direct recipients of benefits from the federal budget. For millions of voters, this tangible increase in the efficiency of the state apparatus, together with the mass construction of roads, appears to be an acceptable price to pay for giving up abstract democratic freedoms.
For millions of poor voters, federal budget aid and new roads proved more important than democratic freedoms
At the same time, social assistance is presented not as the realization of a citizen’s constitutional rights, but as a personal gift from the head of government. Photos of Modi on sacks of free food, on vaccination certificates, and on billboards create a sense among the population of the leader’s continuous personal involvement in the struggle to solve their everyday problems.
Nevertheless, this total digitization has turned into a new form of administrative coercion for the poorest segments of the population. To receive help from the state, one must regularly undergo biometric identification. Yet the system often experiences glitches — fingerprint scanners break, the internet in remote villages is unstable, and linking personal Aadhaar numbers is prone to errors. These glitches result in the automatic freezing of bank accounts, delays in pension payments, and the exclusion of entire families from lists of those receiving vital foods.
International media outlets investigated the case of Santoshi Kumari, an 11-year-old girl from Jharkhand who died of hunger after her family’s ration was cut off because it was not linked to Aadhaar properly. “There are tens of thousands of such cases in the country. In at least 10-15 states, people have died of starvation,” says Colin Gonsalves, a lawyer representing the victims. Rigid and inhumane digital bureaucracy has turned technological progress into a tool of marginalization against those who were unable to seamlessly integrate into the new digital reality.
In parallel with the digitization of social welfare, the state has begun to demonstrate unprecedentedly harsh methods of maintaining order and suppressing dissent on the ground. The streets of Indian cities are rapidly being covered by networks of video cameras equipped with facial recognition systems, and security forces are ever more actively monitoring social media and geolocation to identify critics of the authorities.
In everyday life, ordinary Indians are forced to deal not only with official representatives of the law but also with grassroots religious-nationalist groups that operate with the obvious connivance — and sometimes the direct support — of the state. Organizations such as radical cow protectors or the nationalists’ youth wing Bajrang Dal have taken on the functions of an informal morality police, coming down on Christian and Muslim communities and their way of life.
Nationalists and cow protectors enjoying state support have taken on the role of morality police, interfering in the private lives of Christians and Muslims
They conduct inspections of freight transport on highways, interfere in citizens’ private lives, obstruct interfaith marriages, and monitor compliance with religious norms in daily life. In some regions, the official police are effectively merging with such activists, who are granted the status of law enforcement volunteers.
Activists track interfaith marriage applications at state registry offices (where lists of couples to be married are traditionally posted publicly), carry out raids on newlyweds’ homes, and demand the opening of criminal cases against Muslims. On Valentine’s Day, militants police the dress code and intimidate women who wear clothing “unbecoming to Indian culture.” In parks, cafés, and shopping malls, they hunt down young couples, demanding proof of kinship or forcing them to marry on the spot.
All of this creates an atmosphere of total ideological control in which citizens feel continuously watched — even if there is not a single uniformed police officer nearby.
Local bureaucracy, which was historically oriented toward cooperating with regional politicians and elected councils, has also been placed under strict federal control. The government in New Delhi has built a system to monitor district magistrates and heads of regional agencies through regular video conferences and mandatory targets for nationwide campaigns.
As a result, local officials increasingly orient themselves to directives from above, ignoring the needs of local residents and the decisions of municipal democratic institutions. The state apparatus is becoming a monolithic and pliable instrument in the hands of the central authorities.
“New Indians” against freedom
A directive from above alone cannot accomplish an authoritarian turn; instead, it requires the silent consent and day-to-day conformism from thousands of rank-and-file functionaries — a tax inspector who initiates an audit of an opposition publication or a judge who postpones for years the consideration of a sensitive constitutional suit, even if they do not personally support the regime’s increasingly hardline ideology. Most often they are guided by routine pragmatism, understanding that in the new reality their career prospects are in direct dependence on their ability to read unspoken political signals.
A key role in legitimizing this order belongs to India’s growing urban middle class. For the Indian petit bourgeois, new overpasses and a rising stock market are quite sufficient compensation for the arrests of human rights activists.
For the Indian petit bourgeois, new overpasses and a rising stock market are quite sufficient compensation for the arrests of human rights activists
The readiness of Indian society for an authoritarian-nationalist transit is confirmed by specific sociological surveys that record the erosion of the country’s longstanding democratic consensus. According to a Pew Research Center study, India now shows one of the highest levels of support for autocracy in the world.
Overall, 85% of Indian respondents agreed that rule by a strong leader or the military is an example of good governance. At the same time, 82% of those surveyed supported the idea of handing power to unelected technocratic experts. The share of those who consider representative democracy the best form of government, meanwhile, fell from 44% in 2017 to 36% in 2024.
In parallel, a study by the Centre for the Study of Developing Societies (Lokniti-CSDS) recorded a drop in the authority of the Election Commission of India. In 2019, 51% of voters expressed high trust in the commission, but by 2024 that figure had collapsed to 28%. At the same time, 21.7% of respondents said the commission works “completely” under pressure from the central government, and 44.7% expressed fear that under the pretext of audits real voters would be excluded from the rolls.
In key regions, the level of trust in the Election Commission fell even further: from 56% to 31% in Uttar Pradesh, and from 68% to 41% in West Bengal. These statistics clearly show the mechanics of autocratization: the state systematically dismantles institutions, relying on a significant part of the electorate to consciously reject the values of liberal democracy in favor of effective dictatorship.
The specifics of Indian autocracy
Despite common basic features — ressentiment, witch hunts, harsh control over the media, talk of a unique civilization, digital hypercontrol — the Indian blend of autocracy differs fundamentally from its Chinese or Russian counterparts.
China is a closed one-party system without even a semblance of elections or a legal opposition. India, meanwhile, retains real multiparty competition, its citizens freely take part in voting, and opposition parties have the opportunity to campaign openly and win (even if the odds are being increasingly stacked against them).
Comparison with Russia also reveals key differences: whereas in Russia elections lack competitive intrigue, in India the electoral process at least remains unpredictable. The enormous logistical scale of Indian elections and their administration by independent technical entities make total falsification of results from a single center practically impossible.
Closer analogues of the Indian regime are the competitive authoritarian systems of Erdoğan in Turkey and the recently ousted Orbán in Hungary. All three cases are characterized by a concentration of power in the hands of a national leader, pressure on independent media, and active use of religious and civilizational rhetoric to legitimize their rule.
However, the Indian model has three fundamental differences from the other two cases. First, India is a gigantic federation whose key states are governed by strong regional parties with their own financial and electoral base, which prevents the establishment of a rigid power vertical on the Turkish model.
In Turkey, after suffering sporadic defeats in the 2024 municipal elections, Erdoğan moved to direct administrative suppression of the opposition Republican People’s Party (CHP), arresting popular mayors and replacing them with government appointees.
In India, such a scenario would be extremely hard to execute nationwide. The states of West Bengal, Tamil Nadu, and Kerala are an insurmountable barrier to the expansion of Modi’s nationalist ideology, preserving alternative centers of power.
Second, the ruling BJP relies on the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, a mass movement with a century-long history, united by a common ideology and deeply rooted in the nation’s everyday life. Unlike the Hungarian system of political loyalty built on the distribution of state money and privileges, this network can operate even without such support.
Third, Modi’s government has built a system of direct digital patronage, forming a multimillion-strong class of social benefit recipients who perceive assistance as the leader’s personal care.
The limits of Indian authoritarianism clearly showed in the general parliamentary elections of 2024. Despite administrative pressure and unequal financial conditions, voters deprived Modi’s party of an absolute one-party majority, forcing it to form a coalition government with regional forces.
This development confirmed the researchers’ conclusions that Indian society retains a deeply rooted “democratic spirit,” and the country’s electoral institutions remain a functioning channel of civic oversight.
“Cockroaches” vs. the authorities
In the face of the system for suppressing the opposition built by the Indian state, the main threat to Narendra Modi’s regime paradoxically turned out to be not a classic political party but an absurdist youth movement. In the spring of 2026, the country’s political landscape was blown up by the so-called Cockroach Party (Cockroach Janta Party, or CJP).
In a matter of weeks, the movement transformed from an internet meme into a real force capable of bringing hundreds of thousands of people into the streets — and of using their leverage to secure resignations in the federal government. Its phenomenon exposed the fragility of authoritarian populism when confronted by grassroots self-irony and the consolidated anger of a young generation deprived of social mobility.
The movement’s emergence was catalyzed by a gaffe by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant. In mid-May 2026, during one of the hearings, he spoke disparagingly of unemployed young people who go into activism, social media, and journalism, comparing such young people to cockroaches and social parasites.
Although the judge soon tried to disavow his statement, citing the fact that he had meant only people with fake degrees, his words hit the very nerve of Indian society. Against a backdrop of record youth unemployment and a sense of total hopelessness, these words were perceived as the quintessence of the ruling elite’s attitude toward its own citizens.
The response was a lightning-fast initiative by 30-year-old political strategist and activist Abhijeet Dipke. The next day, May 16, he announced the creation of a new political force whose very name, Cockroach Janta Party, was a direct mockery of the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party.
The Cockroach Party’s manifesto was written in a pointedly mocking vein. The movement declared itself to be the voice of the “lazy and unemployed,” stating that if you have no job and plenty of free time, you automatically qualify as a “cockroach” and can join the party. This post-ironic approach had an effect. Instead of justifying themselves to the authorities or trying to play by the rules of traditional politics, young people appropriated the insulting label, making the cockroach a symbol of resilience and survival in a toxic environment.
The growth dynamic was impressive: in less than a week, the party’s Instagram page gained almost 18 million followers — twice the audience of the official account of Prime Minister Modi’s party, which took years and giant budgets to build.
The success of CJP is explained by the fact that the movement filled a gap that had gone unfilled by the traditional Indian media, which are under the tight control of loyalist big businesses. However, the Cockroach Party completely ignored television format, moving the battlefield into the digital space, where social media algorithms and viral memes proved stronger than government censorship.
Every day, thousands of videos and satirical posts poured onto the web — ridiculing corruption and officials’ incompetence, along with the pompous rhetoric of Hindu nationalism. Government propagandists proved powerless against teenagers and students who openly laughed at themselves and at the absurdity of what was happening.
Government propagandists proved powerless against teenagers and students who openly laugh at themselves and at the absurdity of what is happening
What began as online satire soon transformed into a powerful factor in street politics, testing the limits of the regime’s administrative control. In June 2026, India was rocked by a major scandal over mass leaks of question papers for the nationwide NEET-UG exam, which regulated admission to medical schools. More than 2 million students were forced to retake the tests, which became the last straw for many young people.
The Cockroach Party instantly converted its virtual capital into real mobilization. In New Delhi at Jantar Mantar and in dozens of other cities across the country, mass sit-ins and protest marches began, coordinated by CJP. Students were joined by environmental activists, public figures, and even their parents.
The authorities tried to use their usual repressive methods, and on July 20, police used tear gas, batons, and rubber pellet guns against a crowd of many thousands in New Delhi. However, the attempt to intimidate the “cockroaches” backfired, causing a wave of solidarity across the country. Moreover, the ruling party’s favorite tactic of splitting protesters failed: in CJP’s ranks, Hindus and Muslims, along with members of different Hindu castes, stood side by side, united by common social discontent.
Faced with the risk that the protests might spiral out of control, the government made unprecedented concessions. In late July, Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned, marking one of the rarest cases in which the Modi regime yielded to street pressure. Then the Supreme Court quashed all criminal cases brought against participants in the student protests.
The symbolic weakening of Modi’s regime was also evident in how the leadership of the Cockroach Party learned to deconstruct the image of the prime minister. When in September 2026 pro-government commentators tried to discredit Abhijeet Dipke by questioning the authenticity of his education at Boston University, he publicly proposed that Narendra Modi simultaneously show the people his higher education documents, reminding everyone that the courts had earlier refused to disclose the Indian prime minister’s academic qualifications, making this issue extremely painful for the ruling party. Such audacity on the part of informal politicians destroys the carefully constructed aura of sanctity around the figure of the national leader.
For a long time, the Indian state was held together by a tacit agreement: the authorities could freely crush human rights activists, infringe on Muslims, and demolish their homes without trial — but only so long as the unpleasantness remained on the margins of society, affecting mostly “outsiders.” The urban middle class willingly turned a blind eye to the violence — and in return it got new overpasses, a rising stock market, and familiar rules of the game in business.
But this deal began to fall apart when the police baton came down on their own children. It turned out that the state does not know how to behave otherwise: in response to outrage over the disrupted exams, young people got tear gas in the streets, public insults from judges and the language of force from the government. The image of a sensibly governed country turns out to be extremely hard to maintain when arbitrariness goes beyond isolated ghettos and begins to threaten the future of ordinary families.

articles.title: Trump and Putin, Silicon Valley war lords and rejecting Palantir
articles.body:
Trump and Putin, Silicon Valley war lords and rejecting Palantir
Welcome to our press review of events in the United States. Every Wednesday we look at how the Swiss media have reported and reacted to three major stories in the US – in politics, finance and science.
War has been the dominant theme in the Swiss newspapers in the last week: US interference in the Ukraine war, the rise of warmongering in Silicon Valley and the repeated rejection of Palantir by the Swiss military.
Help us improve the press review
As a reader of our weekly press review, your feedback is important to us. Please take two minutes to answer a short survey and help us improve our journalism. This survey is anonymous and all data is confidential.
👉 [Take the surveyExternal linkExternal link]
The Swiss media has wasted no time in again blasting US foreign policy after Donald Trump lifted sanctions against Russia and apparently took sides with Vladimir Putin against Ukraine.
One phone call between the leaders of the US and Russia has tilted the balance of power decisively against Ukraine, which has been told to stop bombing Russian oil refineries as Russian bombs continue to rain down on its energy infrastructure.
“Under Trump, the US has repeatedly stabbed a beleaguered Ukraine in the back,” opines the Tages Anzeiger. “This misguided policy will never make Moscow willing to make peace but will only prolong the war.”
“The global public should observe closely – and the American people should refuse to be taken for fools.”
Le Temps asks what Trump has to gain from giving Putin the upper hand in his war with Ukraine. The newspaper suggests that Russia could offer its expert services in hacking, trolling and public disinformation.
The newspaper cites several instances when Russian agencies have sought to influence past votes in the US. In each case, the targets have been Democrats. “Russia’s expertise in disinformation could once again prove valuable in discrediting democratic institutions,” says Le Temps.
- Trump policy will prolong Ukraine warExternal link – Tages Anzeiger (German, paywall)
- Le Temps asks what Trump wants from RussiaExternal link – (French, paywall)
Silicon Valley used to be a factory for computing, social media and apps. Now it is increasingly turning to the industry of war, according to the Tages Anzeiger.
Lockheed Martin and Northrop could soon be replaced by the likes of Meta and OpenAI as the manufacturers of military might, the newspaper argues. “It is about who controls the technical foundation of national security.”
This is a far cry from Silicon Valley’s recent ideals, which resembled Californian hippies more than the crew-cuts of West Point. “The culture of the military felt alien to these T-shirt-clad techies. Though Big Tech was powerful, it projected a pacifist image,” writes the newspaper.
But times are changing, personified by Elon Musk being called in by the US Department of Defence to advise on the “future of warfare.”
“The industry’s leading figures are part of a nationalistic revival movement—one that seeks to make the US military, and other armed forces around the world, dependent upon them,” states the Tages Anzeiger.
“Precisely at this moment, Europe must be extremely careful about whom it entrusts with the construction of its national security infrastructure.”
- The Tages Anzeiger connects Silicon Valley with warExternal link – (German, paywall)
Switzerland is not proving to be a happy hunting ground for US data firm Palantir. The magazine Republik has previously reported on cold shouldering by the Swiss army.
Republik, along with WAV Recherchekollectiv, now it has more details – the services of Palantir were rejected five times by Swiss military officials between 2020 and this year.
The main objections revolved around control over data, access of Palantir engineers to data and guarantees of confidentiality of sensitive military information. For now, the Swiss armed forces appear unconvinced by Palantir’s credentials in these areas.
But this does not exclude the possibility of future Palantir contracts, Republik states. Defence minister Martin Pfister is refusing to rule out future cooperation with the US data firm, despite pressure from some parliamentarians.
“A back door for Palantir, therefore, remains open,” the magazine writes.
- Republik’s report on PalantirExternal link – (German, paywall)
The next edition of ‘Swiss views of US news’ will be published on Wednesday, October 28. See you then!
If you have any comments or feedback, email english@swissinfo.ch

articles.title: Russia is ready to help resolve Iran-US dispute, Putin says
articles.body:
Russia is ready to help resolve Iran-US dispute, Putin says
TEHRAN— Russian President Vladimir Putin has said Moscow is ready to help resolve the dispute between Iran and the United States, citing Russia’s longstanding relationship with Tehran and expressing interest in Washington’s assessment of the situation in West Asia.
Putin made the remarks on Wednesday during a meeting with US President Donald Trump’s special envoy, Steve Witkoff, at the Konstantinovsky Palace in St. Petersburg. The talks also covered the conflict in Ukraine and prospects for restoring economic cooperation between Moscow and Washington.
“I am very interested in hearing the United States’ assessment of the situation in the Middle East and the issue of Iran,” Putin said at the start of the meeting, according to the Russian account of his remarks.
He described Russia’s relationship with Iran as special and based on trust, saying the ties had developed over decades.
“We have special, trusting relations with our partners and friends in Iran, built over decades. If we can do anything to help resolve this crisis, we will be happy to do so,” Putin said.
The offer comes amid continuing tensions between Tehran and Washington and diplomatic efforts to address their differences. Moscow’s statement signals its willingness to play a role in easing the dispute, although Putin did not outline a specific mediation initiative during the opening remarks.
Ukraine conflict remains a key focus
Putin also thanked Trump for his attention to efforts to resolve the conflict in Ukraine, referring to their latest telephone conversation and the need to end the fighting to prevent further loss of life.
Witkoff, in turn, said his recent discussions in Oslo with European officials and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky had been constructive and had produced progress. He said there were areas in which the parties could move towards a cessation of hostilities.
The US envoy expressed hope that Putin would consider resuming negotiations involving Russia, the United States and Ukraine, with discussions focusing on technical issues related to a settlement.
According to Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov, the Ukraine conflict was the principal focus of Wednesday’s meeting.
Witkoff also said that ending the conflict could open up prospects for expanding economic ties between Russia and the United States.
Moscow signals readiness for wider economic cooperation
Putin said Russia was prepared to discuss restoring economic cooperation with Washington, including supplying the US market with large quantities of fertilizer.
He also referred to an agreement reached with Trump during their October 9 telephone conversation on Russian diesel supplies to the United States and international markets.
Putin said diesel prices on global markets had fallen by 5–6% following the announcement of the arrangement. He added that Russia was preparing several tanker shipments, with the first expected to carry 40,000 tonnes and depart within two to three days.
Witkoff thanked Putin on Trump’s behalf for the diesel agreement, which represents a step towards renewed energy trade between the two countries despite their continuing geopolitical differences.
The proposed supplies come as Washington seeks to ease pressure on fuel markets. However, the scale and timing of deliveries will determine how much additional Russian diesel can reach international buyers.
Kushner absent from St. Petersburg meeting
Witkoff arrived in St. Petersburg without Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law, who had accompanied him on previous meetings with Putin. Ushakov said Kushner was unable to travel because of illness. He had also been absent from Witkoff’s recent trip to Norway, where the envoy met European officials and Zelensky.
Wednesday’s meeting brought together discussions on three major issues: the Ukraine conflict, US-Russia economic ties and the situation surrounding Iran. While Ukraine remained the central item on the agenda, Putin’s public remarks on Iran underscored Moscow’s stated readiness to assist in resolving the dispute between Tehran and Washington.

articles.title: Israel may be forced to act as Iran rebuilds military capabilities before election, officials warn
articles.body:
Israel is monitoring Iranian efforts to rebuild its military capabilities following the damage Tehran sustained during Operation Roaring Lion, with security officials warning that developments could force Israel to defend itself despite Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's desire to avoid escalation ahead of the elections, according to assessments discussed in recent Israeli security consultations.
Intelligence indicating that Iran is working to restore its military capabilities following the blows it sustained during Operation Roaring Lion was examined during security discussions held in Israel.
In recent weeks, Iranian measures indicating renewed military preparations have been identified. Israeli officials believe that the completion of these preparations could significantly strengthen Iran's combat capabilities. Previous assessments have also highlighted the speed of Iran's military recovery following the conflict.
According to officials familiar with the discussions, "Netanyahu wants the elections to take place as planned and on schedule, something that would not be possible if Israel were in a state of emergency involving fighting against Iran."
Nevertheless, the officials stressed that the situation is changing in accordance with the pace of Iran's military preparations and activities, and that Israel's security assessments are being updated as developments unfold.
Israel does not rule out renewed military action against Iran
"It is impossible to completely rule out a situation in which developments on the ground would require Israel to defend itself," the officials said, despite the desire to avoid escalation ahead of the elections.
US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth made a brief, unannounced visit to Israel on Monday, during which he met with Netanyahu at the Israeli Air Force's Ovda Airbase in southern Israel. The meeting between Netanyahu and Hegseth took place amid heightened security discussions.
The meeting was also attended by Defense Minister Israel Katz, National Security Council head Shmuel Ben Ezra, and other senior officials.
Possible renewal of strikes against Iran
The previously unannounced visit took place amid ongoing Israeli-US security consultations concerning Iran and the possibility of renewed military operations against Iranian nuclear and military facilities.
Neither the Prime Minister's Office nor the Pentagon has issued an official statement regarding the content of the discussions. Hegseth's arrival in Israel was not preceded by a public announcement or the release of an official agenda.
The meeting was held at a military base in southern Israel rather than at the Prime Minister's Office in Jerusalem or the Kirya military headquarters in Tel Aviv, against the backdrop of American military activity at the base and ongoing discussions between the two countries concerning Iran.

articles.title: Russia willing to resume trilateral talks with Ukraine – Moscow
articles.body:
Russia willing to resume trilateral talks with Ukraine – Moscow
Russia is ready to resume three-way negotiations with the US and Ukraine to discuss security arrangements for when the conflict has ended, Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov has said.
The announcement followed nearly three hours of talks between Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff at Constantine Palace in St. Petersburg on Wednesday. Jared Kushner joined by video link after illness prevented him from traveling.
Ushakov said Putin told Witkoff that Moscow was “in principle, ready to resume” trilateral negotiations in mid-November, with the main topic being a post-conflict security system for Russia and Ukraine. Witkoff indicated that Trump would welcome the proposal, the aide added.
The presidential aide noted that earlier attempts to restart trilateral talks were derailed by Kiev having carried out massive attacks on Moscow and other cities during Russia’s recent parliamentary elections. Polling stations were targeted on the main voting day, with election commission personnel killed.
However, the situation has since been “re-evaluated, taking into account the signals received from the Americans,” Ushakov said, adding that Putin had praised the mediation efforts of Trump, his administration, and special representatives in seeking mutually acceptable solutions.
The Russian president also presented an “objective picture of the situation along the line of contact, where Russian troops hold complete strategic initiative,” and noted that Moscow’s forces are conducting a “relentless offensive in all key areas” and effectively destroying military-industrial, energy, and logistics facilities in Ukraine.
Beyond Ukraine, the participants discussed the October diesel agreement, under which Washington eased sanctions on Russian fuel exports. Both sides said the deal served their interests and would help stabilize global fuel markets. Other joint economic projects are also approaching implementation, Ushakov added.
Russia, Ukraine and the US last held talks in Geneva in February, following two rounds in Abu Dhabi. Further negotiations, however, were put on hold after the US and Israel launched their war against Iran, disrupting access to the UAE.
Ushakov told Russian media that Abu Dhabi was again being examined as a possible venue for renewed talks, noting that Putin has yet to choose the members of a future Russian delegation.
Asked by reporters whether the Ukraine conflict was approaching its end, Ushakov suggested it is “moving in that direction.”

articles.title: Air Force’s Top Planner Lays Out Vision for Fighter Fleet Mix by 2035
articles.body:
Roughly two of every five fighters in the Air Force fleet could be F-35As by 2035, according to a new fighter force structure report the service submitted to Congress on Oct. 16.
Lt. Gen. David Tabor, deputy chief of staff for plans and programs, revealed the new estimate during an Oct. 20 media roundtable at the Pentagon as he explained the report’s estimates of the future force’s mix of different types of fighters.
The Air Force did not provide a full copy of the report to reporters.
About 40 percent of the fleet could be F-35s, Tabor said. Another 20 percent would be a combination of F-22 Raptors and F-47s as the sixth-generation fighter replaces the Raptor. The Air Force built 186 operational F-22s, and Tabor said the Air Force still plans to replace them with roughly an equivalent number of F-47s. The remaining 40 percent of the fleet would likely be split evenly between F-15 Eagle variants and F-16 Fighting Falcons, Tabor said.
Today
2035
- F-35
- F-22 / F-47
- F-15
- F-16
Source: Air Force figures cited by Tabor. Excludes A-10s. Percentages are approximate.
View data table
Currently, the fighter fleet—not counting A-10s—is split roughly 45 percent F-16s, 30 percent F-35s, 15 percent F-15s, and 10 percent F-22s.
Beyond the mix of the fighters, the force structure report also provides a new estimate of the total number of fighters the Air Force says it will need in the years to come: 1,509 combat-coded aircraft by 2035.
That’s up from the 1,271 the service estimated it would have in 2026 and the 1,369 combat-coded fighters it was shooting for by 2030 in last year’s report, Tabor said. The additional 140 jets would be a mixture of F-35s, F-15EXs, and F-47s.
The data used for the previous report was “pretty old,” Tabor said, so the service’s researchers set out to compile fresher and more accurate information. This analysis was going on before combat operations against Iran broke out earlier this year, he said, and was not driven by the war.
The Air Force’s analysis was based on geographic combatant commanders’ reported requirements to achieve their goals at “medium risk,” Tabor said, and he cautioned that is based on their subjective assessments of what they will need—and will likely change in the future.
“Certainly, world events and changing requirements in the combatant commands will change that number,” Tabor said. “Capabilities that we bring on to platforms will change the number, and I think really importantly, technology will change the number.”
Getting to the new 2035 goal depends on two key factors falling into place, Tabor said. First, Congress will need to provide the funds the Air Force needs to buy the jets. And the defense industrial base—in particular, prime contractors Lockheed Martin and Boeing—must produce enough aircraft in time.
Top Air Force officials have for years said the service needs to buy 72 new fighters each year to replace its older, retiring jets and modernize the fleet. The fiscal 2027 budget request doesn’t reach that level, proposing 38 new F-35s and 24 F-15EXs for a total of 62. Tabor said those purchases can “ramp over time” to hit the numbers the Air Force needs.
“The question is, can industry produce at those levels?” Tabor said. “They’ve assured us that they can, and we believe them, but we also actually need to see it manifest.”
Right now, 2027’s funding levels remain a big question mark. The administration’s strategy for funding the Pentagon this year relies on a budget reconciliation bill to add additional funding priorities on top of the proposed “base” appropriations.
The Air Force’s proposed budget counted on $2.34 billion coming through reconciliation to pay for 14 of those 38 new F-35s. If reconciliation doesn’t pass, Tabor said, the Air Force is not out of options. It could try to find money in the base budget to pay for more F-35s, he said—though that would require pulling billions from other critical programs.
“We just lose 14 times [an] F-35’s worth of other capabilities that we were planning on,” Tabor said.
Or, he said, the purchases could be pushed out to 2028, which would further put the Air Force behind on reaching its fighter fleet goals.
“It is really imperative that we get the resourcing we need in order to modernize the Air Force the way we want it to be,” Tabor said. “We need it all.”
In the meantime, the clock is ticking on large portions of the Air Force’s fleet such as older F-15s and F-16s, which are aging and reaching the end of their lifespans.
The Air Force is considering buying a new version of the F-16, which is tentatively being referred to as the F-16G. But the Air Force has not yet made any decision on that, Tabor said, “and we’re not in a position where that decision has to be made immediately.” That decision likely won’t be made as part of the 2028 budgeting process, he said, but perhaps the years that follow.
Older F-16s will reach the end of their lifespans in the mid-2030s, Tabor said, and “we are very conscious of that.” The simple—“and maybe the lazy”—way to approach that problem, Tabor said, is to automatically replace them with new F-16s. But that might not be the best strategy, he said.
“There is a spectrum of capability that we might want to replace the F-16s with,” he said. “It’s not urgent, frankly. What we don’t want to get to is a point where it is urgent, and we haven’t done the homework and decided ‘hey, this is really the right place to be.’ We do have time to churn through that and make sure that we have a good option going forward.”
One advantage to buying more F-16s, which Lockheed Martin now builds in Greenville, S.C., is that “it’s practically a ready-made aircraft,” Tabor said—if the Air Force wants to stick with the same type of capabilities.
Another potential wrinkle is the Pentagon’s push to expand its multiyear procurement authorities. The Air Force is eyeing such agreements for the F-35 and F-15EX, though its request is pending before Congress. More multiyear procurement deals will help provide industry more financial stability, Tabor said, which could make it easier for them to expand and stabilize production of fighters.
But while the Air Force is rapidly preparing to add hundreds of autonomous drone fighters known as Collaborative Combat Aircraft to its fleet—the goal is 500 airframes by 2032—Tabor said they’re not yet changing the service’s calculus on what fighter force it will need in the future.
“CCA is very much a reality,” Tabor said. “It is going to be a part of our future, and there is absolutely a world in which the incorporation of CCAs into the force will mitigate the requirement for the number of fighters. That’s not the CCA that we have right now, but it is advancing very, very rapidly. We’re confident that it will play a major role in future versions of the fighter force structure report.”

articles.title: China and Russia push Japan’s jet scrambles to 4-year high
articles.body:
- Japan’s Air Self-Defense Force scrambled fighters 442 times from April to September 2026, up from 265 in the same period of 2025.
- Scrambles against Russian aircraft rose from 59 to 152, while those against Chinese aircraft and drones climbed from 198 to 285.
Japan’s Air Self-Defense Force scrambled fighter jets 442 times between April 1 and Sept. 30, about two-thirds more than the 265 scrambles in the same period last year, according to Joint Staff Office figures reported by USNI News. The rise came as Chinese and Russian military aircraft flew near Japan far more often, and the six-month total for the first half of Japan’s 2026 fiscal year is the highest first-half count since fiscal 2022, when JASDF fighters launched 446 times.
None of the flights crossed into Japanese sovereign airspace, and the report lists no airspace violations during the period. Japan scrambles fighters against foreign aircraft approaching the country and entering its Air Defense Identification Zone, a monitoring area that reaches well past the 12-nautical-mile (22 km) territorial limit into international airspace.
Chinese aircraft and drones accounted for 285 scrambles, or about 65 percent, up from 198 a year earlier. The sharper change came from Russia, as JASDF fighters launched 152 times against Russian aircraft compared with 59 in the first half of fiscal 2025, which is more than in the first half of any of the four previous fiscal years listed in the report. The remaining five scrambles were classed as “other.”
The Joint Staff Office pointed to three patterns behind the numbers: Russian Il-20 intelligence-gathering flights over the Sea of Japan and the Pacific, Chinese Y-9 intelligence flights over the East China Sea, and long-range joint flights by Chinese H-6 and Russian Tu-95 bombers. Japan reported Y-9 flights on five consecutive days from Sept. 3 to Sept. 7, after we reported on an Aug. 12 Y-9 sortie through the same corridor between the Danjo Islands and Okinawa.
The southwest, which faces Taiwan and the East China Sea, remained the busiest sector, with the Southwestern Air Defense Force logging 201 scrambles against 189 a year earlier. The Northern Air Defense Force, which covers Hokkaido and northern Honshu opposite Russia’s Sakhalin Island, more than doubled its count from 53 to 112. The Central Air Defense Force rose from nine to 27.
The steepest jump came in the Western Air Defense Force, which covers Kyushu, Shikoku and western Honshu and went from 14 scrambles to 102. USNI News, citing the Joint Staff flight-path map, attributed the increase to Chinese activity over the East China Sea and to Russian aircraft flying from the Sea of Japan to the East China Sea to link up with Chinese formations.
The largest single event came on June 27, when two H-6 bombers and two J-16 fighters flew from the East China Sea into the Sea of Japan. There they joined two Russian Tu-95 bombers, two Tu-142 maritime patrol aircraft and a Su-35 fighter. The combined group flew back to the East China Sea, where the Russian bombers and patrol aircraft met another two H-6s and four J-16s, passed between Okinawa and Miyako Island and continued on a long-range flight over the Pacific south of Shikoku.
South Korea also scrambled fighters that day after nearly 10 Chinese and Russian aircraft entered and left its own air defense zone, and Seoul lodged a protest with both countries the next day. It was the first joint bomber flight around Japan since a December 2025 mission that paired two Tu-95s with two H-6s and eight J-16s. Beijing and Moscow describe such patrols as normal cooperation, while Japan’s 2026 defense white paper says repeated joint activities are “obviously intended as demonstration activities against Japan.”
The report also lists 25 publicly announced cases of unusual flight activity during the six months. Chinese Y-9 flights account for 13 of them, twice accompanied by a TB-001 reconnaissance and strike drone, while Russian Il-20 flights appear 10 times. The only other bomber entry covers July 21, when a single Tu-95 and a Su-35 flew over the Sea of Japan.
The surge follows a quieter year. Japan recorded 595 scrambles in all of fiscal 2025, including 214 against Russian aircraft, and monthly counts climbed late in that year, reaching 79 in December 2025. That same month, Japan accused J-15 fighters from the carrier Liaoning of directing their radar at two JASDF F-15s southeast of Okinawa.
The pace held through the summer, with 90 scrambles in July and 76 in August, as Chinese intelligence aircraft and drones and Russian intelligence planes kept up flights around Japan.

articles.title: Germany's military warns of 'significant' Russian sabotage threat
articles.body:
Germany's military warns of 'significant' Russian sabotage threat
BERLIN, Oct 21 - Germany's armed forces classified the threat of Russian sabotage against their own troops and facilities as "significant" for the first time, the second-highest level on their internal threat scale, according to a Bundeswehr assessment reported by German broadcasters WDR and the Sueddeutsche Zeitung on Wednesday.
A defence ministry spokesperson confirmed the assessment, telling reporters: "We are noting that we face a significant sabotage threat overall for the Bundeswehr."
The reassessment was triggered by the discovery in mid-September of a crashed drone carrying a tin of high explosives near the Wunstorf air base in Lower Saxony, WDR and Sueddeutsche Zeitung reported.
CROSSED 'RED LINE'
The internal document, seen by WDR and the Sueddeutsche Zeitung, said Russia had crossed "a previously anticipated red line of harmful intent involving kinetic and/or lethal effects" against Germany and the Bundeswehr through the use of weaponised drones.
The Wunstorf drone resembles one laden with explosives that was used in a failed attack at Leipzig/Halle airport in August. But unlike the Leipzig incident, which authorities said targeted civilian cargo aircraft, investigators believe the Wunstorf drone was aimed at Bundeswehr aircraft, the document is cited as saying.
Germany has blamed Russia for the Leipzig attack.
Moscow denied involvement and has consistently rejected accusations of carrying out sabotage or hybrid attacks in Europe.
The report also cited a pattern of suspected Russian reconnaissance across Germany, including drone overflights of the Arrow 3 missile defence site in Saxony-Anhalt, and a camouflaged camera found filming a strategically important railway station in Minden, Westphalia.
Intelligence services expect the situation to worsen in the short term, with further actions likely in the near future, the document says, according to WDR and Sueddeutsche Zeitung.
The defence ministry spokesperson said preventive measures were being tailored to individual sites and could range from increased guard patrols to additional technical security such as infrared cameras and fence surveillance systems.
The assessment comes just over a week after German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said Germany faced a "shadow war" and called for expanded intelligence powers.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Wednesday that Russian disinformation and hybrid attacks posed the biggest threat to Germany. "My view is that our people are still underestimating this big threat to our society... This is a fundamental attack against the entire political order we achieved after 1990." REUTERS

articles.title: UAE-made armored vehicles seen again in Russia
articles.body:
- Russia’s Gyurza SOBR unit in the Moscow region has been seen with a Cobra-LAMV armored vehicle made by Emirati company Streit Group.
- Ukraine, the European Union, Switzerland and Canada have sanctioned Streit Group over vehicles supplied to Russia’s National Guard.
Armored vehicles built by Emirati manufacturer Streit Group have been spotted again in Russian service, this time with Gyurza, the special rapid response unit (SOBR) of Rosgvardia’s Main Directorate for the Moscow region, which was photographed operating a Cobra-LAMV 4×4. The light armored vehicle is built on a Toyota Land Cruiser chassis and marketed by Streit to police and internal security forces. It continues to turn up with Russia’s National Guard even though Ukraine, the European Union, Switzerland and Canada have all sanctioned the company over its vehicles reaching Russia.
Cobra vehicles first appeared in Russia in October 2024, when a Russian military blogger published video of a shipment of more than 20 Streit-built Spartan, Cobra and Cougar armored vehicles bound for Russian forces, as we were first to report. In September 2025, Rosgvardia units were filmed training with Spartan SUT vehicles, including one fitted with an 82 mm (3.2-inch) mortar in the rear compartment, we reported at the time. Every one of these deliveries reached Russia well after the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Ukraine was the first to respond, listing Streit Group in 2023, and the European Union and Switzerland followed in October 2025 before adding founder Guerman Goutorov personally to their sanctions lists in May 2026. Canada sanctioned the company in August 2026 for supplying vehicles to Rosgvardia, a move Russia’s ambassador in Ottawa dismissed as having no practical effect, and the new Moscow-region sighting shows that the vehicles keep reaching Russian units regardless.
The Canadian measures carry particular weight because Streit started out as a Canadian business founded in Ontario in 1992 by Goutorov, a Russian-born businessman who served five years in the Soviet police before emigrating to Canada in the early 1990s. He later moved the company’s headquarters to the Ras Al Khaimah free trade zone in the United Arab Emirates, where Streit grew into one of the world’s largest armored vehicle makers with production sites on several continents. Goutorov’s Canadian citizenship shields him personally from Ottawa’s sanctions, and he has appealed his listing in the European Union.
Streit’s links to Russia go well beyond finished vehicles, since the company opened an armored vehicle plant east of Moscow and another in Tatarstan in 2009 and kept trading with Russian suppliers after both the 2014 and 2022 invasions. Customs records show that between 2015 and 2022 it imported 41 shipments of parts from Russian truckmaker Kamaz and 38 shipments of VPK-Ural vehicle kits, including six from the sanctioned Arzamas plant in the two weeks before Russian troops crossed into Ukraine. The company also worked with Russia’s Military-Industrial Company on armored vehicles that were later used by Wagner Group fighters in several conflict zones.
Russia is far from the only controversial destination for Streit vehicles, which have repeatedly surfaced in conflict zones under arms embargoes or in the hands of armed groups. In Yemen, Houthi military media released footage of armored vehicles captured from Saudi-backed forces. In Iran, a Toophan MRAP displayed at the Eghtedar 40 military exhibition in Tehran in 2019 was photographed and described as the same design as Streit’s Typhoon, although Iranian sources present the vehicle as a domestic development.
UN expert panels have accused Streit of breaking arms embargoes on Libya and Sudan and criticized the sale of hundreds of its vehicles into South Sudan, as we reported in 2016. Its vehicles have since been delivered to Khalifa Haftar’s forces in eastern Libya and seen with riot police in Belarus and with Guinea’s military junta. In 2015, Streit’s U.S. subsidiary paid a $3.5 million fine and Goutorov personally paid $250,000 over unlicensed exports of armored vehicles to Afghanistan, Iraq, Nigeria and other countries.
Streit has denied wrongdoing every time its vehicles have surfaced in such places, insisting that it follows UAE export law, ships its vehicles without weapons and bears no responsibility for how buyers modify or use them after sale. The company has never explained how its armored vehicles continue to reach Rosgvardia units more than four years into Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine.

articles.title: Putin ‘Ready’ for Three-Way Ukraine Talks in November, Kremlin Says
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin told US envoy Steve Witkoff that Moscow was ready in principle to resume three-way negotiations with Ukraine and the US around mid-November, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said on Wednesday, Oct. 21.
Ushakov said Putin conveyed that position during their meeting in St. Petersburg. The proposed discussions would focus on postwar security arrangements.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The president informed Steve Witkoff that we are, in principle, ready to resume the aforementioned trilateral negotiations,” Ushakov told journalists, according to Interfax Russia.
The aide added that Moscow’s main proposed topic was establishing a security framework for Russia and Ukraine after the fighting ends.
Ushakov also said Witkoff indicated that US President Donald Trump would welcome Russia’s willingness to return to negotiations. The Kremlin aide provided that description of the envoy’s response.
The announcement set out Moscow’s position and a proposed timeframe, rather than a jointly announced agreement among the three countries on when negotiations would take place.
The Kremlin has repeatedly said it is open to direct talks with President Volodymyr Zelensky, but it has demanded that the Ukrainian leader come to Moscow, effectively derailing the proposals.
Witkoff brings proposals from Oslo
The Kremlin’s statement followed Witkoff’s arrival in St. Petersburg with proposals discussed with Ukrainian and European leaders.
Russian Su-30 Crashes Near NATO Borders, Pilots Eject
During Wednesday’s meeting, the US envoy said he had brought documents outlining possible approaches to ending Russia’s war against Ukraine. He urged Putin to consider restarting negotiations involving representatives of all three countries, including technical working groups.
Witkoff described the preceding discussions in Oslo as productive and said they could move toward a ceasefire. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Putin would review the proposals.
The visit marked the US envoys’ first trip to Russia since Sept. 5, when Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with Putin and senior Russian officials for three hours before traveling to Kyiv.
Before Wednesday’s meeting, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Moscow would listen to US proposals but ruled out political concessions.
Ukraine seeks strong security guarantees
Security guarantees were also central to Zelensky’s talks with Witkoff and Nordic leaders in Norway on Tuesday, Oct. 20.
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said Witkoff would take proposals developed during the Oslo discussions to Russia’s leadership. The talks covered Ukraine’s security, territorial questions, sanctions and postwar prosperity.
Zelensky said a draft document included several types of guarantees, which Kyiv would present to the Russian side before assessing Putin’s response.
The Ukrainian president also confirmed that US intelligence sharing for early warnings of Russian attacks had resumed after a week of interruptions.
He said he expected progress within 48 hours on Patriot interceptors, intelligence cooperation and restrictions affecting Starlink terminals. Those issues formed part of the broader discussions over Ukraine’s ability to defend itself while diplomacy continued.
Kyiv rejects Ukraine peace talks without Ukraine
The proposed Russia-US-Ukraine format comes as Zelensky has rejected any attempt to negotiate Ukraine’s future without Kyiv.
Speaking in Oslo, he responded to reports of a possible separate meeting involving Trump, Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping. Zelensky said those leaders could hold their own discussions, but any negotiations on Ukraine’s future require Ukrainian participation.
He distinguished that potential summit from the three-way meeting he had proposed involving the US, Ukraine and Russia.
The Ukrainian president said the security proposals discussed in Oslo included arrangements resembling NATO’s Article 5 collective defense commitment. He emphasized that Ukraine needed strong guarantees after the war ends, and Kyiv was awaiting feedback from Witkoff’s discussions in Russia.
Støre likewise reaffirmed that decisions about Ukraine’s future could not be made without Ukraine’s involvement.
