articles.title: Why Rubio is seeking India’s help after coercion over Russian oil
articles.body:
Why Rubio is seeking India’s help after coercion over Russian oil
After spending years pressuring New Delhi to cut back its Russian oil purchases, and isolate Moscow, Washington has now changed tack and is seeking India’s help to bring down elevated domestic fuel prices that are largely of its own making.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who skipped New Delhi entirely on his second visit to India this year, made clear what had brought him to the country – the massive refining capacity of Reliance Industries, owned by billionaire Mukesh Ambani.
“I’m also here in my capacity as the National Security Adviser,” Rubio said in Mumbai. “Energy is related to national security … we’re going to go see a company that has a tremendous amount of refining capability.”
President Donald Trump’s administration is showing a new urgency to bring down the high fuel prices that threaten Republicans’ prospects in November’s midterm elections. US retail diesel prices reached a record average of about $6.32 a gallon on Tuesday.
American refineries are already operating at close to capacity, and Washington is working with India to increase refining output and bring more petroleum products to global markets, US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said in Houston the same day.
“Energy politics is inseparable from American geopolitics,” Jindal School of International Affairs adjunct professor and former Jawaharlal Nehru University professor Anuradha Mitra Chenoy told RT. “The US is using energy as a geopolitical instrument, and that is central to understanding Rubio’s visit.”
From Russian oil tariffs to Venezuelan crude
Washington has regularly used energy sanctions to achieve its geopolitical aims. First it took Iranian, and then Venezuelan, crude off the market with the threat of sanctions. Since the Ukraine conflict began, Washington also pressured India to stop buying Russian crude. The argument was that choking off Moscow’s oil revenues would help end the conflict, which is now in its fifth year.
At the same time, the US continued to supply Ukraine with weapons and funds, and started a war with Iran that disrupted energy supplies from the Middle East.
New Delhi has maintained that providing affordable energy to its 1.4 billion people is central to its oil-purchasing decisions. India imports about 85% of its energy requirements, and Russia remains one of its biggest sources of oil.
But the pressure reached a breaking point when the US Congress passed a law last month that threatened “bone-crushing sanctions” on major buyers of Russian energy. New Delhi warned that the proposed measures could affect bilateral relations and global energy markets.
However, as the affordability crisis in America got worse, and Trump’s rhetoric failed to bring down domestic fuel prices in a connected global market, the administration swiftly changed course.
Trump announced a deal with Russia to buy diesel for the domestic market. And cleared the deck for Rubio’s visit by waiving off sanctions on Moscow’s top oil buyers – which includes China and India, allowing Russian oil to flow more freely into global markets.
“None of these tariffs are meant to punish or harm India,” Rubio said in Mumbai, adopting a more conciliatory tone than has come out of Washington until recently.
Why Reliance, and Jamnagar, matter to Washington
Washington’s top diplomat held talks with Mukesh Ambani at Jamnagar in India’s Gujarat state on the second day of his visit. The Reliance refinery in Jamnagar is the largest single-site refining complex in the world, and can process around 1.4 million barrels of crude a day.
It is also one of the few facilities capable of processing large volumes of Venezuela’s extra-heavy crude, which is good for producing diesel – showing its importance to a US administration worried about domestic fuel prices.
Jamnagar already plays a major part in keeping global fuel prices in check – by selling fuel refined from Russian crude to markets including Europe, which sanctions the same crude.
And it is buying more Venezuelan oil, accounting for more than 74% of the nearly $3.6 billion worth of Venezuelan crude imported by India between April and August, according to figures shared by the Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI) think tank.
Rubio wants Reliance to buy, and process, more of the Venezuelan crude, which the US now controls after kidnapping the country’s President Nicolas Maduro.
“The refining capability exists,” GTRI founder Ajay Srivastava told RT. “The question is whether expanding purchases makes commercial sense.”
Venezuelan crude is cheaper but it also costs more to refine, he pointed out. He also questioned the wisdom of India buying more of the South American country’s oil, which was once subjected to US sanctions.
“It would be very unwise for India to stop using Russian oil,” Chenoy said, pointing out that there are only a limited number of major sources available internationally, and Russia remains one of the most important.
Reliance is also involved in a proposed refinery project in Brownsville, Texas, under a long-term agreement to purchase its output. The facility, which Trump called a $300 billion project in March, is designed to process lighter American shale crude.
The Indian conglomerate “helps utilize and unleash the energy that is being developed in the Western Hemisphere,” Rubio told the Indian Express, describing his visit as an opportunity to identify ways of diversifying energy supplies.
Rubio dodges a Musk-ignited controversy
Ahead of his meeting with Ambani, Rubio had to sidestep the controversy ignited by trillionaire Elon Musk.
The world’s richest man, a prominent donor to the Republican party, had accused Ambani earlier this month of obstructing the launch of his Starlink satellite internet service in India.
Musk targeted Ambani, sarcastically addressing him as “Prime Minister Ambani” and questioning whether his company would allow Starlink to compete in the country.
Starlink, Ambani’s Jio Satellite Communications, and Bharti Group-backed Eutelsat OneWeb are all at broadly the same stage of regulatory approval for satellite internet connectivity in the country, with security assessments underway, according to India’s Communications Ministry.
Reliance also dismissed suggestions that it was blocking competition.
“Elon Musk is a private citizen,” Rubio told the Indian Express, adding that Musk had the right to express his views.
Rubio also sought to assuage concerns about the India-US trade deal, which has been holding fire despite months of tortuous negotiations. Indian Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman described the talks as deadlocked earlier this month, saying both sides were finding it “very difficult” to make further concessions.
“We are weeks, not months, away from, I think, finalizing it,” Rubio said. “I would say we are about as close as you can be without having executed the agreement.”
India has been holding off on finalizing the deal as it wants to lock in a competitive advantage in the US market relative to rival exporter nations.
Pragmatism back on the table
The US administration turning on the charm, so to speak, suggests that Washington’s energy and political interests are taking precedence over its geopolitical considerations and moral grandstanding.
With pragmatism back on the table, Rubio’s visit could mark a step toward easing bilateral tensions and strengthening cooperation beyond the immediate fuel crisis driving the change.
Still India must “carefully examine what it is being asked to commit to, what commercial benefits it can expect, and the risks of future changes in US policy,” Srivastava said.

articles.title: U.S. Army awards $308M for digital investigation software
articles.body:
- The U.S. Army awarded Authentic8 a $307.7 million modification to set up a department-wide contract for its Silo digital investigation software.
- The Army solicited a single bid for the sole-source deal, which covers secure browsing tools used for open-source intelligence and dark web research.
The Pentagon is spending up to $307.7 million on software that lets its analysts browse the darkest corners of the internet without leaving a trace, after the U.S. Army awarded California-based Authentic8 a department-wide deal for its Silo platform on Oct. 20.
Silo is designed for the kind of online detective work that military intelligence now depends on, from monitoring Telegram channels and extremist forums to tracking weapons sales on dark web marketplaces, while hiding the fact that the person on the other end works for the U.S. government.
The problem Silo tries to solve is simple: every time an analyst opens a website from an official network, that site can log the visit, fingerprint the browser and, in the worst case, push malicious code onto a military computer. Silo moves the whole browsing session onto Authentic8’s own cloud servers, so nothing from the website ever reaches the user’s machine, and it lets investigators choose where they appear to be connecting from, so a visit from an Army analyst in Virginia can look like an ordinary user in another country.
That capability has become more valuable as open-source intelligence has grown into a core part of modern warfare, with Russia’s war against Ukraine showing how much can be learned from soldiers’ social media posts, geolocated videos and commercial satellite images. Analysts who dig through that material regularly visit sites run by hostile governments, militant groups and criminal networks, where a careless click from a government address can tip off the target or expose the analyst’s own network to hackers.
The Army ran the purchase as a sole-source deal and received a single bid, after telling industry in August that its requirement was specific to Authentic8’s product and that it planned to buy directly from the company unless another firm could show it offered the same capability. The award gives commands across the Department of War one place to order Silo licenses, add-on tools and support, with the amount and location of the work decided order by order rather than fixed up front.
Authentic8 is already a familiar name in federal law enforcement and financial investigations, with the Department of the Treasury, the Internal Revenue Service and the U.S. Secret Service among the agencies that have bought Silo for secure browsing and dark web research. The new contract expands an initial award made in September into a much larger vehicle that the whole department can use, which puts the Redwood City company’s tools on track to become a standard part of the military’s online investigation kit.

articles.title: Ukraine hits data center of Russia’s top ban
articles.body:
Ukraine hits data center of Russia’s top ban
Ukraine continued striking Russian data centers this week, hitting one belonging to Sberbank, Russia’s largest bank. The state-owned lender is also a sweeping online conglomerate, developing its own artificial intelligence model and operating an extensive ecosystem of digital services. Although the strikes did not cause serious disruptions to banking services, the ongoing Ukrainian campaign could undermine Russians’ confidence in the banking system.
- Ukraine attacked a data center in the city of Balakovo, in the Saratov region, approximately 1,000 kilometres from Moscow. Sberbank has been building the facility since 2021 and described it as the largest in Russia. A week earlier, Ukrainian drones knocked out three of Yandex’s six major data centers. Yandex is one of Russia’s largest IT companies.
- Following the attack, users in Russia began complaining about problems with Sber’s services (the bank’s umbrella brand encompasses its digital products), the Samokat grocery delivery service, and the GigaChat AI service. Some other websites unrelated to Sber also experienced technical issues, including the Kontur business ecosystem and the Ozon marketplace. The disruptions peaked at 11:10 a.m. Moscow time on October 14, after which the number of error reports began to decline.
- Sberbank customers barely noticed the effects of Ukraine’s attack on the data center because the bank’s core banking systems are hosted at other sites, technology expert Anastasia Bezrukova told the business newspaper Vedomosti. According to her, the Balakovo data center was being built to expand existing infrastructure. It was also intended to house the country’s most powerful supercomputer and provide backup capacity for Gostekh, a cloud platform serving federal and regional government agencies. Sberbank has two other data centers that remain untouched: one in Moscow and another in Moscow Oblast.
- Earlier, following Ukrainian attacks on Yandex data centers, Russian users experienced serious disruptions to Yandex Pay, the company’s payment service. For several days, they were unable to make payments or transfers. Some users complained that the problems with Yandex Pay prevented them from making their monthly loan and mortgage payments.
- Strikes on data centers and the subsequent disruptions to banking services are unlikely to trigger a systemic crisis in Russia’s banking sector, but they could further erode public confidence in it. Amid mobile internet disruptions, rising taxes, and widespread anxiety fueled by rumors of a possible new wave of mobilization, Russians have been withdrawing increasing amounts of cash and using it to pay for purchases. According to September data from the central bank, the share of cashless transactions in retail turnover fell for the first time in the second quarter of 2026, dropping by 0.5 percentage points to 88.4%, the data shows. Previous crises — the pandemic, the beginning of the war against Ukraine, and Yevgeny Prigozhin’s attempted military mutiny in 2023 — led to noticeable increases in the amount of cash in circulation.
Why the world should care
A potential increase in cash in circulation could have two consequences. The first is an expansion of the shadow economy, which could potentially affect tax collection, although the impact is unlikely to be significant. The second is a liquidity shortage in the banking sector, which could affect banks’ financial results and slow the decline in lending rates as the key interest rate falls.

articles.title: Russia ready for 3-way talks on Ukraine war, Kremlin says
articles.body:
Russian leader Vladimir Putin is “in principle” ready for Moscow to resume talks with Washington and Kyiv, the Kremlin said Wednesday.
During a meeting in St. Petersburg with U.S. President Donald Trump’s special envoy, Steve Witkoff, Putin said Moscow is ready to restart trilateral negotiations in November, Yuri Ushakov, a senior Putin aide, told reporters.
Ushakov added that the “conflict in Ukraine is coming to an end,” and said trilateral talks “may take place in Abu Dhabi.”
Advertisement
Witkoff confirmed on X that discussions “will continue with trilateral talks between the United States, Russia, and Ukraine at the technical level.”
His visit was the latest in a new round of U.S. attempts to bring Moscow to the negotiating table to end its war against Ukraine. The special envoy also met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Oslo on Tuesday, subsequently announcing a proposal for a three-way leaders’ negotiation.
There have been several rounds of talks between the U.S. and Russia since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. The most recent discussions stalled in February when the U.S. and Israel launched their war against Iran.
Previous negotiations were largely political theater and failed to yield any broader breakthrough on halting hostilities, prisoner-of-war exchanges or a truce regarding strikes on energy infrastructure.
Earlier this week, the Wall Street Journal reported Moscow proposed a potential high-level summit with China and the U.S. to negotiate a deal on ending the war in Ukraine.
On Wednesday, footage emerged of Witkoff praising Putin during their face-to-face talks in St. Petersburg, after the Russians released a U.S. prisoner from captivity.
Posting on X, Witkoff said: “These discussions were constructive, and will continue with trilateral talks between the United States, Russia, and Ukraine at the technical level.”

articles.title: Exclusive: Corbyn vows to pursue Gaza inquiry despite UK refusal
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Exclusive: Corbyn vows to pursue Gaza inquiry despite UK refusal
Jeremy Corbyn has vowed to continue pressing for an inquiry into Britain's possible complicity in Israel's genocide in Gaza after the UK government rejected his renewed calls for an investigation, the former Labour leader told The New Arab.
Corbyn, who now represents Islington North for Your Party, is seeking an independent public inquiry into Britain's military, economic and political cooperation with Israel since October 2023, including arms supplies, surveillance flights and the use of Royal Air Force (RAF) bases.
The former Labour leader first introduced the Gaza (Independent Public Inquiry) Bill in June 2025 before reintroducing the legislation in the 2026–27 parliamentary session. The latest version was published on 2 September and is awaiting its second reading.
However, the government has resisted calls to establish an inquiry, arguing that its policies and actions relating to Gaza have already undergone extensive parliamentary scrutiny.
"The UK's policy and actions relating to the conflict in Gaza have been subject of extensive parliamentary scrutiny through ministerial statements, debates, Select Committee scrutiny, and oral and written Parliamentary Questions," Middle East Minister Stephen Doughty said in a written response to Corbyn's request.
The refusal comes despite hopes that Prime Minister Andy Burnham's government would take a different approach after he apologised for his predecessor Keir Starmer's words and actions regarding Israel's genocide in Gaza.
"We're not going away, we're not giving up because I think this cause is far too important and far too great," Corbyn told The New Arab.
Corbyn said an inquiry could answer questions about Britain's supply of F-35 fighter jet components to Israel and RAF reconnaissance flights over Gaza.
UK companies manufacture around 15% of the components used in F-35 fighter jets, which Israel has deployed in its assault on Gaza, according to the Campaign Against Arms Trade.
Between December 2023 and July 2025, the RAF conducted more than 600 reconnaissance flights over Gaza, according to Action on Armed Violence (AOAV).
The Ministry of Defence maintained that the flights were conducted "solely to locate hostages", though AOAV questioned whether their scale and persistence were consistent with humanitarian aims.
"We do need a very profound apology to the Palestinian people for the way in which the British government has maintained a supply of arms and military corporation with Israeli Defence Force throughout this whole horrific period, particularly since October 2023," Corbyn said.
In 2016, while Labour leader, Corbyn apologised for the Labour Party's role in the Iraq War following the publication of the Chilcot inquiry's findings.
The inquiry found that Saddam Hussein did not pose an imminent threat to Britain at the time of the 2003 invasion and that intelligence about Iraq's alleged weapons of mass destruction had been presented with unjustified certainty.
Corbyn was among the Labour MPs who opposed the Iraq War and subsequently pushed for an inquiry into Britain's role in the invasion and its aftermath, which resulted in hundreds of thousands of deaths, according to various estimates.
"One day the British Prime Minister will say we need an inquiry. I hope it's soon," Corbyn told The New Arab.

articles.title: Ukraine has shown heroism, but military aid to it has depleted U.S. weapons stocks – Hegseth
articles.body:
Ukraine has shown heroism, but military aid to it has depleted U.S. weapons stocks – Hegseth
Kyiv • UNN
U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said that support for Ukraine under the Biden administration had depleted American weapons stocks. He did not provide specific data on the scale of the reduction.
U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth said that Ukraine had demonstrated heroism in confronting Russian aggression, but that the large-scale military assistance provided to Kyiv under the previous U.S. administration had depleted the United States' weapons stocks, UNN reports.
Details
According to the Pentagon chief, Ukrainian troops made significant efforts to defend their country and received substantial support from international partners, including the United States.
Ukraine made heroic efforts, and significant assistance was provided to it. So significant that under the previous administration, weapons stocks were depleted
The Pentagon spoke about the consequences of military assistance to Ukraine
In his statement, the American secretary linked the reduction in U.S. military reserves to the volume of weapons that Washington transferred to Ukraine during Joe Biden's presidency.
At the same time, Hegseth did not specify which categories of weapons he was referring to or the extent to which the corresponding stocks of the U.S. military had been reduced.
The United States remains an important weapons supplier to Ukraine. In particular, European partners continue to rely on American production when providing Ukrainian troops with the necessary systems and ammunition.
The Pentagon chief's statement is his assessment of the consequences of Washington's previous policy. The minister's quoted remarks contain no specific data that would make it possible to assess the scale of the alleged depletion of U.S. military stocks.

articles.title: Starlink slowdown makes Ukraine’s Shahed-hunting drone maker rethink air-launched interceptors
articles.body:
Ukrainian drone maker Wild Hornets is rethinking projects it is currently working on, including launching interceptors from aerial platforms, because of limits on SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet. Spokesman Mike Orliuk told The War Zone (TWZ) this on 20 October. The company builds Sting interceptors, which it says destroyed over 15,000 Shaheds and Gerberas, a cheaper Shahed lookalike, in a year. Orliuk said Sting’s current operations are unaffected.
The stakes rise as Russia shifts to faster drones. Ukrainian defense technology adviser Serhii Beskrestnov counted more than 2,500 jet-powered Gerans, Russia’s version of the Shahed, in August. President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 16 October that these drones fly faster than 400 km/h. He added that some Ukrainian interceptors chasing them work through Starlink. When the link was slowed, Ukraine could not intercept some of them, he said.
How Sting stays connected
“Our own communications system provides the basic connection to our interceptors,” Orliuk said. The company’s remote-control technology can draw on various internet sources, he added, though the military often uses Starlink. Even then, the terminal does not need to move at high speed. It only links the command center to a ground station, which Orliuk compared to a cell tower.
“For these needs, everything is operating normally with Starlink at the moment,” he said.
An air-launch project under review
“Some drones carry a terminal on board and need to fly at high speed with it,” Orliuk said. “In such cases, Starlink’s limitations make their operation impossible.”
That is why the company is rethinking the air-launch project. Wild Hornets has made no clear decision yet but will test alternatives, Orliuk said. He declined to describe them.
“I believe, in any case, depending on a single solution is very risky,” he said.
Musk pointed at the US military over Ukraine’s satellite limits. Now a US official says the administration had nothing to do with them
Other firms share the concern
Orliuk said he has spoken with other companies that rely far more on Starlink and have expressed concerns. He pointed to growing interest in Europe’s Eutelsat network, though “creating something like Starlink won’t be easy.”
Who ordered the slowdown remains unclear. The order to slow Ukraine’s Starshield service came from inside the White House, two US officials and a Western official said. A US official told TWZ the president never made such a request. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on 17 October that the slowdown had “nothing to do with the White House” and called “a report on that” “categorically false,” without saying which report he meant.

articles.title: Nuclear safety risk grows: Russian-occupied nuclear plant’s cooling pond keeps sinking, Russia runs short of diesel and staff, Ukraine says
articles.body:
The Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant is short of cooling water, diesel, and qualified staff, Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR) said on 20 October, warning of rising risks to nuclear safety. The water level in the plant’s cooling pond fell to 12.27 meters on 12 October, down from 12.86 meters in July, while the plant needs at least 15 meters to fully meet its needs, according to HUR. Russian managers are also considering cutting the number of backup generators kept on automatic standby, which would inevitably raise the risk of emergencies, the intelligence agency said.
Europe’s largest nuclear plant has been under Russian control since March 2022. Its six reactors have been in cold shutdown since April 2024, but they and their spent fuel still need constant cooling, which depends on water, on a single remaining external power line, and on diesel generators as the last resort. The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) warned on 16 October that depleted diesel reserves increase the risk that nuclear safety is challenged if the plant loses power again, and that the situation may become acute in winter.
A pond with no source to refill it
The cooling pond has been sinking since Russia destroyed the Kakhovka dam in June 2023, cutting off the reservoir that fed it. Energoatom, Ukraine’s state nuclear operator, recorded 15.70 meters in October 2023. By June 2025, the level had fallen below 14 meters against a norm of above 16, Oleh Korikov, head of Ukraine’s State Nuclear Regulatory Inspectorate, said.
HUR’s figures show the decline continuing this year, from 12.86 meters in July to 12.63 in early August, 12.55 at the end of August, and 12.34 at the start of October. In 2025, the IAEA said groundwater wells on site were supplying cooling water for the safety systems. Its team had not been allowed to inspect a new dam in the cooling channel, access IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi called essential to assess the cooling water situation.
Diesel for a blackout that Russia cannot supply
If the plant loses external power, its diesel generators would burn about 150 metric tons of fuel a day in a prolonged blackout, HUR said. The occupation administration cannot deliver enough, so reserves stay minimal. Russian managers are also looking for covert fuel supplies, including low-quality fuel, without informing the IAEA mission, according to HUR.
The IAEA has already reported fewer generators on automatic standby. Since late September, only four of the plant’s 20 emergency generators would start automatically in a blackout, with the rest needing manual connection, which Grossi said deviates from normal practice. No diesel deliveries have reached the plant since March, the agency said on 16 October.
The plant spent nearly three weeks on generators after losing its last external line on 20 August, EP reported, until the Ferosplavna-1 line was restored under an IAEA-brokered ceasefire. The main 750 kV Dniprovska line remains out. HUR said the Kremlin rejected Ukraine’s proposal to supply power through it, which raises the nuclear safety risks.
Russia blacked out Europe’s largest nuclear plant 15 times since occupying it in 2022
A plant short of the people who know it
About 5,000 people now work at the plant, against roughly 11,000 before the full-scale invasion, and only 1,450 were on site, HUR said. The plant lacks specialists who know its equipment, as well as the experts needed for repairs and for reconnecting it to external power. Russian managers plan training courses for applicants from Russian regions to replace Ukrainian staff, according to HUR.
In Enerhodar, the city where the plant’s staff live, mobile, internet, electricity, and water supplies keep failing, HUR said.

articles.title: Russia wants AI to help design its next aircraft
articles.body:
- Russia’s United Aircraft Corporation said it is evaluating new software, including artificial intelligence, to speed up the design of future aircraft and modifications.
- UAC is already running a pilot project with Sberbank’s GigaChat AI for generative design at the early stage of a new aircraft.
Russia’s United Aircraft Corporation is looking at artificial intelligence and other new software to speed up the design of future aircraft and cut the cost of developing new versions of existing ones, the state-owned planemaker said in a statement on its social media.
UAC, which builds nearly all of Russia’s military and civil aircraft, from Su-57 and Su-35 fighters to the MC-21 airliner, said its engineers are evaluating new software products, including AI technologies, as the company moves its design work onto digital models.
The company said digital models let its engineers analyze far larger volumes of data and test many more aircraft layouts before choosing the best one, which makes developing new modifications faster and cheaper over an aircraft’s life cycle. UAC added that it is taking a measured approach to AI and will only use the new tools where they make sense and help solve specific engineering problems.
“Digital technology makes it possible to take a larger sample and understand a problem more deeply. Over the life cycle, this will be faster and cheaper when creating the next modifications,” UAC specialists said.
The statement follows remarks by UAC general designer Sergey Korotkov, who said on Oct. 13 that there is no reason not to use AI in aircraft design as long as it helps with the task at hand and is applied thoughtfully. UAC has already been testing the idea, and in May its chief executive, Vadim Badekha, said the company was running a pilot project with Sberbank to use the bank’s GigaChat AI model for generative design of a new aircraft at the early design stage, with plans to extend it later to strength and aerodynamic calculations.
The shift to domestic digital tools has been driven largely by sanctions, since Western design software vendors such as Dassault Systèmes, Siemens and Autodesk pulled out of Russia after the 2022 invasion of Ukraine and left the country’s aerospace industry without the programs it had relied on for decades. UAC says it has since replaced software at its design bureaus with Russian products, equipping about 4,000 engineering workstations and swapping out nine key product lifecycle management modules, and on Oct. 16 it said digital design had cut some aircraft system calculations, such as cabin heat balance and hydraulic networks, from months to days.
Those efforts come as UAC struggles with delays on its most important civil programs, which have had to replace Western parts and systems with Russian-made equivalents. President Vladimir Putin said in June that the MC-21 had been set back by almost two years, partly because of problems with the wing, and First Deputy Prime Minister Denis Manturov said certification of the version built entirely with Russian components is now planned for the end of 2027.

articles.title: ‘You are a humanitarian also, sir’: the US feeds Putin with lies as Ukraine’s children take cover and die | Andrew Roth
articles.body:
They say the first casualty of war is truth. For the Trump administration, the road to peace with Russia now encompasses some extraordinary lies.
Steve Witkoff delivered one as he sat down with Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg on Wednesday, aiming to close the deal on Russia’s land grab in Ukraine with the White House’s strategy of maximum pressure on Kyiv and saccharine flattery of the Kremlin.
“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian,” said Witkoff, a real-estate mogul who, thanks to being Trump’s friend, is now the US’s senior envoy and diplomat to end the largest European conflict since the second world war. “You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that. I commend you.”
In Putin’s 26 years in power, it is a rare moment when he has been granted that specific honour. Skim through Russia’s past wartime exploits – from the bombing campaigns in Chechnya and Georgia and Syria, to the thousands of Russian citizens jailed for dissent, to the violent deaths of prominent opposition journalists and politicians in barely disguised assassinations and poisonings – and it will be difficult to identify Putin’s credentials as a humanitarian.
And that is before looking to Ukraine, where Russia chose to launch a full-scale invasion that has claimed hundreds of thousands of lives. The Guardian recently obtained a Russian strategy document showing the Kremlin’s potential to black out Ukrainian cities this winter, cutting off up to 90% of electricity to cities such as Kyiv and Odesa and Kharkiv – where millions of people live – to intentionally create a humanitarian catastrophe. And judging by the nightly barrages levelled at power plants for cities across Ukraine, the Kremlin has decided to move forward with that strategy until Kyiv surrenders.
As Witkoff met Putin on Wednesday, schoolchildren in Kharkiv hastened down a reinforced stairway, sirens announcing the arrival of Shahed drones overhead. This is no ordinary bomb shelter; it is one of 10 underground schools Kharkiv has constructed because of Russia’s regular bombing of the city less than 20 miles from the border.
Parents had welcomed the schools because they were safe, said teachers, and this was the one way that young people could have an uninterrupted school day during a war that could last years more – and reignite even if a shaky peace deal is reached.
“We all believed in Trump. We all really had hopes for America and for Trump to stop this monster Putin,” said Olena Svytlychna, the head of the education department of the Novobavarskyi region in Kharkiv, sitting in the school’s cafe on Wednesday.
“And now we have doubts, we don’t believe them. And we are very scared.”
As Witkoff spoke, the families of six people killed in a drone strike in a park near Kharkiv this week were holding funerals. The youngest victim of the strike was a one-year-old girl, Anhelina, who was killed as she was sitting strapped into her stroller in a playground. Her mother, Inna Mariukhna, a local schoolteacher, was also killed in the strike. The final death toll was four adults and two children, Anhelina and an 11-year-old girl.
Those lives have barely earned a mention from the White House as it pushes for Ukraine to capitulate as quickly as it can this week – and crucially before the 3 November midterm elections when voters will deliver a referendum on Trump’s leadership for the last two years.
Shortly after the bombing, Trump told reporters on the White House lawn that Russia “has been fine on Ukraine”. After taking criticism for that remark, he mentioned the attacks in passing just to downplay the shelling of civilians: there were “some people in a town that got hit or whatever, but mostly young soldiers” died, he said from the Oval Office on Tuesday.
For the White House, those words cost little. Witkoff’s goal was to bring home a US citizen, a 74-year-old retired teacher from Michigan, who had been detained in Russia. But if Witkoff wants to buy a peace deal by 3 November through flattering Putin, then this will only be the White House’s opening salvo in its war on truth.

articles.title: North Korea Sends 12,000 Workers to Russia to Build Shahed Drones
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
North Korea Sends 12,000 Workers to Russia to Build Shahed Drones
North Korea has reportedly sent 12,000 workers to Russia to help manufacture Shahed-type attack drones at the Alabuga Special Economic Zone in Tatarstan, expanding Pyongyang’s involvement in Russia’s military production supporting its war against Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to a joint report by the Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) and the George W. Bush Institute on October 14, North Korean workers receive approximately $2.50 per hour, while the North Korean government reportedly takes between 70% and 90% of their earnings.
The report identifies three main groups involved in drone manufacturing at Alabuga: Russian students and young workers, foreign recruits from other countries, and North Korean nationals. Researchers raised concerns about coercive labor practices affecting all three groups, particularly the systematic withholding of wages from North Korean workers.
Russian students are recruited through Alabuga’s educational programs, which combine technical training with industrial work. Some reportedly work shifts lasting up to 12 hours, with their pay tied to strict production targets.
Workers have also reportedly faced threats of financial penalties for disclosing details about the facility’s operations, including to family members.
The Alabuga industrial complex is a major Russian production site for Geran-2 drones, based on the Iranian-designed Shahed-136, which Russia regularly uses in attacks against Ukrainian cities and infrastructure.
Satellite imagery published in September showed additional production buildings and warehouses under construction at the site, indicating continued expansion of its manufacturing infrastructure.
North Korea’s involvement in Russian drone production comes amid growing military cooperation between Moscow and Pyongyang. Beyond providing personnel, North Korea has reportedly sought to incorporate lessons from Russia’s use of drones in Ukraine into its own military development programs.
Analysts have also indicated that Pyongyang is working to expand domestic production of Shahed-type drones and smaller unmanned aircraft, potentially benefiting from Russian technical expertise.
Earlier, Bloomberg reported on September 17 that approximately 25,000 North Korean nationals were working at Russian drone manufacturing facilities, including Alabuga. Many reportedly entered Russia on student visas to circumvent international sanctions, while North Korean authorities confiscated most of their earnings.

articles.title: India & United States to boost defence, energy ties, Marco Rubio says trade deal close
articles.body:
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and US ambassador to India Sergio Gor stand for the national anthem, as they attend a Freedom 250 reception at the Jio World Convention Centre in Mumbai.
External affairs minister S Jaishankar met his US counterpart Marco Rubio in Mumbai, agreeing to further expand cooperation in energy, defence and technology ties and committing to an early conclusion of the trade deal still under discussion.While Rubio emphasised the role that the US can play in the diversification of India's energy and defence supplies, Jaishankar said in a post on X that they also discussed people-to-people ties, alluding to India's concerns over immigration and H-1B governance issues.
Speaking at the US anniversary celebrations later, Jaishankar said in Rubio’s presence that Indian talent and skills have helped shape the tech era in the US.The ministers met ahead of a likely meeting between PM Narendra Modi and President Donald Trump next month in Manila on the margins of the ASEAN summit, and also before Modi's visit to the US in December for the G20. Both sides are also working to schedule a Quad leaders’ summit in Manila.A State Department readout said Jaishankar and Rubio discussed regional and global issues, including developments in West Asia. Rubio reiterated that increased energy trade with the US can play a transformative role in diversifying India’s supply chains while meeting its sizable consumer demand.
Rubio’s second visit to India is taking place against the backdrop of US’ Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act meant to penalise countries purchasing Russian oil and Trump’s subsequent suspension temporarily of related tariffs. India maintains that its oil procurement is essential not just for its own energy security but also stability of the global markets. Rubio lauded “substantial progress” made by India in diversifying its energy portfolio.Rubio focused on reducing India's reliance on Russia also in defence as he stressed deepening of defence interoperability, framing enhanced technology purchases by India as a win-win situation for both nations.According to the US readout, Rubio also commended recent progress in bilateral defense and civil nuclear cooperation, and advocated increased purchase of US technologies and systems, which can enhance the security and prosperity of both countries.Rubio said in a post on X that he and Jaishankar reaffirmed the importance of advancing the US-India strategic partnership. The ministers will meet again on the sidelines of the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting in Atlanta later this month. Both will also join their counterparts from Japan and Australia for a meeting of the Quad foreign ministers in Atlanta.According to the MEA, Jaishankar and Rubio welcomed the progress made in negotiations on the India–US Bilateral Trade Agreement (BTA) and reaffirmed their commitment to working towards its early conclusion. Rubio said both sides were “as close as you can be without having an executed agreement”.“I think there's a small number of items left to wrap up. So, I think that will happen shortly...and hopefully have some good news to announce fairly soon, and perhaps the leaders can sign it thereafter,” said Rubio, addressing the US travelling media.
Shortly after his arrival, Rubio laid a wreath at Mumbai’s Taj Mahal Palace Hotel to honor the 26/11 terrorist attacks victims 166 victims, strongly condemning the attacks and reaffirming the US “unwavering solidarity” with the people of India.“Secretary Rubio underscored the Trump Administration’s commitment to dismantling terrorist networks and ensuring that those responsible for acts of terrorism are brought to justice, including individuals facing charges for their roles in planning the 2008 Mumbai attacks,” said the State Department, without naming Pakistan.According to the Indian readout, the visit reflected the sustained momentum of high-level exchanges between the two countries, underscoring the importance both sides attach to further advancing the India-US COMPACT for the 21st century. Modi and Trump had launched the COMPACT (Catalyzing Opportunities for Military Partnership, Accelerated Commerce & Technology) initiative last year to drive transformative change across key pillars of bilateral cooperation.

articles.title: Russia attacks Ukraine with Iskander-K missiles and 186 drones, air defences down 150 UAVs
articles.body:
Russia attacks Ukraine with Iskander-K missiles and 186 drones, air defences down 150 UAVs
Russia attacked Ukraine with Iskander-K cruise missiles and 186 drones on the night of 20-21 October. Air defence forces have destroyed or jammed 150 UAVs, while another 10 remain airborne.
Source: Ukraine's Air Force
Details: The attack began at 18:00 on 20 October. Russian forces launched Iskander-K cruise missiles from the airspace over Rostov Oblast. The number of missiles launched and how many were intercepted have not been reported.
Russia also attacked Ukraine with 186 Shahed loitering munitions (88 jet-powered), Gerbera attack drones, S-8000 Banderol/Dan-T drone- and air-launched cruise missiles and Parodiya decoy UAVs.
The drones were launched from the Russian cities of Oryol, Kursk and Primorsko-Akhtarsk as well as from temporarily occupied Donetsk, Chauda and Hvardiiske (Crimea).
Aircraft, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare assets, unmanned systems units and mobile fire groups from Ukraine's defence forces have been involved in repelling the attack.
Quote: "As of 08:30, [Ukrainian] air defence forces had destroyed or jammed 150 Shaheds (63 of which were jet-powered), S8000 Banderol/Dan-Ts, Gerberas and drones of other types. Another 10 attack drones remain airborne, combat work is ongoing!
Hits by aerial assets have been recorded at 27 locations and the fall of downed aerial assets (debris) at 13 locations."
Background:
- Russian drones attacked Kyiv from the evening of 20 October and into the morning of 21 October.
- At around 07:00, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported that a Russian drone had hit a 24-storey residential building in the Sviatoshynskyi district at the level of the 19th floor. A fire broke out.
- Parked cars caught fire in the Desnianskyi district after a drone crashed onto them. A drone strike on a transport infrastructure facility in the Solomianskyi district caused a fire and another drone was reported to have crashed in an open area.

A flight-tested attack drone similar to Iran’s Shahed model that its Taiwanese maker says could reach military targets in mainland China is meant to swamp PLA air defences, analysts said.
Drawing on battlefield lessons from Ukraine and the Middle East, military experts broadly agree on the utility of such low-cost systems, but differ on how the drone could be deployed in a conflict with Beijing should it enter service.

articles.title: U.S. Midterms Loom Over a Deadlock Between Trump and Tehran
articles.body:
Iran may have found a weapon in the American electoral calendar. With the midterm elections two weeks away, Tehran is intensifying attacks on shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz, calculating that higher energy prices will deepen President Donald Trump’s political troubles and make another U.S. military campaign too costly to contemplate.
The wager is seductive: an American president anxious about diesel prices and his party’s prospects in the midterms, Iran seems to believe, will have little appetite for another major war.
Trump’s declaration that he will refrain from striking Iran before the Nov. 3 vote appears to vindicate this view, even as he periodically threatens to use force again. Having survived two rounds of war and absorbed punishing economic losses, Iran’s leaders believe they can endure a little longer. By disrupting Gulf commerce, they gain leverage their conventional forces cannot provide. They also hope to make that leverage permanent and compel Washington to accept Tehran’s authority over passage through the world’s most important energy chokepoint.
Yet the past nine months of war against Iran have made it clear that renewed military conflict before the midterms or after the elections is unlikely to resolve the disputes between the U.S. and Iran. The two countries will eventually have to sit across the negotiating table to resolve their long-running disputes.
Miscalculations in Tehran and Washington
Tehran may be misreading how political peril shapes an adversary’s decisions. Trump could decide that appearing powerless as Iranian attacks push up prices is more damaging than another round of military strikes. Reports that his administration has considered fresh strikes suggest the military option remains in play. A serious attack on American forces could turn Trump’s promise of restraint into a political liability overnight.
The political situation in Israel adds a combustible variable. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faces an Oct. 27 election with his bloc struggling to secure a majority. He has staked his political reputation on the claim that only he can neutralize the Iranian threat.
With Tehran rebuilding its missile and drone capabilities and uncertainty surrounding its nuclear program, Netanyahu may see renewed strikes as both a strategic opportunity and a means of restoring his standing at home. Such a gamble could deepen Israel’s insecurity, but electoral desperation seldom improves anyone’s judgment.
The convergence of these calculations makes the coming weeks particularly perilous. Iran thinks Trump’s electoral weakness will constrain him. Trump and Netanyahu might each conclude that a show of force could rescue their political fortunes. Each side imagines it can calibrate the violence and manage the aftermath. The experience of this year’s conflict, in which successive rounds of fighting outran diplomatic efforts to contain them, offers little reason for that confidence.
Even if October passes without another conflagration, November brings its own hazards. After the midterm elections, the political constraints Trump has publicly imposed on himself will disappear. With substantial American forces already positioned in the region, Washington may be tempted to break the deadlock through another round of attacks. Tehran, fearing another surprise attack, might choose to strike Israel or U.S. military assets in the region first. What might seem like prudent preparation in Washington or Tehran could help bring about the war it is meant to deter.
The underlying impasse is as stubborn as ever. Washington wants a nuclear agreement and believes its blockade will ultimately compel Iran to negotiate. Tehran insists on upfront economic relief and an end to the war before substantive talks on the nuclear issue can begin.
America can point to tankers still transiting Hormuz, but shipping that depends on costly military protection and remains under threat is a poor substitute for normal trade. Iran can inflict considerable damage on the oil exports of its Gulf neighbors, but it has so far failed to turn that leverage into meaningful American concessions.
Dangers of a wider war
Another surge in hostilities would widen this gulf rather than bridge it. American and Israeli aircraft can destroy missile launchers, production facilities, and infrastructure, but Iran has repeatedly demonstrated that it can retaliate and survive. Iran’s response could extend further to target Gulf energy infrastructure, maritime commerce, data centers, and other critical networks.
The Houthi confrontation with Saudi Arabia already offers a grim illustration of how quickly the costs can spread. The war in Yemen has been reignited with devastating consequences, including deadly attacks on civilian airports and a spiraling cycle of retaliation. The fighting now threatens to draw in Turkey and Pakistan to support Saudi Arabia, as the three countries recently signed a mutual security pact known as the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement.
A new campaign could leave Iran poorer, Israel more exposed, and the U.S. burdened with an even more expensive regional commitment, while markets around the world absorb another shock.
The outlines of a diplomatic bargain have been visible for months: reciprocal steps to reopen Hormuz, calibrated sanctions relief, and a resumption of nuclear negotiations. The difficulty lies in sequencing and trust. Tehran fears that surrendering its maritime leverage first would invite fresh demands; Washington worries that easing pressure would reward coercion without securing lasting constraints on Iran’s nuclear program. Addressing those fears will require reciprocal steps and credible verification. More bombing won’t help.
Leaders contemplating an October surprise or an offensive after the midterms must remember that uncomfortable truth. Military force may alter the balance of pain without resolving the disputes each side will eventually have to confront across the negotiating table.
After another round of death and destruction, they could find themselves negotiating over the same issues, with less trust, greater bitterness, and far fewer resources to rebuild what they have broken. Their choices will be no easier then; the cost of reaching an agreement will be far greater.

articles.title: Witkoff to Putin: ‘You are a humanitarian … I salute that’
articles.body:
Russia's President Vladimir Putin, right, greets U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff during a meeting in St. Petersburg on Oct. 21, 2026. | Pool photo by Gavriil Grigorov via AFP/Getty Images
Steve Witkoff, the United States’ special envoy, praised Russian ruler Vladimir Putin during face-to-face talks in St. Petersburg, calling him “a humanitarian.”
“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian. You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that, I commend you, and I thank you again,” Witkoff said Wednesday in a Russian state media video clip posted on social media.
Witkoff’s visit is the latest U.S. attempt to bring Moscow and Kyiv to the negotiation table, four-and-a-half years after the Kremlin launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Advertisement
The American envoy met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Oslo on Tuesday, and is expected to propose trilateral talks between the two leaders and U.S. President Donald Trump.
Russia’s strikes on Kyiv and Kharkiv continued overnight, killing three people, local mayors reported.
Putin’s assault on Ukraine killed 328 civilians in September alone, according to the United Nations, while Kremlin forces bombard energy infrastructure across the country heading into winter.

articles.title: Moscow and Beijing could seal major gas pipeline deal by year-end – Russian deputy PM
articles.body:
Moscow and Beijing could seal major gas pipeline deal by year-end – Russian deputy PM
Russia and China could finalize agreements on a major new gas pipeline by the end of the year, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Aleksandr Novak said on Wednesday, in a potential breakthrough that would significantly expand Moscow’s energy exports to Asia.
Speaking to reporters on the sidelines of talks between Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin and his Chinese counterpart Li Qiang in St. Petersburg, Novak said the planned Power of Baikal pipeline was among the issues discussed.
“Our companies – Gazprom and China National Petroleum Corporation – are negotiating a second route for gas supplies from Russia to the People’s Republic of China,” he said. “We are waiting for our companies to complete commercial negotiations and hope they will reach the relevant agreements by the end of the year.”
Li arrived in St. Petersburg on Tuesday for the regular meeting of the Russian and Chinese heads of government.
Russia already supplies gas to China through the Power of Siberia, a more than 3,000-kilometer pipeline launched in 2019. It carries gas from the Chayandinskoye field in Yakutia and the Kovyktinskoye field in Irkutsk Region through Russia’s Far East and across the border near Blagoveshchensk, connecting to a Chinese network extending toward Shanghai. Its annual export capacity is 38 billion cubic meters (bcm), with deliveries reaching 38.8 bcm in 2025.
The planned Power of Baikal, previously known as Power of Siberia 2, would open a major new energy corridor. The roughly 2,600-kilometer pipeline is designed to deliver up to 50 bcm annually from Russia’s Arctic gas fields on the Yamal Peninsula to China via Mongolia, including the Soyuz Vostok transit pipeline.
Unlike Power of Siberia, which draws gas from eastern Siberia, the new route would tap western Siberian reserves that previously supplied Europe, giving Moscow a major new outlet for gas following the collapse of much of its European market. Novak said the project was renamed Power of Baikal to distinguish it from the existing pipeline and reflect its planned route along the southern shore of Lake Baikal. The precise route remains subject to final commercial agreements.
Together, the two pipelines would give Russia a combined nominal export capacity of around 88 bcm annually to China – roughly 80% of the 110 bcm combined capacity of Nord Stream and Nord Stream 2, built to supply Russian gas to Europe via the Baltic Sea.
Gazprom and CNPC signed a legally binding memorandum on the project in September 2025, envisaging deliveries of 50 bcm annually over 30 years. A final supply contract, however, was not signed. Pricing is a key sticking point, with media reports suggesting Beijing is seeking rates close to Russia’s domestic prices, while Moscow has pushed for more commercially favorable terms. President Vladimir Putin said last year that pricing would follow a market-based formula similar to that used for European supplies, stressing that there would be “no charity” on either side.
The expansion comes as Russia accelerates its energy pivot toward Asia in light of Western sanctions and EU efforts to phase out Russian supplies. Before the Ukraine conflict escalated in 2022, Europe was Russia’s largest pipeline gas market, with Gazprom providing around 40-45% of the bloc’s total gas imports. Deliveries subsequently plunged as Brussels pursued alternative suppliers and imposed successive sanctions on Russia.
Meanwhile, China has emerged as Russia’s largest pipeline gas customer, with Power of Siberia reaching its full contracted capacity and further export routes under development.
Unlike oil, which can be redirected by tanker, pipeline gas requires extensive infrastructure, making Power of Baikal a key project in Moscow’s efforts to replace lost European demand. Moscow has repeatedly accused Western governments of undermining European energy security through their sanctions policies.
The shift also follows the September 2022 sabotage of the Nord Stream pipelines that previously brought Russian gas to Germany beneath the Baltic Sea. Novak said on Wednesday that Moscow remains ready to resume deliveries through the one Nord Stream pipeline string out of the four that remained undamaged.
“We have one of the four strings in working condition. If European consumers and politicians want it, supplies can, of course, be delivered through that line,” he said. The decision rests primarily with European countries, particularly Germany, where the pipeline terminates, Novak added. He said the three damaged strings could also be restored if demand and economic conditions justified repairs, suggesting it would not take long to bring them back to working order.
Russia has repeatedly offered to resume energy supplies to Europe, particularly in light of the disruptions to global markets caused by the Middle East crisis, but says its proposals have received no response from European governments.
